sources.news_title: UH-OH! Trump’s Economic Advisor Forgets to Blame Biden for Trump’s Latest Rise in Inflation
sources.text:
One of the most prominent promises made by Donald Trump during his 2024 campaign to reoccupy the White House was that he would bring consumer prices down. He swore that he would do that on day one, and that it would be easy. We are now at day 632, and things have only gotten worse.
Click here to post this article on Twitter or Click here to post on Bluesky
The American people are well aware of Trump’s failures with regard to the economy. Despite his lying about this being the “Golden Age,” people know what their groceries cost, and their gas, and their healthcare, and their housing, etc. Trump’s deceit and uncaring attitude are among the primary reasons that he is floundering at record lows for job approval.
SEE THIS: HOW CONVENIENT! Trump Says the Iran War and High Gas Prices Will End – Right After the Elections?
Most experts agree that the dismal economy we are suffering through are due to Trump’s neglect, incompetence, and ego. The war he started against Iran has resulted in higher costs for energy. His ridiculous, unwarranted tariffs account for the rise in virtually everything else. But in Trump’s twisted mind, and the minds of his MAGA-pologists, President Biden – who left office nearly two years ago – is the culprit who caused the fiscal fiasco that has plagued the Trump years.
Political observers have wondered when the timeline would flip from the seemingly endless Biden Effect, to one where Trump actually takes responsibility for his own mistakes and misdeeds. Well, we might be getting close to that now. In an interview on Fox News Wednesday morning, the chairman of Trump’s Council of Economic Advisors, Kevin Hassett, had the following exchange with Fox’s Stuart Varney…
Varney: We got the last Consumer Price Index report before the midterms. In September price is up 0.6%. Moved up a bit, a bit hotter, 3.7% over the last year. Here’s what Kevin Hassett had to say about it this morning.
Hassett: Because the Houties started attacking the Saudi pipeline. And other Iranian proxies from Iraq were attacking refineries and so on. That we had a negative shock to energy again in September. But inside the topline number there’s a lot of good news. [Insert a bunch of Hassett lies] If you look at core inflation, it was basically at the Fed’s target on average over the last three months. But this month was a blip up.
Top Trump econ advisor claims today's high inflation report was a "blip"
— FactPost (@factpostnews.bsky.social) 2026-10-14T15:53:19.076038849Z
This may be the first time that Hassett has ever answered a question about Trump’s poor performance that didn’t begin with “But Biden…” In fact, the reasons that he does cite are all problems of Trump’s making. It was Trump’s reckless and illegal attack on Iran that led to associated battles in the region with the Houties, Saudi Arabia, and Iraq. And the targeting of oil refineries was a possibility that a competent leader would have prepared for.
What’s more, the Federal Reserve’s target for inflation is 2.0%, way below the 3.7% that Hassett is preposterously calling a blip. At least he didn’t blame Biden again. But has he finally recognized how ridiculous that is? Or did he just forget?
While it’s a welcome relief that Hassett didn’t push to blame Biden again, he still tried to downplay any notion that the economy is troubled. But how could he? Trump would have his head. After all, here is what Trump said about the rise in inflation…
Question: Are you concerned about the latest inflation number?
Trump: No, I love it. The numbers were great. I love the inflation.
Q: Are you concerned about the latest inflation number?Trump: No, I love it. The numbers were great. I love the inflation.
— FactPost (@factpostnews.bsky.social) 2026-10-14T18:34:08.197711334Z
Trump has expressed his love for inflation before. It’s just another indicator of how out of touch he is with ordinary people. And for the record, the video here was cut off right before he explained why he loves inflation. Here is what he said…
“Because as soon as this war is over. You know, I can say it now, something you didn’t know. Did you know we’ve been taking out millions of barrels of oil? Nobody knows it.”
HUH? So Trump loves inflation because he’s going to steal Iran’s oil when the war is over? That war, which he said would only last a few weeks, is now in its eighth month. Does he think that the American people love inflation for that period of time, and who knows how much longer?
Furthermore, everybody knows about Trump’s stated intention to steal Iran’s oil. He has said it repeatedly in public. He brags about it saying that “to the victor goes the spoils.” The only problem is that Trump is losing. And therefore, unfortunately, so are the American people. And they know that Trump and his MAGA Republican enablers are solely to blame.

sources.news_title: Higher Energy Prices Pushed U.S. Inflation Up to 3.7% Ahead of Midterm Elections
Republicans head into midterm elections with US inflation at 3.7%. Then a report shows it's the highest before midterms since 1990
sources.text:
US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics released on Wednesday, The Guardian reported. This figure represents an increase from the 3.4% rate recorded in August, marking the highest inflation rate before a midterm election since 1990, excluding the pandemic era.
These numbers are hitting household budgets hard, especially as we head into the colder months. Gasoline was the primary driver here, accounting for over half of the overall price increases with a 34% jump from last year. Fuel oil prices have surged by 74% compared to last year. Travel isn’t looking much cheaper either, with air travel costs climbing 22.4%.
Price increases this year have been largely driven by the US-Israel war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to soar. According to data from AAA, average gas prices are currently over a dollar per gallon more expensive than they were last year. Diesel, which is essential for keeping our domestic supply chains moving, also hit a record high last month. Research from Brown University suggests these higher energy prices have cost Americans more than $1,020 per household, totaling $133bn for all US consumers.
These rising costs are tied heavily to global instability
The economy is consistently cited as a top issue for voters, and this latest report shows just how much inflation is outpacing earnings. According to a recent survey from Reuters/Ipsos, 78% of Americans blame the current Trump administration’s policies for these price hikes. This sentiment even extends to the president’s base, with 57% of Republicans who support Donald Trump expressing blame toward the administration.
President Trump has attempted to shift the focus to external factors. In a post on social media on Tuesday, he claimed that Yemen’s Houthi group was attacking Saudi Arabia in a deliberate attempt to influence the elections. He wrote, “They’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran … in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE.”
During a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, later that same day, the president defended his economic record, describing his support for families as “substantial.” He noted, “Every time they want to try and get me, they say ‘affordability’,”
These elevated prices are putting significant pressure on the Federal Reserve to continue using interest rates as a tool to cool the economy. The Fed already raised rates last month for the first time since 2023. This has direct consequences for everyday borrowing, as the 30-year mortgage rate has climbed to 7.40%.
Richard Carter, who serves as the head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot, summarized the situation in a statement. “Inflation in the US has come in higher than expected, in a blow to Donald Trump ahead of November’s midterms,” Carter said. “The president has been desperate to show he is getting inflation under control and providing the environment for rate cuts, even going so far as allowing Russian diesel back into the market, but those moves are proving too little too late as the war in the Middle East continues to have a grip on the global economy.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding the latest report.
Published: Oct 14, 2026 03:35 pm

sources.news_title: U.S. inflation heats up as Fed rate hike returns to the table | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
U.S. inflation heats up as Fed rate hike returns to the table
WASHINGTON >> U.S. consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged, dealing another blow to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections and putting an interest rate increase later this month back on the radar.
The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department today showed a broadening of price pressures beyond energy, raising concerns among economists that underlying inflation could be getting sticky. There was also an AI-related boost to inflation last month. Financial markets now see the Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision at its Oct. 27-28 meeting as a closer call than before the data was released.
The report added to surveys this month that showed a further deterioration in consumer sentiment and a plunge in Trump’s approval rating, driven by angst over the rising cost of living. A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed about 78% of Americans blamed Trump’s policies, including tariffs and the Middle East conflict, for rising prices, which are outpacing wages.
“The inflation we’re experiencing right now is largely the result of erratic policy from the executive branch,” said Kyle Moore, chief economist at the Century Foundation, a progressive think tank. “Worse still, the directionless war in Iran continues to disrupt global supply chains. This administration has also been wholly unwilling to moderate the pace of the AI and data-center buildout.”
The CPI rose 0.6% last month after climbing 0.4% in August, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said, in line with economists’ expectations. In the 12 months through September, the CPI advanced 3.7% after rising 3.4% in August.
A 9.1% surge in gasoline prices accounted for more than half of the increase in the CPI over the month. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran is driving up energy prices. Other motor fuels, which include diesel, soared 11.9% last month and were up 60.9% on a year-over-year basis. Diesel prices at the pump are at record highs, and there are fears that those costs will soon feed through to higher prices at the supermarket.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
Food prices were unchanged after gaining 0.1% in both July and August. Grocery store prices dipped 0.1% over the month as beef prices dropped 1.0% and the cost of dairy and related products eased 0.9%. Egg prices declined 1.3%.
But prices for nonalcoholic beverages surged 0.9%, while fruits and vegetables cost 0.5% more, with banana prices shooting up 1.0%, in what could be early signs of rising trucking costs being passed on to consumers.Lettuce prices rebounded 3.9% as a cyclospora outbreak faded.
Grocery prices rose 1.8% on a year-over-year basis.
Average hourly earnings for all employees declined 0.7% in September from a year ago, after falling 0.3% in August, underscoring the squeeze on consumers in what economists call the bottom of a K-shaped economy.
Economists said this data raised doubts about whether consumers could maintain their robust pace of spending.
“While much of the lost purchasing power is due to rising energy costs, there is no reason to expect that to fade in the near term,” said Eric Winograd, chief U.S. economist at AllianceBernstein. “The bottom part of the K-shaped economy is losing ground, as anybody who has seen campaign ads on TV the last few weeks has heard.”
With the cost of living rising, the Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits for 2027. The programs benefit nearly 72 million Americans, including retirees, the disabled and certain widows, widowers and children. Social Security retirement benefits will, on average, increase by $75 per month.
Stocks on Wall Street fell. The dollar advanced versus a basket of currencies. Yields on U.S. Treasury notes and bonds rose.
Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI rose 0.3% in September, matching the gain in August. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the so-called core CPI would increase 0.2%. The core CPI was lifted by a 0.4% advance in the cost of shelter, including hotel and motel rooms. Owners’ equivalent rent, a measure of the amount homeowners would pay to rent or would earn from renting their property, rose 0.3%.
Airline fares rose 1.2% amid higher jet fuel prices. Consumers paid more for gardening and lawn care services, likely reflecting worker shortages amid a crackdown on undocumented immigrants. The costs of recreation and education also rose, as did those of hospital and dental services. Overall services prices increased 0.4%. They were also up 0.4% excluding energy.
Core goods prices rose 0.3%, pushed up by a 0.7% increase in the cost of used cars and trucks. Apparel prices climbed 0.3% and the cost of toys rebounded 4.2%, suggesting some lingering pass-through from tariffs. But prescription medication was cheaper.
Prices for computers and peripherals jumped 1.3%, reflecting AI-related investment, while the cost of computer software and accessories rebounded 0.4%.
In the 12 months through September, core CPI inflation was 2.6%, compared with 2.4% in August.
The U.S. central bank tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index for its 2% inflation target. Financial markets raised the chances of a rate hike at the Fed’s meeting this month to roughly 37% from about 22% prior to the release of the CPI report, CME Group’s FedWatch Tool showed.
The odds of a rate increase this month had diminished following underwhelming payroll gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE inflation readings for July and August.
The Fed in September raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range, its first hike in three years, and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead.
Most economists continue to expect the Fed will hold rates steady this month and raise them in December.
Based on the CPI data, economists’ estimates for core PCE inflation ranged from 0.3% to 0.4%, which would mean a year-over-year reading of 3.1%. Producer price data being released on Thursday could impact those estimates. Core PCE inflation was 0.2% in August and 3.0% on a year-over-year basis.
“What is interesting is that the primary drivers of inflation are supply-side policies that are better addressed by the fiscal authority,” said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. “However, that is not going to happen anytime soon, which leaves the Fed to address a re-establishment of price stability.”

sources.news_title: Inflation report raises Fed rate-hike odds
sources.text:
Investors are bracing for the Federal Reserve to again hike interest rates after the Labor Department said Wednesday that consumer prices rose more in September than economists had expected.
The inflation report, which comes two weeks before the central bank’s next meeting and three weeks before Election Day, is heightening concerns about the Iran war’s effect on the cost of goods beyond food and energy.
With consumer sentiment already nearing a record low, the Trump administration is frantically trying to put a positive spin on the data — and discourage the central bank from acting.
Adviser Kevin Hassett told Fox Business it’s a “blip,” while adviser Peter Navarro wrote an editorial on why it proves “the Fed should hold its fire.”
All eyes are on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who is slated to speak in Bangkok later this week.

sources.news_title: Powered by spikes in energy prices, inflation surges to 3.7% • Maine Morning Star
sources.text:
Powered by spikes in energy prices, inflation surges to 3.7%
A gas station advertises gas and diesel prices in Forest Glen, Md., on Oct. 5, 2026. More than half a dozen states have enacted tax relief to ease the burden on consumers as fuel prices continue to surge. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom)
Inflation grew to a 3.7% annual rate in September, according to an Oct. 14 report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August.
In the last consumer price inflation report before midterm elections, with voters already fed up with higher prices, September’s number was the highest since May, when it was 4.2%.
“Inflation has wiped out wage gains for 6 months now,” Heather Long, the chief economist for Navy Federal, wrote in a social media post. “It’s a financial squeeze. Americans are trying to work more hours to make up for it, but many are still falling behind.”
Spikes in energy prices were largely responsible: Gas is now up 34% for the year, and fuel oil, which includes diesel, is up 72% as the Iran war drags on.
States including Georgia, Kentucky, Illinois, Indiana, North Carolina, Ohio and Utah have enacted gas tax relief measures recently to battle rising prices. North Carolina expects to lose more than $362 million in tax revenue for the fiscal year because of a gas tax holiday.
New York state estimates fuel oil prices are up 67% from last year, with home heating oil at $6.21 a gallon as of this month. Connecticut announced plans Oct. 13 for additional state aid for home heating assistance, partly because of high prices for delivered oil.
Other than energy, the largest factor was food away from home, up 3.5%. The only decreases were medical care products, down 3.3%, and used cars and trucks, up for the month but still down 1.5% for the year. So-called “core” inflation outside of volatile food and energy was a more modest 2.6%.
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at [email protected].

sources.news_title: Hotter-Than-Expected CPI Signals Stubborn Inflation and Rising Costs
sources.text:
Shoppers hoping for a respite from rising inflation were again disappointed in September, as prices ballooned again, far overshooting the Federal Reserve’s target rate.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI), which measures the cost of goods and services across the United States, rose by a seasonally adjusted 0.6 percent last month and a headline 3.7 percent over the past 12 months, according to the report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics released Wednesday. Economists had projected a headline rate of 3.6 percent.
By comparison, the annual rate of inflation seen in August was 3.4 percent, while the core rate was 2.4 percent.
With mercurial energy and food costs removed from the equation, the CPI rose 0.3 percent during September and 2.6 percent from the previous 12 months, beating out economists’ projections of 0.2 percent and 2.5 percent, respectively, for the time period.
Not surprisingly, the ballooning price of oil was the driving force behind the inflationary bump as the war in Iran rages on and energy exports remain tied up in the Strait of Hormuz. On Friday, President Donald Trump made a stunning about-face in temporarily drawing down sanctions on Russian oil exports and making a deal with President Vladimir Putin to purchase over 300,000 tons of diesel in an effort to lower domestic gas prices.
The move appears a scramble on the part of the White House as the index for gasoline shot up 9.1 percent in September, accounting for more than half of the all-items increase for the month. According to the BLS, the energy index grew 5.2 percent throughout the month, far outpacing the 2.1 percent growth seen in August.
Apparel prices, too, grew 0.3 percent month over month in September, hitting an un-adjusted 3.4 percent for the previous 12 months. This, after data from Dr. Sheng Lu, professor of fashion and apparel studies at the University of Delaware, revealed that the value of apparel imports to the U.S. market rose 0.2 percent year over year in August but fell by a notable 6.3 percent in quantity. In other words, the same goods have gotten more expensive.
“With apparel and footwear prices continuing to increase over already elevated inflation rates, affordability will be on the mind of everybody who wears clothes and shoes in the United States,” American Apparel and Footwear Association president and CEO Steve Lamar told Sourcing Journal.
	The leader of the Washington, D.C.-based trade organization fingered the president’s trade policy, centered on punishing duties levied against trade partners, as a key factor precipitating the heightened prices seen at retail.
“The time for meaningful tariff relief for this industry—already the most highly tariffed industry in the country—is long overdue,” he added.
According to the Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America, footwear prices rose by 3.4 percent—the same as apparel—year over year, with men’s shoes up 4.5 percent, women’s up 3.9 percent, and children’s up 0.4 percent.
“Today’s report is another reminder that the affordability challenges facing American families have not gone away,” said Matt Priest, the group’s president and CEO. “Consumers are already navigating higher costs across their household budgets, and tariffs add another layer of expense to products people buy every day. Footwear companies are working hard to keep shoes affordable, but there is a limit to how much additional cost businesses can absorb before those pressures reach consumers.”
Gazing into a crystal ball reveals some uncomfortable truths. FDRA expects to see broader inflation, it said, with footwear import costs and oil prices continuing to impact prices at retail. While import costs have been on a downward trajectory and are expected to continue to fall, protracted geopolitical upheaval will persist in driving up the cost of oil, putting pressure on the industry. As a result, FDRA surmised, shoe prices may continue to rise heading into 2027, “though at a more moderate pace.”
Stocks fell as Wall Street took in the news on Wednesday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.4 percent, the S&P 500 declining 1.3 percent and the Nasdaq Composite tumbling 2.01 percent as of press time, deepening losses seen Tuesday.
With consumer prices still on the rise and outpacing projections, the Federal Reserve is under pressure again to raise interest rates—a decision that could have a marked impact on the outcome of the midterm elections in November.
According to CME Fed Funds futures, there is now 47 percent chance the central bank’s Oct. 27-28 meetings could yield a decision to raise rates (up from a 22 percent chance just yesterday).
The Fed’s final meeting of the year on Dec. 9 will be another opportunity for a rate hike as it endeavors to beat back inflation to its 2 percent target rate. CME projected a 93 percent probability of at least one increase, and a 41 percent chance of two hikes, before the end of the year.
This article was updated to reflect comments from Matt Priest and the FDRA.

sources.news_title: U.S. Inflation Hits 3.7 Percent - by Jan Wondra
sources.text:
On Wednesday, October 14 the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics announced that the rate of annual inflation across the country during the month of September hit 3.7 percent.
That number was higher than economists expected, led by a sharp rise in energy costs. Gas prices rose 9.1 percent during the month of September, and grocery prices are rising.
Bureau of Labor Statistics
The trend is concerning.  It exceeded the August annual inflation figure, which rose to 3.4 percent.
The monthly Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.6 percent in the space of one month. The inflation rates have wiped out Americans’ economic gains since January, 2025.
The news comes on top of last month’s unemployment data, which rose to 4.2 percent. That’s an average; if you’re a minority, that figure stands at 7 percent. The entire country added only 29,000 new jobs in September, a sign the economy is slowing, and many of us are struggling to make ends meet.

sources.news_title: US September inflation rate at 3.7% defies forecasts, impacting daily expenses
sources.text:
U.S. inflation rose at an annual rate of 3.7% in September, exceeding economist expectations of 3.6%. The acceleration was driven primarily by a surge in energy prices, increasing the cost of essential goods and services for American households.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI), which measures the price changes of a standard basket of goods, indicates that the cost of living is rising faster than anticipated. This shift translates into direct financial pressure on families, particularly as energy costs-which affect everything from commuting to home heating-spike.
The economic strain is reflected in public sentiment: a recent CBS News poll found that 90% of Americans identify prices as the most critical factor shaping their view of the economy. For these households, the 3.7% headline figure represents a tangible decrease in purchasing power and a heightened struggle with daily affordability.

sources.news_title: New Inflation Report Delivers Painful Surprise - American Liberty News
sources.text:
The latest figures show rising costs for gasoline, shelter, airfare, and other expenses.
U.S. inflation accelerated more than expected in September, reaching 3.7% annually as gasoline prices surged more than 34% from a year earlier, putting additional pressure on American households and presenting a fresh economic challenge for President Donald Trump and Republicans just three weeks before the midterm elections.
The Consumer Price Index report released Wednesday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that annual inflation climbed from 3.4% in August, exceeding economists’ expectations of 3.6%. Consumer prices increased 0.6% in September alone, up from a 0.4% monthly increase in August.
Gasoline accounted for more than half of the monthly increase, reflecting the growing economic consequences of the war involving Iran and disruptions to global energy supplies. (RELATED: Trump’s Diesel Deal With Putin Comes As Attacks Escalate)
The figures represent the final major inflation reading before the Nov. 3 midterms, when voters will decide control of Congress amid persistent concerns about affordability and the cost of living.
Gasoline prices surge as energy costs climb
Energy prices drove much of September’s inflation increase, with gasoline rising 9.1% in a single month after climbing 3.9% in August.
Gasoline prices were 34.2% higher than in September 2025, while the overall energy index increased 5.2% for the month and 20.4% over the preceding year.
Fuel oil prices rose even more sharply, jumping 15.3% in September and 74.2% annually, threatening substantially higher heating expenses for households that rely on oil during the winter.
The increases follow months of instability in global energy markets stemming from the conflict involving Iran, which has disrupted oil supplies and driven up fuel costs.
According to Yahoo Finance, the national average gasoline price reached approximately $4.33 per gallon in September, citing figures from AAA.
Diesel prices also climbed above $6.20 per gallon, increasing expenses for trucking companies, agricultural producers, and businesses that depend on commercial transportation.
Higher diesel costs can eventually reach consumers through more expensive shipping, food distribution, and other goods.
Inflation spreads beyond gasoline
Although energy accounted for much of September’s increase, the Labor Department reported higher prices across several other major categories.
Shelter costs rose 0.4% during the month, accelerating from August’s 0.3% increase. Housing expenses were 3.2% higher than a year earlier.
Prices also increased for used cars and trucks, recreation, education, medical care, clothing, and airline tickets.
Airline fares were particularly expensive, rising 22.4% over the preceding 12 months.
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, also accelerated, rising to 2.6% annually from 2.4% in August.
Core prices increased 0.3% in September, indicating that inflationary pressure extended beyond the energy sector.
The increase presents another challenge for the Federal Reserve, which has struggled to bring inflation back toward its long-term 2% target.
The central bank measures that target using the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, but the latest CPI figures provide further evidence that inflation remains elevated. (RELATED: Fed Reverses Course With First Interest Rate Hike In 3 Years)
Grocery prices provide some relief
Food prices offered a rare bright spot in Wednesday’s report.
The overall food index was unchanged in September, while grocery prices declined 0.1%.
Prices for meats, poultry, fish, and eggs fell 0.5%, while dairy products became 0.9% cheaper.
However, fruits and vegetables increased 0.5%, and nonalcoholic beverages rose 0.9%.
Restaurant prices climbed another 0.2% during the month.
Over the preceding year, food prices increased 2.5%, with groceries rising 1.8% and restaurant meals becoming 3.5% more expensive.
The modest decline in grocery prices provided some relief for families, although it did little to offset years of accumulated price increases.
Federal Reserve faces pressure to raise rates again
The inflation report has intensified expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again as policymakers attempt to contain rising prices.
The central bank increased rates in September, and Wednesday’s unexpectedly strong inflation reading prompted traders to raise their expectations for another increase in October.
Higher interest rates can slow inflation by discouraging borrowing and reducing consumer and business spending.
However, additional increases would also make mortgages, automobile loans, credit cards, and business financing more expensive.
Federal Reserve officials must weigh those consequences against the risk that inflation will become more entrenched.
The acceleration in core inflation adds to those concerns, particularly as higher shelter costs and other consumer expenses continue to strain household budgets.
Trump faces growing affordability concerns before elections
The latest inflation figures arrive at a politically difficult moment for the Trump administration, with Republicans preparing to defend their congressional majorities in the Nov. 3 elections. (RELATED: Mike Johnson Says He Plans To Stay GOP Leader Even If Republicans Lose The House)
A recent survey by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of American adults approved of Trump’s handling of the cost of living.
Only 26% approved of his handling of the economy overall.
The administration has explored measures to address elevated fuel costs, including proposals involving diesel exports and direct financial relief.
However, the ongoing conflict involving Iran has complicated efforts to stabilize energy markets, leaving American consumers exposed to higher gasoline, diesel, and heating fuel prices.
Those increases have particularly significant consequences for working families, retirees on fixed incomes, and Americans who depend on their vehicles for daily transportation.
Higher transportation and energy expenses also threaten to increase operating costs for businesses, potentially adding to inflation in other sectors.
Next inflation report will arrive after Election Day
Wednesday’s figures will be the final official monthly inflation report available to voters before the midterm elections.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics has scheduled its October CPI report for Nov. 10, one week after Americans cast their ballots.
Although grocery prices declined slightly in September, rising fuel, housing, transportation, and other expenses continue to squeeze household budgets.
The trajectory of inflation in the coming months will depend heavily on global energy markets, developments in the Iran conflict, and the Federal Reserve’s response.
For now, the latest figures leave the Trump administration confronting renewed concerns about affordability as voters prepare to decide which party will control Congress.

sources.news_title: Powered by energy price spikes, inflation surges to 3.7% in last report before midterm elections
sources.text:
Powered by energy price spikes, inflation surges to 3.7% in last report before midterm elections
A gas station advertises gas and diesel prices in Forest Glen, Md., on Oct. 5, 2026. More than half a dozen states have enacted tax relief to ease the burden on consumers as fuel prices continue to surge. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom)
Inflation grew to a 3.7% annual rate in September, according to an Oct. 14 report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August.
In the last consumer price inflation report before midterm elections, with voters already fed up with higher prices, September’s number was the highest since May, when it was 4.2%.
“Inflation has wiped out wage gains for 6 months now,” Heather Long, the chief economist for Navy Federal, wrote in a social media post. “It’s a financial squeeze. Americans are trying to work more hours to make up for it, but many are still falling behind.”
Spikes in energy prices were largely responsible: Gas is now up 34% for the year, and fuel oil, which includes diesel, is up 72% as the Iran war drags on.
States including Georgia, Kentucky, Illinois, Indiana, North Carolina, Ohio and Utah have enacted gas tax relief measures recently to battle rising prices. North Carolina expects to lose more than $362 million in tax revenue for the fiscal year because of a gas tax holiday.
New York state estimates fuel oil prices are up 67% from last year, with home heating oil at $6.21 a gallon as of this month. Connecticut announced plans Oct. 13 for additional state aid for home heating assistance, partly because of high prices for delivered oil.
Other than energy, the largest factor was food away from home, up 3.5%. The only decreases were medical care products, down 3.3%, and used cars and trucks, up for the month but still down 1.5% for the year. So-called “core” inflation outside of volatile food and energy was a more modest 2.6%.

sources.news_title: Core Inflation Holds Steady in September, Energy Costs Push CPI Higher
sources.text:
September’s core inflation rate provided a bright spot to the monthly Consumer Price Index (CPI) report released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Wednesday.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and food products, increased a seasonally-adjusted 0.3% in September, matching August’s month-to-month rise, the BLS reports. The 12-month core inflation of 2.6% in September was higher than August’s 2.4% 12-month rise – but, that was the lowest monthly year-to-year increase in five and a half years.
The last month that annual core inflation was as low as it was in August was March of 2021, former President Joe Biden’s second full month in office, when it was 1.6%. The next month, it jumped to 3.0%, ending a 12-month streak under 2.0%. It has not fallen below 2.0% - the Federal Reserve’s target rate – in any month since.
September’s all-items index increased 0.6% from the previous month’s 0.4% growth and 3.7% from September of 2025. In August, consumer prices rose 0.4% over the month and 3.4% from a year earlier. Monthly growth matched analysts’ expectations, but the annual increase was slightly higher.
The index for food was unchanged in September, as a 0.1% drop in the cost of food at home offset a 0.2% increase in the price of food away from home. In all, food prices were 2.5% higher than a year earlier.
The shelter index rose 0.4% in September and 3.2% from a year earlier. In August, the food index increased 0.3%.
The index for all energy increased 5.2% over the month after rising 2.1% in August. Compared to September of 2025, energy prices were 20.4% higher.
The gasoline index was up 9.1% in September, accounting for more than half the monthly all-items increase. Compared to a year earlier, gasoline prices were 34.2% higher. In August, the gasoline index posted a 3.9% monthly rise.

sources.news_title: Inflation climbs in September as gas prices surge - Regional Media News
sources.text:
Inflation climbed to a 4-month high in September as the Iran war continued to drive up gasoline prices, according to federal government data released on Wednesday. The reading came in slightly above economists’ expectations.
Prices rose 3.7% in September compared to a year earlier, marking an uptick from an annual inflation rate of 3.4% in the prior month.
Inflation stands well above a rate of 2.4% recorded in February prior to the outbreak of the Iran war.
The fresh data arrived as affordability marks a top concern for voters ahead of early November’s midterm elections.
Gas prices jumped more than 9% in September from August, accounting for more than half of the overall price increase last month, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Shelter prices — which include home-owner payments and rental charges — also rose in September.
Food prices proved stable, however. The price of food stayed flat in September from August, putting annual inflation for food at 2.5%. That figure, which includes prices for groceries and food eaten away from home, stands well below the annual pace of overall price increases.
The Middle East conflict drove up fuel prices and catapulted inflation to a three-year high in May, but inflation eased slightly over the summer after a preliminary peace agreement established an on-again, off-again pause in fighting.
The tentative accord between the U.S. and Iran expired in August, however, giving way to continued attacks on oil infrastructure and ships in the region.
Oil exports from the Gulf have improved in recent weeks but heightened shipping costs and persistent risks have kept the national average gas price above $4.30 a gallon, AAA data shows. Prior to the Iran war, the average price of U.S. gas stood below $3 a gallon.
Diesel prices, which feed into supply costs for groceries and just about every other product bought in stores, stood at $6.29 a gallon, according to AAA. That figure amounts to an increase of about 66% since the outbreak of the Iran War.
Last month, consumer sentiment dropped close to the lowest level ever recorded in the 74-year history of the University of Michigan’s monthly survey.
By some measures, the economy remains robust.
Gross domestic product grew over three months ending in June, defying fear of a downturn triggered by the Iran war. Consumer spending, which accounts for about two-thirds of U.S. economic activity, rose 0.6% in August from July, the largest monthly increase since March 2025, government data on last month showed.
In other areas, however, the economy has wobbled. The inflation report came days after monthly jobs data showed sluggish hiring in September.
Employers added 29,000 jobs last month, a sharp slowdown from 162,000 jobs added in August, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics said earlier this month. The figure came in well below economists’ expectations.
Prior to the latest jobs report, hiring had proven largely resilient this year, even as shoppers and businesses weathered higher costs.
The combination of elevated inflation and a sturdy labor market prompted the Fed to raise interest rates a quarter of a percentage point last month, marking the central bank’s first rate increase since 2023.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said at a press conference in Washington, D.C., last month.
In theory, an increase to the benchmark interest rate should slash inflation by slowing the economy and eating away at demand, though the policy typically yields results after a lag time lasting several months.
The next meeting of Fed policymakers takes place on Oct. 28, just days before the midterm elections. Investors peg the chance of another quarter-point rate increase at about 45%, according to CME Group’s FedWatch Tool, a measure of market sentiment.

sources.news_title: New nightmare explodes for Trump ahead of midterms: ‘MAGA you got conned’
Gas Prices Jumped 9.1% in 1 Month, and CPI Inflation Hit 3.7%. Here’s What It Means for Consumer Stocks.
sources.text:
Inflation data continues to move month to month with no rhyme or reason.
After a soft inflation report in August, the September Consumer Price Index (CPI) reading came in hot again this morning, Oct. 14. The CPI rose 0.6% seasonally adjusted in September and was 3.7% higher year over year.
The monthly increase was in line with economists' expectations, while the headline number came in 0.1% higher than expected. Gasoline prices rocketed over 9% higher in the month, accounting for roughly half the headline CPI's gain.
Stripping out more volatile food and energy prices, core CPI rose 0.3% in September and 2.6% year over year, each 0.1% higher than economists expected.
Image source: Getty Images.
How it impacts consumer stocks
Generally speaking, higher inflation and gas prices hurt consumer stocks from an operational perspective.
Transporting consumer goods from suppliers to stores becomes more expensive due to higher gasoline prices, a cost that can be passed on to consumers.
Consumers also feel the pinch as they pay more for gas and most other items, squeezing their budgets and reducing their purchasing power.
While a 0.6% monthly increase is a big jump, it was largely expected due to higher oil prices in September amid escalating tensions between the U.S. and Iran. But the surprise came in core inflation, which removes energy and food prices.
"CPI came in hot and it wasn't just fuel prices, as core inflation ran at a 3.7% annualized pace in September and 3.2% over three years," the Carson Group's Chief Macro Strategist Sonu Varghese said, according to CNBC. "The only surprise is that investors keep getting surprised by broad-based inflation. And we've yet to see the full impact of higher diesel prices and the AI boom."
US Core Consumer Price Index MoM data by YCharts
Despite operational struggles and potential margin pressure, consumer staple stocks can actually outperform when inflation is rising. That's because economic pressure can lead investors to worry about a potential recession.
People are unlikely to cut many consumer staples, such as food and toiletries, from their budgets unless they simply can’t afford them, since these are necessities.
The State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLP +2.22%) had risen nearly 1.2%, as of 11:56 a.m. ET and is nearly 9.7% higher year-to-date, as some investors have rotated into these safer stocks.
Consumer stocks may face more pressure if interest rates continue to rise
Following the CPI report, the odds of a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's October meeting rose from roughly 22% yesterday to nearly 44% today, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool, which tracks federal funds futures.
If the Fed still views inflation as too high and not making progress toward its 2% target, it is likely to raise interest rates at least one more time this year, if not more.
While the goal of rate hikes is to slow the economy, they will pressure consumers in the near term by raising borrowing costs, which can also lower purchasing power.
This may not be good for consumer stocks because safer assets, such as U.S. Treasury bonds, become more attractive when rates rise. Even consumer stocks with strong dividend yields don't look so appealing with bond yields in the 5% to 6% range.

sources.news_title: Consumer prices accelerate in September on costlier gasoline; core CPI firmer
sources.text:
Consumer prices accelerate in September on costlier gasoline; core CPI firmer
Key takeaways:
- Consumer Price Index rose 0.6% in September
- Gasoline prices surged 7.1% in September
- Core CPI inflation increased 2.6% year over year
- Senior Citizens League projects 3.5% Social Security COLA for 2027
WASHINGTON – U.S. consumer prices accelerated in September amid a surge in gasoline costs, dealing another blow to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November 3 midterm elections and putting an interest rate increase later this month back on the radar.
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.6% last month after climbing 0.4% in August, the Labor Department‘s Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Wednesday. In the 12 months through September, the CPI advanced 3.7% after rising 3.4% in August.
Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI would gain 0.6% over the month and increase 3.6% on a year-over-year basis. Gasoline prices soared 7.1% in September, data from the US Energy Information Administration showed.
The report followed surveys this month showing a further deterioration in consumer sentiment and a plunge in Trump’s approval rating, driven by angst over the rising cost of living. A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed about 78% of Americans blamed Trump’s policies, including tariffs on imports and the US-Israeli war with Iran, for rising prices, which are outpacing wages.
Underlying inflation picks up
Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI gained 0.3% in September, matching the gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI inflation increased 2.6% after advancing 2.4% in August. The US central bank tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index for its 2% inflation target. The core CPI measure is lagging core PCE inflation, which increased 3.0% in August, because of the different weights assigned to the components in the baskets.
The Fed last month raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range, the first hike in three years, and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead. Prior to the CPI report, financial markets assigned a roughly 22% chance of a rate hike at the October 27-28 policy meeting, CME Group’s FedWatch Tool showed.
The odds of a rate increase this month diminished following underwhelming payroll gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE inflation readings for July and August. Economists had expected the Fed to raise rates in December.
The September CPI inflation report was keenly awaited by millions of retirees and other Social Security recipients trying to figure out how much their benefits will increase next year.
The Social Security Administration uses the CPI for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers data from the third quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026 to determine the annual cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits for 2027.
The programs benefit older Americans who have retired as well as the disabled and certain widows, widowers and children.
The Senior Citizens League, one of the nation’s biggest seniors groups, projected a 3.5% COLA raise in 2027. That would be up from 2.8% in 2026, and would lift the average monthly benefit for retirees by $67.90 to $2,007. The Social Security Administration will announce the COLA increase for 2027 later on Wednesday.
Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; editing by Andrea Ricci and Paul Simao.

sources.news_title: Fed rate hike call seen tight as inflation heats up
sources.text:
Fed rate hike call seen tight as inflation heats up
Summary
The Federal Reserve is facing a closer-than-expected decision on an interest-rate hike in Washington later this month after consumer prices rose 3.7 percent year over year last month. Gasoline prices linked to the Middle East war drove part of the increase, while broad-based price pressures also emerged in software and toys. Interest-rate futures now imply roughly even odds of an October hike as policymakers weigh persistent inflation against a cooling labor market.
Key Facts
- Core consumer prices, excluding food and energy, rose 2.6 percent year over year, exceeding economists’ 2.5 percent projection.
- The Fed raised its policy-rate target range to 3.75 percent-4.00 percent in September.
- Software prices increased 28 percent from a year earlier, the largest increase ever recorded in the data, while toy prices also posted a record rise.
- The Federal Open Market Committee is scheduled to meet October 27-28.
- Fed officials are weighing whether further tightening could unduly slow the labor market as job gains cool despite low unemployment.
A Federal Reserve interest-rate decision later this month may be a closer call than previously thought after Labor Department data showed consumer prices were up 3.7 percent last month from a year earlier, well above the Fed's 2 percent target and moving in the wrong direction.
Higher gasoline prices from the Middle East war were a main driver. Excluding volatile food and energy prices, the core Consumer Price Index (CPI) was up 2.6 percent, more than the 2.5 percent economists polled by Reuters had projected.
The Fed lifted the policy rate in September to a target range of 3.75 percent-4.00 percent to bring down too-high inflation, and officials have said they are looking closely for signs of broadening price pressures that could keep inflation high even if gas prices fall, necessitating more policy tightening. Wednesday's data contained plenty of such signs.
"The surprise was not concentrated in any one item, like it was with wireless in the August report, but instead reflected a number of components showing strength, i.e., it was broad-based," wrote Omair Sharif, founder of Inflation Insights.
Software prices were up 28 percent from a year earlier, the largest increase ever, and toy prices also notched a record rise, the data showed -- emblematic of inflationary impulses from both AI-driven demand and higher tariffs under the Trump administration.
"This means that inflation is broadening out, something that is not a good omen for the Fed and would raise the probability for an increase in rates at the end of the October FOMC meeting," wrote Raymond James Chief Economist Eugenio Aleman, referring to the Fed's rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee, which next meets October 27-28.
In recent weeks several of the Fed's most influential policymakers have signaled there's time to weigh more data before delivering what most believe will be at least one more rate hike by year's end, and traders had bet heavily against a second straight hike under Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh -- especially just a week before November elections that will decide if Trump's Republican party holds on to majorities in Congress.
After Wednesday's economic data, interest-rate futures are priced for around even odds of an October rate hike, a place of unusual uncertainty around the outcome of a Fed decision just two weeks away.
Fed policymakers are also weighing the risk of tightening too fast and unduly slowing the labor market. Unemployment has been low, but job gains have also cooled.
"September CPI keeps inflation concerns alive, with core inflation still sticky, but weaker jobs data and fragile consumer sentiment mean the Fed still has room to hold in October," PPHC Chief Economist Martin Beck said.

sources.news_title: "Flashing Red": Rate-Hike Odds, Bond Yields Explode Higher After Hotter-Than-Expected CPI
sources.text:
"Flashing Red": Rate-Hike Odds, Bond Yields Explode Higher After Hotter-Than-Expected CPI
Tl;dr: "This inflation report is flashing red for the Fed," according to Olu Sonola, Head of US Economics at Fitch Ratings.
"Energy pushed the headline number higher, as expected, but the real problem is that core inflation remains stuck above 3%. Higher energy costs are beginning to seep into broader services prices, increasing the risk that this inflation burst will persist. A rate hike at the end of the month is now firmly on the table, but December remains the more likely move."
We don’t know if these numbers will ultimately prove to be a game changer for the Fed, but they sure don’t fit the message we’ve heard recently from some policymakers saying they have time to assess how the data plays out.
There does not appear to be any quirky one-off 'excusable' data-points (like last month's phone bill and information processing surge) for the doves to 'look through' which explains why October is now well and truly back on the table and December is a definite.
* * *
Expectations were for a hot headline and cool core heading into this morning's most-watched macro signal from CPI with the October FOMC decision on the line. FedSpeak has clearly pushed the market to back away from a hawkish view, today's data may force a change.
Headline CPI did indeed come hot in September - but as expected - at +0.6% MoM, which pulls it up 3.7% YoY (hotter than the 3.6% YoY exp)...
- The index for gasoline rose 9.1% in September, accounting for over half of the monthly all items increase. The energy index increased 5.2% over the month following a 2.1% increase in August. Electricity CPI rose 0.2% over the month. In contrast, the natural gas index decreased 0.3% in September.
- The shelter index rose 0.4% in September after rising 0.3% in August.
- The index for food was unchanged in September, as the index for food away from home increased 0.2% and the index for food at home fell 0.1%. It increased 2.5% over the last year. 
  - Three of the six major grocery store food group indexes decreased in September, while the other three indexes increased. The meats, poultry, fish, and eggs index decreased 0.5% over the month, as the beef index fell 1.0%. The index for other food at home decreased 0.2 percent in September. The dairy and related products index decreased 0.9% over the month, as the milk index declined 2.0%.
- The energy index increased 20.4% YoY due in large part to the index for gasoline rising 34.2% over the same period. The natural gas index increased 5.0% YoY and the electricity index rose 4.4% YoY.
Core CPI also printed hotter than expected, up 0.3% MoM (+0.2% MoM exp). That has pulled Core CPI up 2.6% YoY (above the expected 2.5%)...
Indexes that increased over the month include recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, medical care, and apparel. Conversely, the index for communication was among the small number of major indexes that decreased in September.
- Shelter CPI increased 0.4% MoM, after rising 0.3% in August.
	
  - Index for owners’ equivalent rent rose 0.3% in September, and the index for rent increased 0.2%.
  - Lodging away from home index rose 2.0% in September after rising 2.4% the previous month.
- Index for recreation increased 0.5% over the month after being unchanged in August.
- Used cars and trucks index rose 0.7% in September, and the education index increased 0.6%.
- New vehicles index, the personal care index, and the motor vehicle insurance index also increased over the month.
- Index for airline fares increased 1.2% in September, and the index for apparel rose 0.3%.
- The medical care index increased 0.1% in September after falling 0.2% in August. The index for hospital services rose 0.7% over the month.
- Prescription drugs index declined 1.2% in September.
- Index for physicians’ services was unchanged over the month.
- Communication CPI declined 0.2% in September after rising 2.3% in August.
- Index for household furnishings and operations was unchanged over the month.
Services was the big driver of Core's jump (with Shelter dominating)...
Both Goods and Services price gains accelerated in September...
But it was Energy that was the biggest driver of the jump...
With Fuel Oil (Diesel) prices exploding higher...
And that is only going to get worse!
The much-watched 'SuperCore' CPI also ticked up to +2.96% YoY...
With prices rising broadly...
Short-term annualized CPI remains energy-driven...
Worse still, this is why consumer sentiment is so low. Real wages continue to fall (for the sixth straight month) with a large drop last month...
Finally, expectations were for some modest volatility today relative to the last few CPI days...
...but the dismally low volume/liquidity of the last couple of days may exaggerate any move.
Rate-hike odds have soared to 50% for October...
The market is now pricing in at least 2 more hikes in 2027 (on top of 1.5 hikes in 2026)...
...and 2Y yields are spiking...
Christopher Hodge at Natixis confirms that these numbers put October in play:
“We had said that anything near consensus would not likely shift the narrative for the Fed for October, but this is far enough from consensus to make it a debate. We still think the Fed does not ultimately go – the arguments laid out by Williams and Jefferson suggests that there is no rush to tighten again right now, but today at least gives the hawks more ammo at the meeting.”
The bottom line is that this print signals reasonably broad-based price pressures too (not just energy). Prices for recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, medical care, and apparel all increased. Some of that may be tariffs and the energy story, but some of it also suggest sticky inflation.
And that is what Warsh and his pals fear most... you can't "look through" that!

sources.news_title: US inflation rises before midterm elections, fuelling rate hike fears
sources.text:
US inflation rises before midterm elections, fuelling rate hike fears
Economists divided on Fed rate hike as inflation creates uncertainty in run-up to US midterm elections in a tense market.
United States consumer prices jumped in September in the final inflation report before the midterm elections, increasing chances of an interest rate hike later this month.
Annual inflation accelerated to 3.7 percent, up from 3.4 percent in August. On a monthly basis, prices rose by 0.6 percent, according to the Consumer Price Index report released by the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Wednesday.
Petrol prices led the surge as tensions between the US and Iran, as well as Russia and Ukraine, weighed on global energy prices. Petrol prices rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for more than half of the CPI monthly increase, according to the BLS. They were up 34.2 percent from the same time a year ago.
“The directionless war in Iran continues to disrupt global supply chains, driving up the prices of food and fuel,” Kyle Moore, chief economist at The Century Foundation, an economic think tank, said in a statement provided to Al Jazeera.
Petrol prices have continued to climb. The average price for a gallon of petrol is $4.33 ($1.14 per litre), compared with $4.31 a month ago, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. Diesel prices are higher, at $6.29 per gallon (1.66 per litre), compared with $6.23 a month ago.
In a post on X, Patrick DeHaan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, said, “2026 has now seen more days with average gas prices over $4/gal than any year before: 158 days.”
Shelter costs also jumped 0.4 percent from the previous month, following a 0.3 percent increase in August. Food costs were a bright spot in the report, remaining unchanged overall.
Food away from home, including restaurant meals, rose 0.2 percent, but that increase was offset by a 0.1 percent decline in food-at-home prices, which track grocery costs.
At the grocery store, poultry prices jumped 0.7 percent, fruit and vegetable prices rose 0.5 percent, and juice prices increased 1.1 percent. However, milk prices dropped 2.1 percent and beef prices fell 0.9 percent.
Amid heavy investment in AI infrastructure, prices for computer software and accessories have jumped 28 percent from the same time last year.
“The AI boom is playing a huge part, and we have all read about the hundreds of billions being poured into data centers, AI firms, and models,” Rami Cassis, principal of Parabellum Investment, said in comments provided to Al Jazeera.
Fed pressures
The inflation data comes days before the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision later this month. Last month, the US central bank raised rates by 25 basis points, bringing the target range to 3.75–4.00 percent, the first hike in three years.
Economists are divided over whether the Fed will raise rates again or hold them steady. According to CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, there is a 52.9 percent chance that rates will remain in the 3.75–4.00 percent range, while a 47.1 percent chance of a quarter of a percentage point hike that would bring them to 4.00–4.25 percent.
The inflation data puts pressure on Republicans before the midterm elections on November 3. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that about 78 percent of Americans blamed US President Donald Trump’s policies for price increases.
US markets trended downward following the inflation report. The Nasdaq fell 0.8 percent and the S&P 500 dropped 0.6 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was roughly flat in midday trading.

sources.news_title: Trump gets an ugly October surprise at the worst possible time
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has been hit with a fresh blow with an unwelcome October surprise just before the midterms, which contradicts his final pitch to American voters on the campaign trail.
Within a week of the president declaring that “prices are coming down very fast,” inflation is climbing again, and the latest numbers from his government are much worse than economists projected.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics revealed that the Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% year-on-year in September, up from 3.4% in August, while economists had anticipated 3.6%. During the month, prices rose 0.6%, up from 0.4% in August.
This is the final inflation report before voters make their decision on November 3. This presents a new challenge for the president and Republicans, battling to keep their majority in Congress to convince voters that the economy is doing fine.
Most of the increase came from gasoline, which rose a whopping 9.1% in a single month and was 34.2% higher than a year earlier. In total, energy costs climbed 5.2% for the month and 20.4% annually, per the Labor Department figures.
Core inflation rose to 2.6% annually from 2.4%, and shelter costs increased 0.4% in September. Airfares, used cars, and recreation got pricier, but food prices, however, were flat for the month, with grocery prices coming down slightly.
At the G7 summit in June, Trump claimed that the U.S. has “the strongest economy we've ever had” and called affordability a “fake word made up by the Democrats.” During a Pennsylvania rally in December 2025, he also called affordability a hoax. However, he has toned down that rhetoric at the campaign rally amid voter backlash.
Poll after poll has shown that Americans care about the prices of everyday goods that affect their lives. A CBS News poll released earlier this month found nine in 10 Americans said prices are the No. 1 factor in determining their view of the American economy.
The promises are clashing with the reality that families are spending more on essentials while their incomes struggle to keep up. Per an MS Now report, the price of goods is outpacing workers' salaries for the last five months.
From a political standpoint, the timing could not be worse: Trump is trying to reassure voters about the economy with fewer than three weeks to go, but the next CPI report won't arrive until Nov. 10, a week after Election Day.
The September figures will therefore be the last official look at consumer inflation voters will have before they decide who will control Congress.

sources.news_title: Americans' Paychecks Fall Behind Inflation for Third Straight Month as Gas Prices Surge 34%
sources.text:
Americans' Paychecks Fall Behind Inflation for Third Straight Month as Gas Prices Surge 34%
Real pay fell 0.5% in a month as petrol prices drove the spike
The dollar in an American worker's pocket bought less in September than it did in August, and less again than the month before that. For the third month running, pay rises failed to keep pace with the cost of living.
Real average hourly earnings, which measure take-home pay against prices, fell 0.5 per cent over the month, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on 14 October. That was the sharpest monthly drop since the spring and the third consecutive decline, after slips of 0.1 per cent in July and August. Over the full year, the real value of an hour's work was down 0.7 per cent.
The reason sits in a simple gap. Nominal pay rose just 0.1 per cent in September, lifting average hourly earnings to $37.81 (about £28.36). Prices rose six times faster.
Consumer prices climbed 0.6 per cent on the month and 3.7 per cent over the year, up from 3.4 per cent in August and the highest annual reading in more than a year, the bureau's Consumer Price Index showed. For production and non-supervisory workers, who make up the bulk of the private-sector workforce, real hourly pay fell 0.6 per cent on the month.
Why Gas Is Driving the Pain
Petrol did most of the damage. The gasoline index jumped 9.1 per cent in September alone and accounted for more than half of the entire monthly rise in prices, the bureau said. Measured over 12 months, gasoline has climbed 34.2 per cent.
That one category has bent the whole figure out of shape. The broader energy index rose 20.4 per cent over the year, and fuel oil, which heats millions of homes, soared 74.2 per cent. Drivers at the pump and families eyeing winter heating bills are absorbing the hit first.
Strip out food and energy and the picture cools, though not by much. Core inflation, the gauge economists track for the underlying trend, held at 0.3 per cent for the month and 2.6 per cent over the year. Shelter, the single biggest line in most household budgets, rose 3.2 per cent annually. Airline fares were up 22.4 per cent.
Groceries offered the only real relief. The cost of food at home edged down 0.1 per cent over the month, with beef off 1.0 per cent and milk down 2.0 per cent, though the shopping bill still ran 1.8 per cent higher than a year ago.
What Economists Are Watching
The monthly gaps look trivial on their own. Strung together, they chip away at living standards, and September extended a run that began in the spring when real pay first turned negative.
Jared Bernstein, an economist at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, has called the real hourly wage the fundamental building block of working Americans' living standards. When it falls month after month, households feel it not in a statistic but in what a week's pay no longer covers.
Markets were braced for a hot reading. Forecasters had clustered around 3.6 per cent, so the 3.7 per cent print barely moved the needle for traders. For households, the forecast was beside the point. What registers is the receipt at the pump and the total at the till, and in September both moved the wrong way.
A Report That Almost Did Not Arrive
The September figures carry an unusual back story. The report was delayed by the federal government shutdown, which had frozen most data collection across Washington.
The bureau recalled furloughed staff specifically to finish the September index, because the number anchors the annual cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security, the payment that supports tens of millions of retirees. Released the same day, that September reading is the one the government uses to set how far benefits rise in 2027.
So one of the most closely watched economic indicators in the country was produced almost alone, while much of the rest of the statistical machinery stayed dark. The message it carried was consistent across the board. Prices are rising, the raises meant to offset them are lagging, and both are trailing the real cost of a tank of petrol. The next inflation report, covering October, is due on 10 November.

sources.news_title: US inflation jumps to 3.7% as Iran war drives up prices
sources.text:
US inflation jumped to 3.7 per cent in September as the war in Iran drove a rebound in fuel prices, piling pressure on Americans ahead of the midterm elections and prompting traders to raise bets on Federal Reserve rate rises.
Wednesday’s annual consumer price index figure was up from 3.4 per cent in August and ahead of the 3.6 per cent forecast in a Bloomberg poll of economists.
Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, also came in ahead of Wall Street expectations, rising to 2.6 from the previous month’s figure of 2.4 per cent.
Wednesday’s data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics marks the first time US annual inflation has risen since May. It underlines how the energy shock triggered by the war in the Middle East continues to reverberate across the world’s biggest economy, weeks ahead of November’s midterm election.
READ MORE
US President Donald Trump has tried to contain the economic fallout from the conflict and douse fuel prices, as Democrats tap into voter frustration at the cost of living and seek to wrest control of Congress from his Republican Party.
But Wednesday’s data suggests that less affluent Americans in particular are being increasingly squeezed. Hourly earnings rose by just 3 per cent in September versus a year earlier, marking the sixth consecutive month of declining real wage growth.
“Inflation simply isn’t coming down quickly enough,” said Eric Winograd, chief economist at AllianceBernstein. “The bottom part of the K-shaped economy is losing ground, as anybody who has seen campaign ads on TV the last few weeks has heard.”
The inflation data increased bets that the Fed could raise rates again as soon as this month after it lifted borrowing costs for the first time in three years in September. Expectations of an October increase had faded in recent weeks after central bank officials indicated they were not in a rush to act again.
Following the data release, traders in the futures market were pricing in a roughly 45 per cent chance of an October rise, up from 22 per cent before.
Budget 2027: Does this giveaway budget have potential banana skins that might lie ahead for the Government?
Jeff Schulze, head investment strategist at the Franklin Templeton Institute, said that the latest data “bolsters the case for additional rate hikes, but recent dovish Fed-speak . . . suggests that the bar is high for an immediate hike”.
“I don’t think there is going to be urgency to react to this one report and raise interest rates six days before midterms,” added Joe Lavorgna, chief economist at SMBC Nikko Securities. “The Fed doesn’t want to put itself into a political fight unnecessarily. But they will almost certainly go again in December.”
Treasury yields jumped following the figures, with the two-year rising as much as 0.16 percentage points to 4.95 per cent, approaching the 28-month high it hit in September.
The months-long sell-off in the Treasury market had abated in recent days, as bond investors began to snap up government debt. But the recovery in bonds was almost fully erased by Wednesday morning’s move.
The US dollar strengthened 0.6 per cent against the euro to its highest level since May 2025.
The sell-off in bonds was poised to cascade into the equities market, with futures tracking the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 falling almost 0.8 per cent and those for the blue-chip S&P 500 down 0.2 per cent.
The September inflation rise was largely driven by higher fuel prices, with the BLS’s index tracking petrol prices up 34.2 per cent year on year and 9.1 per cent higher than August’s figure.
Petrol and diesel costs eased during the summer from the initial highs after the war broke out. But they have bounced back in recent months as tensions flared in the Middle East, sending the price of diesel to record highs and prompting a flurry of policy interventions by Trump.
Analysts noted that the rise in core inflation suggested price pressures were becoming more entrenched, with rises in everything from cars and airfares to education and toys.
“Today’s CPI report stands out as the first of the year in which price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once,” said Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede. - Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

sources.news_title: Economists predict inflation worsened last month, driven by pricier gas and semiconductors
sources.text:
Inflation likely worsened in September in one of the last price reports the government will issue before the midterm elections that have been heavily defined by concerns over affordability.
Consumer prices are forecast to have risen 3.6% in September compared with a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August, according to a survey of economists by data provider FactSet. The Labor Department will issue the report Wednesday morning.
On a monthly basis, prices are expected to have risen 0.6% from August to September, FactSet said, up from 0.4% the previous month and the biggest jump since April.
The figures will likely underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which has fallen sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but has ticked higher since the war began in late February. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices.
Ongoing inflation has taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living issue. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices likely rose 2.5% in September from a year ago, up slightly from 2.4% in August. That is closer to the Fed’s 2% inflation target, but it has been stuck at mostly that level since January of this year — just before the Iran war. Core prices are forecast to have risen just 0.2% from August to September.
Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn’t moving quickly enough back to the central bank’s target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9%.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said at a news conference last month. Inflation reports over the summer “do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved,” he added.
Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year.
By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war’s disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can’t address those bottlenecks.
Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It’s already pushed up the price of air fares about 23% from a year ago. Gas prices jumped about 9% from August to September, a big increase that will drive much of the overall jump in inflation. Rising gas costs are a highly visible sign of inflation and often drive down measures of consumer sentiment about the economy.
Prices at the pump have ticked lower in recent weeks, though they remain higher than a month ago. Gas prices averaged $4.34 a gallon nationwide Tuesday, up a few cents from a month earlier.
Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients.
The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed into costs for consumer electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones.
On September 1, Nintendo increased the price for its Switch 2 gaming system by 11% to $499.99. And Apple’s newest iPhone, the iPhone 17, cost about 10% more than its previous upgrade, though some of that likely reflects greater capabilities.
