sources.news_title: US inflation rises to 3.7% in September as gasoline prices surge
sources.text:
US consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged, dealing another blow to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November 3 midterm elections and putting an interest rate increase later this month back on the radar.
The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department on Wednesday showed a broadening of price pressures beyond energy, raising concerns among economists that underlying inflation could be getting sticky. Financial markets now see the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision this month as a closer call than before the data was released.
The report added to surveys this month that showed a further deterioration in consumer sentiment and a plunge in Trump's approval rating, driven by angst over the rising cost of living. A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed about 78% of Americans blamed Trump's policies, including tariffs on imports and the Middle East conflict, for rising prices, which are outpacing wages.
"The last mile back to target could remain bumpy and keep interest rates elevated," said Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial. "The report complicates the Fed's decision this month, as the road back to price stability is looking increasingly difficult to navigate."
The CPI rose 0.6% last month after climbing 0.4% in August, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said. The increase in the CPI was in line with economists' expectations.
A 9.1% surge in gasoline prices accounted for more than half of the increase in the CPI over the month. The US-Israeli war with Iran is driving up energy prices. Diesel prices have vaulted to record highs and there are fears that those costs will soon feed through to higher prices at the supermarket.
Food prices were unchanged after gaining 0.1% in both July and August. Grocery store prices dipped 0.1% over the month, but rose 1.8% on a year-over-year basis. Beef prices dropped 1.0% in September and the cost of dairy and related products eased 0.9%. But prices for nonalcoholic beverages surged 0.9%, while fruits and vegetables cost 0.5% more.
In the 12 months through September, the CPI advanced 3.7% after rising 3.4% in August.
CORE INFLATION ABOVE EXPECTATIONS
Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI gained 0.3% in September, matching the gain in August. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the so-called core CPI would rise 0.2%. The core CPI was lifted by a 0.4% increase in the cost of shelter, including hotel and motel rooms. Owners' equivalent rent rose 0.3%.
There were increases in the costs of recreation and education. Prices for used cars and trucks increased 0.7%, while airline fares rose 1.2% amid higher jet fuel prices. Apparel prices climbed 0.3%.
In the 12 months through September, core CPI inflation increased 2.6% after advancing 2.4% in August. The US central bank tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index for its 2% inflation target.
The core CPI measure is lagging core PCE inflation, which increased 3.0% in August, because of the different weights assigned to the components in the baskets.
Financial markets raised the chances of a rate hike at the Fed's October 27-28 policy meeting to roughly 52% from about 22% prior to the CPI report, CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed. The odds of a rate increase this month had diminished following underwhelming payroll gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE inflation readings for July and August.
US Treasury yields were mostly higher while the dollar advanced versus a basket of currencies. US stocks opened lower.
The Fed in September raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range, its first hike in three years, and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead. Economists had expected the Fed to raise rates in December.
The September CPI inflation report was keenly awaited by millions of retirees and other Social Security recipients trying to figure out how much their benefits will increase next year.
The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits for 2027. The programs benefit older Americans who have retired as well as the disabled and certain widows, widowers and children.

sources.news_title: Inflation Jumps Higher In Final Report Before Midterm Elections
sources.text:
Inflation accelerated in September as surging gasoline prices drove consumer costs higher, delivering another blow to Republicans’ chances to retain both the House and Senate in November’s election.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August, according to data released Wednesday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). The report landed less than three weeks before November’s midterm elections, as polling showed President Donald Trump and Republicans struggling with voters over inflation and the economy.
Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly increase in consumer prices. Gas prices were 34.2% higher than a year earlier, while fuel oil prices surged 74.2% over the same period.
Consumer prices climbed 0.6% in September alone, exceeding economists’ expectations and raising the prospect of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike as Americans contended with mounting financial pressures.
The broader energy index climbed 5.2% during September and 20.4% over the past year, reflecting the continued fallout from disruptions to global energy supplies amid the conflict involving Iran.
An August Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 47% of registered voters considered the cost of living the single most important factor in deciding their congressional vote, while 71% of Americans disapproved of Trump’s handling of the issue.
A separate Gallup poll released Tuesday found that 51% of Americans trusted Democrats more to keep the country prosperous, compared with 37% who favored Republicans. The 14-point Democratic advantage was the party’s largest advantage since 2007.
Inflation also extended beyond the gas pump. The index excluding volatile food and energy prices, commonly known as core inflation, rose 0.3% in September and 2.6% over the previous 12 months, up from 2.4% in August. (RELATED: Diesel Hits Record Even As Oil Prices Fall)
Housing costs continued climbing, with the shelter index rising 0.4% during September and 3.2% over the past year. Used cars and trucks increased 0.7% over the month, while airline fares climbed 1.2% and recreation costs rose 0.5%.
Food prices offered some relief, remaining unchanged overall in September. Grocery prices slipped 0.1%, although the broader food index remained 2.5% higher than a year earlier.
The inflation figures complicated the Federal Reserve’s effort to rein in prices without further weakening the labor market. The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point in September, its first increase since 2023, bringing the target range to 3.75% to 4%.
Following Wednesday’s report, interest rate futures traders raised the probability of another increase at the Fed’s Oct. 27-28 meeting to nearly 45%, according to the Financial Times, up from approximately 22% before the data was released.
The latest figures followed a disappointing September employment report showing employers added just 29,000 jobs while the unemployment rate reached 4.2%, leaving policymakers confronting persistent inflation alongside signs of a slowing labor market.
Financial markets reacted sharply to the inflation data, with Treasury yields rising and stock futures falling as investors reassessed the likelihood of additional Fed tightening.

Slowing wage growth, ever-increasing prices put the squeeze on Americans’ budgets ahead of midterm elections
Today’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) report shows prices rose 0.6% in September and are up 3.7% over the past year, the fastest pace since May. Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% in September alone, accounting for over half of the monthly increase in overall prices, and are up 34% from a year ago. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, rose 0.33% in September, the largest monthly increase since April.
Americans are increasingly frustrated with Trump's failure to bring down high prices. Consumers' views of current economic conditions are at an all-time low, and 82% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living. Instead of working to rein in inflation, Trump is trying to pull a fast one on voters, spewing empty promises to bring prices down and send Americans a $5,000 “Trump dividend” if Republicans hold Congress, despite having never delivered on the DOGE and tariff checks he promised last year.
Today's inflation report is the last before the Federal Reserve's October 28 interest rate decision. The Fed raised interest rates last month for the first time in three years because of inflation concerns, and most officials anticipate another increase by the end of the year. In its latest meeting minutes, the Fed pointed to Trump's tariffs and higher energy costs, as well as the president’s never-ending war with Iran, as drivers of persistent inflation. Trump’s war and tariffs are raising the prices of nearly everything families buy, and now his actions are raising borrowing costs for families, too.
Groundwork’s Senior Vice President of Policy, Advocacy, and Research Alex Jacquez, released the following statement:
“It’s no wonder Americans have lost faith in Trump’s economy. The president has repeatedly made promises he can’t keep, and despite the band-aid attempts from the White House, there is a gaping hole in our economy just weeks from the midterms. Between the president’s war in Iran and reckless tariffs, his economy is on life support.”
The Groundwork Collaborative is dedicated to advancing a coherent and persuasive progressive economic worldview and narrative capable of delivering meaningful opportunity and prosperity for everyone. “Mr. Belgal’s detention was unlawful from its inception."
Immigrant rights advocates this week demanded the immediate release of Oscar Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican father of two held in US Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody with a bullet lodged in his neck after an ICE agent shot him in front of his young son last week in New York City.
The Legal Aid Society filed an emergency petition Wednesday in the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York seeking Belgal's release, arguing that his continued detention threatens his health and violates his rights.
Masked ICE officers wearing civilian clothing approached Belgal's vehicle on October 8 with firearms drawn, without identifying themselves or presenting a warrant. An officer shattered the driver's-side window before agents fired at least seven shots, striking Belgal in the neck as his 5-year-old son sat in the back seat.
"Rather than providing immediate medical assistance, ICE officers threw Mr. Belgal to the ground, handcuffed him, and left him bleeding and fading in and out of consciousness," the Legal Aid Society said Wednesday. "[New York Police Department] officers ultimately intervened to secure medical assistance. Doctors advised that Mr. Belgal required surgery to remove the bullet and instructed him to return for treatment during the week of October 12. Instead, ICE transferred him into detention."
Belgal is being held at Brooklyn's Metropolitan Detention Center despite suffering a loss of sensation on the left side of his face and impaired hearing in his left ear, according to his attorneys. He has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet.
“Mr. Belgal’s detention was unlawful from its inception. ICE officers shot him in the neck in front of his 5-year-old son, failed to provide him with immediate medical assistance, and now continue to hold him in a facility notorious for medical neglect,” said Perry McAninch and Elyssa Williams, counsel for Belgal and attorneys with Legal Aid.
“With a bullet still lodged in his neck and his serious medical needs unmet, every additional day in custody puts him at further risk," they added. "The court must intervene and order his immediate release.”
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents have shot more than two dozen people since President Donald Trump’s return to office, including more than half a dozen who died. In multiple cases, federal authorities had made allegations against shooting victims that were later contradicted by evidence.
More than 50 people have also died in ICE custody during Trump’s second term.
Belgal's shooting has fueled fresh calls to abolish ICE from progressives, including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). Meanwhile, Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) has introduced legislation aimed at dismantling DHS, which oversees ICE.
The San Diego-based Haitian Bridge Alliance also condemned Belgal's shooting and called for an independent investigation, the release of relevant body camera footage, and accountability for what it called the unlawful uses of force.
“How many more families must be traumatized before we say enough is enough?” Guerline Jozef, the organization's founder and executive director, asked Monday.
“We cannot continue to accept a system where immigration enforcement becomes a license to terrorize communities, endanger children, and take human lives,” she added. “Our humanity is not negotiable. Our dignity is not conditional on immigration status.” 
"What a stain on this government that people in this country are unable to buy and enjoy the work of one of this generation’s greatest writing talents," said lawmaker Jeremy Corbyn. "De-proscribe Palestine Action now."
News out of the British book publishing world encapsulated the UK government's priorities when it comes to Israel and Palestine, one protest group suggested Wednesday.
"We got a Sally Rooney book ban before a single arrest of the more than 2,000 Britons who have participated in Israel’s genocide and now walk our streets," said Defend Our Juries after Irish author Sally Rooney announced she would no longer be able to sell her books in the United Kingdom because of her support for the pro-Palestinian group Palestine Action.
In July 2025, the group was proscribed as a terrorist organization under the Terrorism Act of 2000, with lawmakers voting to ban Palestine Action after some of its members vandalized two military planes at a Royal Air Force base. The UK has provided military and political support to Israel as it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since October 2023, in retaliation for a Hamas-led attack.
Under Section 15 of the Terrorism Act, it is a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison for a person or group to provide funds to Palestine Action.
Rooney, author of novels including Normal People, Conversations With Friends, and Intermezzo, said Wednesday that her publisher, Faber, would not continue to sell her books in the UK because of an opinion she wrote a month after Palestine Action's proscription, saying she planned to continue supporting the group, which is not labeled a terrorist organization in Ireland, and would donate proceeds from her book sales to it.
“As a result, the fulfillment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offense," Rooney said in a statement to The Guardian. "After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”
Faber explained that should it continue to sell Rooney's popular and acclaimed novels in the UK, it would not be able to pass the author's royalties on to her due to her statements about backing the nonviolent group, which has called on the British government to end its support for Israel. Numerous human rights groups and Holocaust scholars have said Israel's bombardment of Gaza and its blocking of humanitarian aid, which have continued despite a ceasefire deal signed one year ago, constitutes a genocide.
"To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher," said Faber in a statement. "As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format. We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories.”
Palestine Action's proscription has led to the arrests of about 3,700 people in the UK—most for simply holding signs that say, “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”
The arrests of nonviolent protesters—many of whom have been senior citizens—have been widely condemned around the world, and Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori said the new outgrowth of the proscription on Wednesday was "a new low in the escalating assault on free speech."
Rooney, Ammori told The Guardian, "took a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced. She has refused to compromise her convictions, even at considerable personal and professional cost. Her work should be celebrated and widely available, not driven off the shelves of British bookshops because she refuses to be complicit in the suppression of solidarity with the Palestinian people."
"No author should have to choose between their principles and their freedom to publish," she said.
The Ireland-Palestine Solidarity Campaign called the banning of Rooney's books "disgraceful and embarrassing for the British government."
Kerry Moscogiuri, the chief executive of Amnesty International UK, told The Guardian that with Rooney pushed into removing her books from stores across Britain, "there is a real danger that others, seeing the price she has paid, will decide they cannot afford to speak out.”
“Writers should not find their books disappearing from shelves because of their political beliefs. Nor should people have to choose between expressing their conscience and pursuing their livelihoods," said Moscogiuri. “Sally Rooney’s willingness to accept the personal consequences of her convictions deserves recognition."
The hip-hop trio Kneecap, from Northern Ireland, expressed solidarity with Rooney, while Member of Parliament Jeremy Corbyn, who represents the progressive Your Party, said the removal of her books was "more proof of the complete absurdity of the proscription of Palestine Action."
"What a stain on this government that people in this country are unable to buy and enjoy the work of one of this generation’s greatest writing talents," he said. "De-proscribe Palestine Action now."
A legal challenge against the group's proscription will be heard by the UK Supreme Court next month.
"Senate confirmation processes and financial disclosures exist to ensure that qualified individuals are appointed and carry out their official duties with integrity. Kushner is not an exception."
A government watchdog on Wednesday filed a lawsuit aimed at blocking Jared Kushner from serving as a top American foreign policy official while lacking confirmation from the US Senate.
In a complaint filed with the US District Court for the District of Columbia, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) alleged that Kushner, who is President Donald Trump's son-in-law, is engaged in "unlawful exercise of government power."
Even though Kushner has been given the role of an informal "envoy," the lawsuit contends that he has been tasked with major responsibilities, such as negotiating an end to Russia's war against Ukraine, that under the Constitution should require Senate confirmation.
"Kushner is one of President Trump’s go-to foreign policy negotiators," the complaint explains. "He represents the United States in the highest profile global conflicts... He negotiates directly with foreign leaders. He fills a crucial and continuing role in shaping and implementing the country’s foreign policy during President Trump’s second term."
Even as Kushner oversees such highly consequential diplomatic efforts, the lawsuit continues, he is still working as a private businessman operating an investment firm that has received billions of dollars in investments from the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates.
"The interplay and overlap between his government role and private business interests present a heightened risk of financial conflicts of interest," the complaint says. "Nonetheless, Kushner continues to exercise significant government power while circumventing the very protections put in place to guard against such conflicts."
Kushner has also been appointed in a manner that has helped him completely evade "transparency and conflict-of-interest obligations, including the filing of public financial disclosures during the appointment process," the lawsuit says.
The complaint urges the court to order Kushner to file financial disclosures and, if it finds him in violation of the US Constitution's appointments clause, bar him from continued government service.
CREW president Donald K. Sherman said the lawsuit is necessary to ensure that Kushner is not using US foreign policy as a vehicle for self-enrichment.
"Senate confirmation processes and financial disclosures exist to ensure that qualified individuals are appointed and carry out their official duties with integrity," Sherman explained. "Kushner is not an exception. He cannot simply opt out and expect the public to simply take him at his word.”
“Flock’s technology isn’t making us safer," the Michigan congresswoman said. "Instead, it has been used to stalk people, misidentify and arrest innocent people, surveil protestors, and wrongfully record our neighbors."
Amid what she called a "mass surveillance crisis," US Rep. Rashida Tlaib announced legislation on Wednesday to ban the use of federal funds for powerful dragnet spying systems—including the automated license plate-reading cameras manufactured by Flock Safety.
Flock has quickly grown into a massive nationwide surveillance network with more than 120,000 of its artificial intelligence-powered cameras installed across 49 states, allowing law enforcement agencies to track and reconstruct Americans' movements, often without warrants.
While supporters describe Flock cameras as a tool to help police solve crimes, there is little evidence that they actually reduce it. There are also many documented cases of cops using the technology to stalk romantic partners, track women who've had abortions, monitor First Amendment-protected protests, and surveil people on behalf of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) as part of its mass deportation push.
“Flock’s technology isn’t making us safer," Tlaib (D-Mich.) said in a statement on Wednesday. "Instead, it has been used to stalk people, misidentify and arrest innocent people, surveil protesters, and wrongfully record our neighbors. My bill would prevent our government on all levels from selling us out to Big Tech companies that trample our civil rights for profit.”
The bill, titled the Get the Flock Out of Our Communities Act, is co-sponsored by Reps. Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas), Summer Lee (D-Pa.), Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), Nydia Velázquez (D-NY), and Bonnie Watson Coleman (D-NJ).
It is part of a growing wave of bipartisan efforts to restrict the use of Flock cameras and other surveillance tech. Reps. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) and Greg Steube (R-Fla.), along with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, have introduced legislation to limit government use or funding of automated license plate readers, while Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) has proposed limits on data collection.
Tlaib's legislation would go further. Its restrictions would also extend beyond license plate readers to other "mass surveillance systems," such as those that employ facial recognition technology and biometric tracking.
It would not only prohibit federal, state, and local governments from using federal funds to purchase, operate, or access automated mass surveillance systems; it would also make state and local governments ineligible for certain federal law enforcement grants unless they stop operating or accessing mass surveillance networks that already exist.
Federal agencies would also be barred from using data derived from these systems, and they'd be required to delete certain data that has already been gathered.
The full extent to which Flock cameras are funded with federal dollars is unknown. But the company itself has identified several federal grant programs that local police departments can apply for to purchase the cameras.
"Federal funds should be used to invest in our communities in real safety solutions. We need good jobs, affordable homes, clean water, and reliable electricity. That’s what’s going to make us safer," Tlaib said at a news conference Wednesday. "Instead, our government is sacrificing our rights to big tech companies that care more about their profits, selling our data, than about our safety."
Tlaib's bill comes as backlash to Flock cameras grows around the country. A recent Data for Progress poll showed 52% of voters viewed Flock cameras unfavorably, while more than 200 cities and counties have canceled their contracts with the company.
“People everywhere are starting to recognize that conflating surveillance with safety makes communities less safe,” said Tawana Petty, a digital and data justice organizer from Detroit. “The persistent abuse of Flock cameras and other surveillance systems by law enforcement agencies across the United States, and the lack of transparency by the companies that market them, has caused an awakening among residents and city government agencies who are ridding themselves of the technologies."
A group of Democratic senators warned the company's CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, that the tax maneuver violates "the spirit and, potentially, the letter" of federal law.
A group of Democratic senators wrote Tuesday that Meta is violating "the spirit and, potentially, the letter" of federal tax law by using a research and development tax credit to save billions of dollars on its massive data center buildout.
In a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, the Senate Democrats noted that the $1.9 trillion company has "indicated on federal regulatory filings that it has used the federal research credit to reduce its federal income tax liability by $6.6 billion between 2023-2025." By one measure, the senators noted, Meta alone could be responsible for "more than 10% of all research credits claimed in the US."
"While it remains unclear exactly how Meta was able to reduce its federal tax liability by over $6.6 billion in the last three years using federal research credits, it appears from published reports that a substantial share is by claiming the research credit related to its massive AI data center build out," wrote the group of lawmakers led by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee.
Last month, The New York Times reported that Meta claims in its federal tax filings that the company's AI data centers are "a giant experiment that could fail," allowing it to "tap into a tax credit intended for research and experimentation." Meta specifically characterizes its expensive, resource-devouring data centers as "pilot models."
"Meta’s own accountants recognize that the strategy is on shaky legal ground," the Times reported. "In disclosures buried in securities filings, the tech giant warns that billions in tax savings are vulnerable to being overturned by the IRS, in large part because of 'uncertainties with our research tax credits.'"
In their letter to Zuckerberg, the Democratic senators wrote that the research tax credit "can be a useful and necessary tool to support our nation’s innovation economy and cutting-edge research."
"Subsidizing your AI data center build is not close to meeting this standard," the lawmakers added, demanding that the company provide specific information on its use of the federal research tax credit and its legal justification for the maneuver.
The senators sent their letter to Zuckerberg about a week after more than two dozen House Democrats demanded that the Trump administration prevent Meta and other tech giants from exploiting an "overly expansive interpretation of qualifying expenditures" to reap billions in taxpayer subsidies to fund data centers that a majority of Americans oppose.
"Allowing ordinary data center construction and deployment costs to qualify would significantly expand the research credit beyond its intended purpose and risk converting an incentive for technological experimentation into a subsidy for capital expenditures that companies would undertake in the ordinary course of business," the House Democrats wrote in an October 7 letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
"Laggards, including the United States and Japan, are continuing to prop up the fossil fuel industry."
For the first time on record, major international public financial institutions are providing more financing for clean energy around the world than for fossil fuels. But wealthy nations, including the United States, continue to pour billions into oil and gas, hampering the global energy transition, according to a new report.
On Wednesday, two environmental advocacy groups—Oil Change International and Friends of the Earth US—published an analysis of new data on public financing from Group of 20 (G20) nations and multilateral development banks for clean energy projects, such as wind and solar, and planet-warming fossil fuels, including oil, gas, and coal.
They found that from 2023-25, public financing for clean energy averaged at least $52.7 billion annually, compared with just $36.3 billion for fossil fuels. The report attributes the shift mostly to multilateral development banks, while G20 nations' own development and export financing continued to favor fossil fuels.
“This new dataset represents a tipping point. Clean energy financing overtaking fossil fuel financing for the first time is an important milestone," said Claire O'Manique, public finance researcher at Oil Change International. "But it doesn't mean we can sit back and count our wins.”
The level of clean energy financing, the group said, is still far below what is needed to limit global warming to 1.5°C above preindustrial levels, a threshold beyond which the risks of devastating climate impacts increase.
That's largely thanks to four main culprits. Canada, Japan, the United States, and Italy accounted for around 75% of fossil fuel financing from G20 countries during this period.
Canada provided an annual average of $12.5 billion in fossil fuel financing—mostly for domestic projects. Japan averaged about $4.5 billion annually despite a G7 commitment to end public support for new international fossil fuel projects by 2022. Italy likewise averaged $3.8 billion annually, breaking a pledge to end international fossil fuel financing.
Over the same period, the US provided an annual average of about $3.6 billion in fossil fuel financing, mostly through its Export-Import Bank, compared with just $1.5 billion for clean energy.
The data from 2025, the first year of President Donald Trump's second term, is particularly striking. That year, the US provided nearly $8 billion in financing for fossil fuel projects compared with just $2.5 million for clean energy—roughly 3,200 times as much.
This included a loan of up to $4.7 billion for a liquefied natural gas project in Mozambique, despite allegations that soldiers guarding the project committed war crimes. British and Dutch backing has since been withdrawn from the project.
"Important progress is being made to move the world’s largest economies away from supporting fossil fuels and shift that financing toward renewable energy projects," said Kate DeAngelis, economic policy deputy director at Friends of the Earth US. "Unfortunately, laggards, including the United States and Japan, are continuing to prop up the fossil fuel industry instead of helping countries transition to sustainable economies.”
The report also found that less than 2% of the clean energy financing tracked reached low-income countries, despite their unmet energy needs. Meanwhile, nearly half of the funds went toward projects in the highest-income countries, according to World Bank classifications.
The five largest recipients of clean energy financing were all high- or middle-income countries: France, Poland, and Spain fall into the former category, while Brazil and India fall into the latter.
"A just transition will not happen at the scale required without governments actively steering it through redirecting and mobilizing public finance," O’Manique said. "Wealthy governments must move first and fastest to phase out fossil fuels at home and meet their climate finance obligations."
"We are running out of time," she said. "Without a fossil fuel phaseout and public finance being redirected to drive a just energy transition, we will continue to see escalating climate disasters that come at a huge human and economic cost, such as the deadly glacial flood disaster in Nepal.”
"In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime."
A nonpartisan watchdog on Wednesday filed a complaint with the State Bar of California over new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia's claims of being an attorney.
The Campaign for Accountability (CfA) has formally asked the California Bar to investigate whether Zacharia, whose stumbling first press briefing on Tuesday was panned by critics, broke state law by falsely identifying herself as a lawyer.
The group's complaint notes that while Zacharia received a Juris Doctor in 2011 from the Pepperdine University School of Law, there is no record of her being admitted to practice law in any US jurisdiction.
"A law degree, standing alone, does not entitle its holder to practice law," the complaint states. "When the White House was asked whether Ms. Zacharia had ever been admitted to a bar, its press office responded only by referring the reporter to President Trump’s social media post announcing her appointment, which described her as 'an attorney.'"
When asked by a reporter on Tuesday about where she passed the bar exam, Zacharia replied that she became an attorney "when I moved to China."
However, the complaint notes that "published reporting indicates... that China does not permit foreign nationals to sit for its national bar exam or to practice Chinese law."
And even if China had allowed her to practice law, the complaint says that this would still not allow her to represent herself as an attorney in the US.
The complaint concludes that Zacharia "appears to have violated" Section 6126(a) of the California Business and Professions Code, which states anyone who makes false claims about being licensed to practice law is guilty of a misdemeanor offense "punishable by up to one year in a county jail or by a fine of up to $1,000, or by both that fine and imprisonment."
Michelle Kuppersmith, executive director of CfA, pointed to Zacharia's repeated statements during television appearances about being a lawyer as a way to "buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson."
"Yet it seems it was all a lie," Kuppersmith added. "In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime. The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has."
"Social Security’s future is on the ballot this November," said one advocate, "and that includes the size of annual COLA adjustments.“
The rising cost of healthcare and other essentials means that the modest cost-of-living adjustment for about 76 million Social Security beneficiaries, announced Wednesday by Social Security Administrator Frank Bisignano, is likely to make only a small difference for senior citizens struggling to afford gasoline and groceries, said economic justice advocates.
Bisignano said the COLA for 2027, effective in January for most beneficiaries, will be 3.6%, amounting to an average of about $75 more per month.
Along with senior citizens, 40% of whom rely on Social Security for at least half their income, about 7.3 million people with disabilities who receive Supplemental Security Income will also receive the COLA increase starting December 31.
The COLA is higher than last year's, when the SSA adjusted monthly earned benefits by 2.8%.
But Richard Fiesta, executive director of the Alliance for Retired Americans, said the new increase "is just not enough to keep up with the cost of food, gas, utilities, and prescription drugs."
"A good chunk" of increased Social Security payments "will be wiped out" by higher premiums for Medicare Part B, which covers medically necessary and preventive healthcare services, said Fiesta. Those premiums are projected to rise to $209.50 per month in January, up from $202.90 per month this year.
Medicare Part D prescription drug plans are also expected to see increased premiums next year, while Social Security beneficiaries, like other Americans, will likely be impacted by continued inflation driven by President Donald Trump's illegal war on Iran and his tariff policy.
Social Security recipients are aware of the limits of the COLA, a poll released Monday by the AARP showed. Seventy-six percent of respondents said a 3.5% COLA would not keep up with rising prices they are facing at the grocery store, gas station, and pharmacy.
Fiesta called on billionaires and the wealthiest 1% of Americans to "pay their fair share" to make it possible to "boost benefits for everyone, implement a COLA that reflects the cost of things older Americans spend money on, and guarantee the program’s solvency for future generations."
While most American workers pay into Social Security year-round, millionaires in the US stop paying into the program just two months into the year because the payroll tax does not apply to income over a certain level. Some of the richest Americans, like Tesla CEO Elon Musk, pay very little into the crucial anti-poverty program by earning most of their money through investments rather than income.
"In just three weeks, older Americans will have an opportunity to elect members of Congress who will make strengthening Social Security a priority. The future of our earned benefits is on the ballot.”
“Strengthening and expanding Social Security must be a national priority," said Fiesta. "It’s time for clear and decisive action. In just three weeks, older Americans will have an opportunity to elect members of Congress who will make strengthening Social Security a priority. The future of our earned benefits is on the ballot.”
At Social Security Works (SSW), which advocates for strengthening the program and regularly debunks myths from the Republican Party claiming that Social Security is unaffordable for the country, Nancy Altman said the COLA increase "will help" some seniors, "but it doesn’t fully account for the costs that Social Security beneficiaries face."
"The Trump administration’s war of choice with Iran and tariff chaos have driven gasoline prices up nearly 40 percent, and caused grocery costs to skyrocket," said Altman, president of SSW.
Part of the problem, said Altman, is the SSA's use of the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which measures price changes for goods purchased by working families, to determine the annual COLA.
SSW has called for the use of the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly (CPI-E) to better reflect how Social Security recipients spend their money.
Meanwhile, Altman said, Republicans including House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) have proposed calculating the COLA using the chained Consumer Price Index (CPI), which would “substantially lower benefits over time," according to an AARP analysis.
“That’s a cut to the American people’s hard-earned benefits," said Altman. "Over time, switching to the chained CPI, as the Republicans have proposed, would shrink yearly benefits by hundreds and even thousands of dollars. Switching to the CPI-E, as the Democrats propose, would increase benefits. This would particularly impact women and Hispanics, who have longer average life expectancies."
She noted that US senators elected in November will have a say in whether Social Security remains fully funded through their six-year terms—and urged Americans to vote accordingly.
In 2032, said Altman, "Social Security is projected to face a funding shortfall. The vast majority of Republicans refuse to support a single penny in revenue increases, even from the ultra-wealthy, to address the shortfall. That leaves benefit cuts, including less generous COLAs, as their only option."
"The bottom line: Social Security’s future is on the ballot this November," she said, "and that includes the size of annual COLA adjustments.“
The September 1 strike, which killed five women and children and wounded more than 70 other Iranians, is but one of several civilian massacres during Trump's illegal war of choice.
More than 70 House Democrats on Tuesday sought answers and accountability from the Pentagon regarding a likely US strike on a September wedding gathering in southern Iran that killed five civilians—all women and children—and wounded over 70 others.
In a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Reps. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.), and Jason Crow (D-Colo.) led 74 lawmakers in demanding an explanation for the September 1 bombing in Kuhestak and details of what the Trump administration is doing to protect Iranian civilians.
“We demand urgent answers regarding the United States’ role in this strike, why the strike proceeded given the clear risk of significant civilian harm, and what steps the [US Department of Defense] is taking to prevent further civilian casualties in Iran,” the lawmakers wrote.
The strike occurred at approximately 9:30 pm local time while preparations were underway for the wedding of the daughter of a local fisher.
According to witnesses interviewed by The Associated Press, around 150 women and children were gathered at the Mallahi family compound. The celebration was following a regional tradition in which women and men gather separately. The bride and groom had not yet arrived, and the main celebration had not begun. A bomb struck the room where dinner would have been served.
Four initial fatalities—two women and two children—were identified by Iranian authorities and human rights groups: 50-year-old Zarkhatoun Taheri, 43-year-old Kolsoum Malahi Najandnia, 16-year-old Mohammad Mallahi, and 4-year-old Amir Mohammad Karimi. A fifth victim, 22-year-old woman Asiyeh Molainejad, died in a hospital on September 3.
Weapons experts concluded the blast was likely caused by a direct hit from a US munition. The Pentagon has not publicly accepted responsibility for the strike, which remains under investigation.
"This incident is regrettably among the latest in a string of civilian casualty incidents arising from the US-led war in Iran," the lawmakers wrote in their letter. "This includes a strike at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran, on the first day of the war that killed a reported 175 civilians, including 120 children."
The United Nations' Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran said it found “reasonable grounds" to believe that the Minab school strike constituted a war crime.
"While it has been reported that a preliminary investigation by the department found that the US military was responsible for the strike, over six months later the department has still not publicly acknowledged responsibility for the strike nor released the findings of its investigation," the lawmakers' letter notes.
"Similarly, reporting and independent analysis indicate that US forces were responsible for a strike at a youth sports hall in Lamerd, Iran, that killed 21 civilians, including 7 children, on February 28. While the department has denied responsibility, analysis by weapons experts found that the damage pattern is consistent with that of an American Precision Strike Missile," the lawmakers continued, referring to Lockheed Martin's next-generation surface-to-surface ballistic missile.
Hegseth, who advocates “maximum lethality” for US forces, has expressed disdain for what he called “stupid rules of engagement” designed to minimize civilian harm. He has overseen the dismantling of efforts meant to mitigate wartime harm to civilians—hundreds of thousands of whom have been killed in US-led wars during this century, according to experts.
“Maximum lethality," combined with AI-powered systems allowing for exponentially faster and more numerous target selection, has raised concerns that have been underscored by actions including US-backed Israeli massacres in Gaza and Lebanon, and US airstrikes in Iran, where tens of thousands of people have been killed or wounded during more than seven months of President Donald Trump's illegal war of choice, according to Iranian government figures.
The Washington, DC-based National Iranian American Council (NIAC) welcomed the lawmakers’ intervention, arguing that Iranian civilians must not be treated as expendable casualties of war.
“The lives of Iranian civilians cannot be treated as an acceptable cost of war,” NIAC president Jamal Abdi said in a statement. “These are families, children, and entire communities whose lives have been irreversibly altered by a military campaign that Congress never authorized."
“Credible allegations of unlawful attacks on civilians demand independent investigations, full public disclosure of the findings, and accountability for any violations of international humanitarian law,” Abdi added. “The Trump administration cannot be permitted to wage an unauthorized war in defiance of US and international law while evading responsibility for its devastating human consequences.” 
"Real wages are falling, and have been falling for months," said one economist.
Data released by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics on Wednesday showed inflation grew faster than expected in September, driven in large part by costs related to President Donald Trump's illegal war with Iran.
The latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed overall prices in September posted a yearly increase of 3.7%, marking the biggest rise in prices since May.
The main drivers of inflation in September were related to energy, which has surged in cost since Iran shut down the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year in retaliation for Trump's unlawful attack in February.
Energy prices increased by an annual rate of 20% in September, with the price of gasoline growing by an annual rate of 34% and the price of fuel oil growing by an annual rate of 74%.
University of Michigan economist Justin Wolfers noted in a Wednesday social media post that average wages are not keeping up with the rate of inflation, meaning workers have seen their purchasing power decrease.
"Real wages are falling," Wolfers wrote, "and have been falling for months."
Jared Bernstein, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress and who served as chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under former President Joe Biden, said the September data showed that "working families are getting squeezed on both sides (wage, price) of the affordability crunch," as workers' inflation-adjusted earnings are now back to where they were at the start of Trump's second term.
Bernstein's observations were echoed by Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, who pointed out that "inflation has nearly wiped out all wage gains since January 2025."
"This is a very different picture from President Trump's first term when wages were up over 15%, well above about 8% inflation," Long added. "It helps explain the frustration many households feel right now with the economy."
Sen. Andy Kim (D-NJ) said that accelerating inflation was yet another sign of Republicans' governing failures.
"Trump and Republicans have no answer for rising inflation caused by soaring gas prices and the war in Iran," Kim wrote. "They're more focused on enriching Trump and his friends and family. This is why we're fighting to take back Congress so we can end the war and bring prices down for you and your family."
Alex Jacquez, senior vice president of policy, advocacy, and research at Groundwork Collaborative, said the CPI report shows why "Americans have lost faith in Trump’s economy."
"The president has repeatedly made promises he can’t keep," Jacquez said, "and despite the band-aid attempts from the White House, there is a gaping hole in our economy just weeks from the midterms. Between the president’s war in Iran and reckless tariffs, his economy is on life support."

sources.news_title: U.S. Inflation Rises to 3.7% as Gasoline Prices Surge in September
sources.text:
U.S. inflation accelerated in September as a sharp increase in gasoline prices pushed consumer costs higher, while rents, airline tickets and used vehicles also became more expensive.
The Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% over the 12 months through September, up from 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. Prices increased 0.6% over the month on a seasonally adjusted basis, following a 0.4% rise in August, according to the agency’s September inflation report. 2026 M09 Results
Gasoline prices jumped 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the monthly increase in the overall index. Grocery prices edged lower, with declines in milk, beef and other products, but the cost of eating away from home continued to rise.
Excluding food and energy, prices increased 0.3% for a second consecutive month. Annual inflation in that measure, commonly called core CPI, rose to 2.6% from 2.4% in August.
Gasoline drives the rise in U.S. inflation
Energy prices increased 5.2% in September, more than twice their 2.1% monthly rise in August. Over the preceding 12 months, the energy index climbed 20.4%, driven largely by a 34.2% increase in gasoline prices.
The September gasoline increase followed a 3.9% rise in August. Earlier in the summer, gasoline prices had fallen 9.7% in June and 2.9% in July, according to the BLS monthly series.
Before seasonal adjustment, gasoline prices increased 6.5% in September. BLS adjusts monthly figures to account for recurring seasonal patterns; its annual inflation comparisons use unadjusted prices.
Household utility costs moved less sharply. Electricity prices rose 0.2% in September and were 4.4% higher than a year earlier. Natural gas prices declined 0.3% during the month but remained 5.0% above their September 2025 level.
Shelter and travel costs climb
Shelter prices increased 0.4% in September, following a 0.3% rise in August. Over the year, the shelter index increased 3.2%.
Rent rose 0.2% during the month, while owners’ equivalent rent increased 0.3%. Lodging away from home rose more sharply, increasing 2.0% after a 2.4% gain in August.
Airline fares climbed 1.2% in September and were 22.4% higher than a year earlier, among the largest annual increases identified in the release.
Used cars and trucks rose 0.7% during the month, following a 0.4% increase in August. Despite those monthly gains, their prices remained 1.5% below the level recorded a year earlier. New vehicle prices increased 0.2% in September and 0.6% over the year.
The education index rose 0.6% during September, while recreation increased 0.5% and apparel rose 0.3%. Personal care and motor vehicle insurance also became more expensive.
Grocery prices edge lower
Food prices overall were unchanged in September after increasing 0.1% in each of the previous two months. Grocery prices fell 0.1%, while food away from home rose 0.2%.
Three of the six major grocery categories recorded monthly declines. The meats, poultry, fish and eggs index fell 0.5%, including a 1.0% decline in beef prices. Dairy and related products dropped 0.9%, with milk prices falling 2.0%.
The category covering other food at home declined 0.2%.
Elsewhere in the grocery aisle, nonalcoholic beverages rose 0.9%, including a 1.5% increase in carbonated drinks. Fruits and vegetables increased 0.5%, and cereals and bakery products edged up 0.1%.
Over the year, grocery prices rose 1.8%. Nonalcoholic beverages were 3.8% more expensive, fruits and vegetables rose 3.7%, and cereals and bakery products increased 2.1%. Dairy prices were 0.7% lower.
Eating away from home continued to record a larger annual increase than groceries. Those prices rose 3.5% over the year, with full-service meals increasing 3.8% and limited-service meals rising 3.2%.
Hospital prices rise as prescription drugs fall
Medical care prices increased 0.1% in September after declining 0.2% in August. Within that category, hospital services rose 0.7%, prescription drugs fell 1.2%, and physicians’ services were unchanged.
Over the year, the medical care index increased 1.5%. Education prices rose 3.8%, and recreation prices increased 2.8%.
Communication prices declined 0.2% in September, reversing part of a 2.3% increase in August. Household furnishings and operations were unchanged.
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, a separate measure based on that population’s spending patterns, increased 3.9% over the year. The chained CPI for all urban consumers rose 3.5%; its recent readings remain subject to revision.
BLS is scheduled to release October’s consumer price report on November 10 at 8:30 a.m. Eastern time.

sources.news_title: US consumer inflation rises more than expected in September
sources.text:
The uptick underscores voter worries over high costs of living, and comes as president Donald Trump is campaigning in US states to shore up support for his Republican party as it tries to retain control of Congress.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.7% year-on-year in September, the labour department said, more than the 3.6% analysts forecast according to MarketWatch.
This was a notable acceleration from 3.4% in August, in one of the last major economic reports before the Nov 3 vote.

sources.news_title: Inflation rises to 3.7% last month as prices stay elevated ahead of midterms
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gasoline and many other goods and services became more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before midterm elections that have focused heavily on issues related to affordability.
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month.
The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn't all linked to oil and gas, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month and higher than economists had expected. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed's 2% target.
Higher inflation will likely put more pressure on the Fed to lift its key interest rate at its next meeting Oct. 27-28. Economists noted that the report showed price increases were spread more broadly across the economy than in recent months.
"The report was worse than expected," Bill Adams, chief U.S. economist at Fifth Third Bank, said in a note to clients. "Price increases were widespread ... affecting a range of durable goods, nondurables, and services."
Wednesday's report is the last major inflation data to be released before the upcoming elections. Ongoing inflation has taken a toll on Trump's standing with U.S. voters. A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living issue. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Gas prices jumped 9.1% just from August to September, the government's consumer price index report said. Rising gas costs are a highly visible sign of inflation and often drive down measures of consumer sentiment about the economy.
With fuel much more expensive, air fares rose 1.2% last month and have soared 22% compared with a year ago. Hotel prices rose 2% from August to September and are up 4.4% compared with a year earlier.
Consumers saw some relief in grocery prices, which actually declined 0.1% last month and are up just 1.8% from a year ago. Ground beef prices fell 0.8% in September, though they are still up 5.4% from last year.
The cost of toys, new and used cars, sporting goods, and shoes all rose at a rapid clip last month, the government said.
Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn't moving quickly enough back to the central bank's target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9%.
Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year.
By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war's disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can't address those bottlenecks.
Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It's already pushed up the price of air fares about 22% from a year ago.
Prices at the pump have ticked lower in the past two weeks to a nationwide average of $4.33 a gallon, according to AAA, though they remain higher than a month ago.
Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients.
The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones.
Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed's preferred inflation gauge.
On Sept. 1, Nintendo increased the price for its Switch 2 gaming system by 11% to $499.99. And Apple's newest iPhone, the iPhone 17, cost about 10% more than its previous upgrade, though some of that likely reflects greater capabilities.

US consumer inflation hotter than expected as midterms loom
Washington (United States) (AFP) – US consumer inflation was hotter than anticipated in September, government data showed Wednesday, as Washington's continued war with Tehran pushed energy costs higher, deepening strains on American households ahead of next month's midterm elections.
Issued on: Modified:
The uptick underscores voter worries over high costs of living, and comes as President Donald Trump is campaigning in US states to shore up support for his Republican Party as it tries to retain control of Congress.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.7 percent year-on-year in September, the Department of Labor said, more than the 3.6 percent forecasted by analysts according to MarketWatch.
This was a notable acceleration from 3.4 percent in August, in one of the last major economic reports before the November 3 vote.
Inflation picked up pace on a month-on-month basis too, accelerating from 0.4 percent in August to 0.6 percent last month.
Gasoline costs accounted for more than half of the monthly CPI jump, surging 9.1 percent in September.
The higher-than-expected inflation reading has raised the odds of a second straight interest rate hike at the US central bank's October 27-28 policy meeting, although many expect the Federal Reserve to proceed cautiously.
Economist James Knightley at ING noted that Fed officials John Williams, Philip Jefferson and Christopher Waller have suggested "that we don't need to see back-to-back interest rate increases," instead leaning towards "a slow and steady" approach.
He expects the Fed will want to be "careful and cautious in terms of its policy tightening."
Traders see a 37.1 percent chance that the Fed will raise rates by another 25 basis points in October, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. The probability was around 22 percent a day prior.
"We expect at least two more rate hikes by early 2027, starting in December," said KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk. "September gave the Fed more reason to hike, even if officials hold in October."
Industries sensitive to interest rates, including housing, are already under pressure from steeper borrowing costs.
Yields on US government bonds spiked after the inflation report. The 10-year Treasury yield, which influences rates on mortgage and auto loans, rose to 5.3 percent from 5.2 percent. But it has since moderated.
Spillover
"Energy lit the match; sticky services, shelter and goods prices kept the fire burning," said KPMG's Swonk of the inflation report.
Energy prices have soared since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, prompting Tehran to block off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for oil and gas shipments.

Diesel prices have soared even more, by 67.7 percent, boosting the cost of transporting goods and threatening further spillovers to consumers.
"Again, the Iran-US conflict has led to higher motor fuel costs that everyone is experiencing," ING's Knightley told AFP.
"The US is also seeing substantial increases in airline fares," he said, adding that this will likely contribute to additional price pressures.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was up 2.6 percent from a year ago.
Although high gasoline and diesel prices drove about half of the September spike in inflation, "it's starting to spill into other areas," warned Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union.
"Airfares, used cars and recreation all had big price jumps," she added. "Americans are seeing their pay totally wiped out by inflation. That's been the case for half a year now."

Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients. The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones. Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. On September 1, Nintendo increased the price for its Switch 2 gaming system by 11% to $499.99. And Apple's newest iPhone, the iPhone 17, cost about 10% more than its previous upgrade, though some of that likely reflects greater capabilities. sources.news_title: U.S. inflation rises to 3.7% in September report - The Daily Bo Snerdley
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – U.S. inflation rose 0.6% in September for an annual rate of 3.7%, according to a new report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The September rate marks a significant increase from the overall 3.4% inflation in July and August. The price index for gasoline rose 9.1% in September, accounting more than half of all price increases. The overall energy index rose 5.2% in September after a 2.1% increase in August.
Across the country, states have passed temporary fuel tax suspensions as oil and gas prices continue to rise. Orphe Divounguy, founder and chief economist of Quantitative Research Group and a former Zillow economist, said the suspensions do not substantially change a household’s fuel bill.
The suspensions, in Ohio, North Carolina and Georgia began in October. The delayed timeline means state progress has little effect on September’s report.
“The benefit is a smaller bill than the household would otherwise face; it does not necessarily free up money for other spending,” Divounguy told The Center Square. “Actual relief depends on local prices and how much of the tax cut reaches consumers.”
Annual core inflation increased by 0.3% in September for an increase of 2.6% over the year after August saw a 2.4% increase. Divounguy said rising energy prices continuing to drive up core inflation could be a cause for concern.
“The question is whether higher energy costs keep spreading into other prices, or whether weaker demand forces businesses to absorb more of those costs,” Divounguy said.
Jeffrey Roach, chief economist for LPL Financial, highlighted how energy prices are having a greater effect on other economic indicators. He said the Federal Reserve’s latest interest rate hike will make future decisions more difficult.
“Inflation pressures are broadening beyond energy, suggesting the last mile back to target could remain bumpy and keep interest rates elevated,” Roach said in a statement to The Center Square. “The latest report complicates the Fed’s decision this month, as the road back to price stability is looking increasingly difficult to navigate.”
The September jobs report, released on Oct. 2, showed wage growth slowed to 3%, lower than overall inflation. Divounguy warned of a continued gap between prices and wage growth remaining a persistent problem for American families.
“Households are feeling the pressure,” Divounguy said. “When spending outpaces income, households have less room to save.”
Overall, the energy index rose by 20.4% in the last year. Fuel oil rose by 74.2% over the last year. Food at home saw a decrease of 0.1% in September as it rose 1.8% over the year.
“Families should plan around their actual grocery bills, fuel use, utility rates, rent renewals, insurance premiums and debt payments,” Divounguy told The Center Square. “Their experience depends on what they buy, which can differ considerably from the national average.”

sources.news_title: Inflation worsened last month in sign that prices remain high as midterms near
sources.text:
Prices remain elevated ahead of midterms after inflation reportedly worsened last month
U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes, and air fares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before the midterm elections that have focused heavily on issues related to affordability.
Related video: President Trump heading to Arizona and Montana today to speak with voters ahead of the midterms
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month.
The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but this year has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn't all linked to gas prices, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that also use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed's 2% target.
Ongoing inflation has taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living issue. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn't moving quickly enough back to the central bank's target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9%.
Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year.
By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war's disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can't address those bottlenecks.
Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It's already pushed up the price of air fares about 22% from a year ago.
Gas prices jumped more than 9% from August to September, Wednesday's report said. Rising gas costs are a highly visible sign of inflation and often drive down measures of consumer sentiment about the economy.
Prices at the pump have ticked lower in the past two weeks to a nationwide average of $4.33 a gallon, according to AAA, though they remain higher than a month ago.
Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients.
The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones.
Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed's preferred inflation gauge.
On Sept. 1, Nintendo increased the price for its Switch 2 gaming system by 11% to $499.99. And Apple's newest iPhone, the iPhone 17, cost about 10% more than its previous upgrade, though some of that likely reflects greater capabilities.

Stock Market Today: Stocks Head Lower as Hot Inflation Puts Another Fed Rate Hike Back in Play
A surprise jump in consumer prices just flipped the Fed's playbook for October, and stocks, yields, and rate-hike odds all moved fast. Here is what the morning data means for your portfolio before the opening bell.
The S&P 500 is headed for a lower open because September consumer prices came in higher than forecast. The report pushed Treasury yields up and put another Federal Reserve rate hike back in play for this month. Premarket trading in funds that track the S&P 500 was down 0.3%. Even after a choppy week, the S&P 500 proxy is still up 14% year to date.
Premarket Snapshot Before the Bell
| Index | Latest Reading | Basis | 
|---|---|---|
| S&P 500 | -0.3% | Delayed premarket ETF proxy | 
| Nasdaq Composite | -0.15% to 27,204 | Tuesday close (the Nasdaq-100 proxy is -0.6% premarket) | 
| Dow | -0.2% | Delayed premarket ETF proxy | 
| Russell 2000 | -1.1% | Delayed premarket ETF proxy | 
| VIX | 15.21, up 0.37 | Monday close | 
Hot CPI Revives October Hike Odds
Consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August and above the 3.6% economists expected. Core inflation also came in above forecasts. Most traders had expected the Fed to hold off on its next hike until December. After the report, they raised the odds of a move this month.
That matters because the Fed already lifted its upper target to 4% from 3.75% in September. The 10-year yield, which closed Tuesday at 5.2%, rose this morning. Higher yields hit small caps hardest because many of those companies carry floating-rate debt. That helps explain why the Russell 2000 proxy is down 5% over the past month.
Banks and Memory Chips Move Stocks
Bank of America (NYSE:BAC | BAC Price Prediction) fell before the open after its profit disappointed, even excluding a $1.2 billion fine. BlackRock (NYSE:BLK) rose after reporting record assets.
Chipmakers are still weighing on tech. Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) lost 3.6% Tuesday on reports of technology advances at Chinese memory maker CXMT. The PHLX chip index has fallen more than 8% in five sessions, and memory stocks extended their declines this morning.
What the Inflation Report Means for Your Portfolio
Analysts expect S&P 500 third-quarter earnings to rise over 30%. Those strong expectations have pulled the index’s forward valuation below 19 times expected earnings, the lowest since 2023. Today’s CPI report tests whether that earnings growth can outrun rising rates. The rally is also narrow: the median S&P 500 stock is up less than 5% this year. For index investors, a few AI names are carrying most of your gains (we highlighted seven of the lesser-known suppliers powering that expansion, from power to cooling, in a free report you can grab here).
Wall Street’s fear gauge, the VIX, measures how much volatility options traders expect from the S&P 500. Near 15, it sits in its normal range, so traders are pricing in caution.

Over the next few days, watch the Fed’s October decision, which is now in doubt, and how bank and chip stocks trade as more earnings come.

sources.news_title: Inflation accelerates to 3.7% in final consumer price report before midterm elections
US inflation jumps to 3.7% in September as Iran war drives gasoline prices higher
sources.text:
US consumer inflation was hotter than anticipated in September, government data showed Wednesday, as Washington's war with Tehran pushed energy costs higher, deepening strains on American households ahead of next month's midterm elections.
The uptick underscores voter worries over high costs of living, and comes as President Donald Trump is campaigning in US states to shore up support for his Republican party as it tries to retain control of Congress.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.7 percent year-on-year in September, the Department of Labor said, more than the 3.6 percent analysts forecast according to MarketWatch.
This was a notable acceleration from 3.4 percent in August, in one of the last major economic reports before the November 3 vote.
Inflation picked up pace on a month-on-month basis too, accelerating from 0.4 percent in August to 0.6 percent last month.
The higher-than-expected reading has left analysts divided over the odds of a second straight interest rate hike at the US central bank's upcoming October 27-28 policy meeting.
Economist James Knightley at ING noted that Federal Reserve officials John Williams, Philip Jefferson and Christopher Waller have suggested "that we don't need to see back-to-back interest rate increases," instead leaning towards "a slow and steady" approach.
He expects the Fed will want to be "careful and cautious in terms of its policy tightening."
But traders now see a 51.5 percent chance that the Fed will raise rates by another 25 basis points in October, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. The probability was around 22 percent a day prior.
Already, industries sensitive to interest rates, like housing, are under pressure from steeper borrowing costs.
Yields on US government bonds spiked after the inflation report. The 10-year Treasury yield, which influences rates on mortgage and auto loans, rose to 5.3 percent from 5.2 percent.
- Spillovers -
Gasoline costs accounted for more than half of the monthly CPI jump, surging 9.1 percent in September, Wednesday's report said.
Energy prices have soared since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, prompting Tehran to block off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for oil and gas shipments.
Average prices at US gasoline pumps have surged more than 45 percent since the start of the Middle East war to $4.33 per gallon, according to AAA motor club data.
Diesel prices have soared even more, by 67.7 percent, boosting the cost of transporting goods and threatening further spillovers to consumers.
"Again, the Iran-US conflict has led to higher motor fuel costs that everyone is experiencing," ING's Knightley told AFP.
"The US is also seeing substantial increases in airline fares," he said, adding that this will likely contribute to additional price pressures.
Excluding volatile food and energy prices, core CPI was up 2.6 percent from a year ago.
Although high gasoline and diesel prices drove about half of the September spike in inflation, "it's starting to spill into other areas," warned Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union.
"Airfares, used cars and recreation all had big price jumps," she added. "Americans are seeing their pay totally wiped out by inflation. That's been the case for half a year now."
Long expects that another interest rate hike will be needed, likely in December.
With the underlying US economy remaining strong as massive spending linked to the artificial intelligence buildout boosts demand for chips and labor, economists also caution that higher costs could continue filtering through to households.
