sources.news_title: Live Coverage of US CPI Report for September
US inflation rises to 3.7% as fuel costs climb ahead of midterms
sources.text:
Higher petrol prices and airfares pushed US inflation to 3.7% in September, adding pressure on households and the Federal Reserve weeks before the midterm elections.
US inflation accelerated last month as petrol, clothing and airfares became more expensive, adding pressure on households just a few weeks before the midterm elections.
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year earlier, the US Department of Labor said on Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices jumped 0.6%, up from 0.4% the previous month.
The annual figure was above the 3.6% forecast by economists surveyed by data provider FactSet.
The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on petrol prices and the persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but has risen since the war began in late February.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% from a year earlier, up from 2.4% in August. Monthly core inflation held at 0.3%.
“CPI came in at 3.7%, slightly above expectations, and similarly core inflation was above predictions, suggesting that prices are feeding into the wider economy,” said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot.
Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and complicated the Federal Reserve’s efforts to bring price rises under control.
A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of US adults approve of President Donald Trump’s handling of the cost of living. Only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Markets react: Will the Fed raise rates again?
Following the higher-than-expected inflation figures, major US stock indices turned negative. Gold fell more than 1.7% to $4,105.50 an ounce, while silver was down more than 4% at $56.91 an ounce.
Oil prices were mixed, with international benchmark Brent trading just above $105.70 a barrel, close to its opening level. US benchmark WTI rose 1.4% to $95.50 a barrel.
Bond yields jumped following the news. The policy-sensitive two-year US Treasury yield rose 13 basis points to 4.93%, as traders increased bets on further Fed rate rises. The benchmark 10-year yield climbed about eight basis points to around 5.3%.
Inflation moving further away from the Federal Reserve’s 2% target was the “last thing” global bond markets needed, according to Robin Brooks, a former Goldman Sachs economist and a senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution.
Carter warned that persistent inflation could push US government borrowing costs higher. “It is not inconceivable that ten-year Treasury yields continue to march higher,” he said.
The figures add pressure on the Fed as it weighs whether to raise rates again at its next meeting on 27–28 October.
Last month, the central bank raised rates for the first time in three years, to a range of 3.75%–4%. Fed chair Kevin Warsh said inflation was not falling quickly enough towards its target.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said at a news conference last month. He added that summer inflation reports “do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved”.
Some Fed officials have since suggested they can wait before raising rates again, although their latest projections point to one more increase this year.
Higher borrowing costs can slow spending and growth, helping to ease inflation. But they cannot resolve supply disruptions such as those caused by the Iran war, leaving the Fed trying to prevent higher energy costs from feeding into broader price rises.
Higher fuel costs feed through to other prices
Warsh has said his goal is to keep the petrol price spike from spreading to other areas of the economy. Higher fuel costs have already helped push airfares up by about 23% from a year ago.
Petrol prices jumped about 9% from August to September, driving much of the overall increase in inflation.
Prices at the pump have eased in recent weeks, though they remain higher than a month ago. Petrol averaged $4.34 a gallon nationwide on Tuesday, up a few cents from a month earlier.
Higher fuel prices also raise shipping costs for businesses, some of which pass those costs on to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said it would raise prices for some snacks and soft drinks to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminium and food ingredients.
The expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure has also sharply increased the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment and electrical components, feeding through to prices for consumer electronics such as gaming devices, laptops and smartphones.

sources.news_title: Trump's midterm nightmare deepens as inflation surges
Annual Inflation Rate Hits 3.7% After Consumer Prices Rose 0.6% In ...
U.S. consumer prices rise by most since April in broad advance
sources.text:
By Jeffrey Sparshott
(Bloomberg) — U.S. consumer prices advanced in September at the fastest pace in five months and a gauge of underlying price pressures rose by more than expected, keeping the squeeze on household budgets ahead of November’s midterm elections.
The consumer price index rose 0.6% from a month earlier, driven by a surge in fuel costs, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data out Wednesday. A key measure of underlying price pressures, which excludes food and energy, was up 0.3%.
The report suggests the economy — and in particular, price increases that are eroding paycheques — will remain front and centre for voters in the final stretch of midterm campaigns. The broad upswing in prices also helps reinforce expectations for additional Federal Reserve interest-rate increases in the months ahead, even if the central bank elects to take a pause at its upcoming policy meeting.
“Americans are seeing their pay totally wiped out by inflation,” Heather Long, the chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said in a note. “Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve isn’t seeing progress on inflation,” and rising fuel prices are “starting to spill into other areas.”
U.S. Treasury yields rose and the S&P 500 opened lower after the release as investors upped bets on an October rate hike to about 50%.
The Fed in September responded to renewed price pressures by raising interest rates for the first time since 2023. Since then, top officials have signalled they have time to weigh incoming data before acting again, though the median forecast of officials lined up with one more increase this year, according to their latest projections.
Wednesday’s report, which showed the CPI advanced 3.7% from a year earlier and core CPI rose 2.6%, is the last reading on consumer prices before the central bank’s Oct. 27-28 policy meeting. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is due to speak late Thursday New York time from the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok.
Surveys show U.S. households have become increasingly frustrated with worsening affordability problems as price increases have outpaced wage growth. A separate report on Wednesday showed that average hourly earnings, adjusted for inflation, fell in September from a year earlier for a sixth consecutive month.
The CPI data showed gasoline, a daily price gauge for many, climbed 9.1% in September from the prior month — the most since the outbreak of the Iran war sent fuel prices surging in March. Medical care services prices, meanwhile, rose 0.3%. Healthcare costs and gas prices tied as voters’ top economic concern ahead of the midterm elections, according to a KFF poll released this month.
Owners’ equivalent rent, a gauge of housing costs which is the largest component of the CPI, continued to climb, advancing 0.3% from the prior month. Grocery prices, however, edged lower, and prescription drug prices also fell.
Broader services prices excluding energy and rents registered a steep advance for a second month. Core goods prices rose by the most since January 2025, reflecting solid increases for used cars and apparel as well as a record jump for toys.
“Obviously we knew there was going to be a spike in energy and fuel prices, but the firm readings for core CPI — which follows up a firmer reading on core CPI in August — those give us concerns that maybe we are seeing more pass-through from fuel prices into other goods and services,” said Ben Ayers, a senior economist at Nationwide.
The report also highlighted ongoing pressures from the data centre buildout: Computer software and accessories prices rose a record 28.4% from a year earlier, while prices of computers, peripherals and smart home assistants rose a record 9.7%.
What Bloomberg Economics Says…
“The surprising acceleration in September core CPI may appear to cement another Federal Reserve interest-rate hike this year, but the source of the pressure pushes against such certainty. The owners’ equivalent rent component printed hot despite a cool housing market most of the year, suggesting a potential aberration.”
— Anna Wong and Troy Durie
The economy is a key topic of debate for candidates in upcoming midterm elections. The unemployment rate is low, consumer spending remains strong and business investment is adding fuel to economic growth. But many voters blame President Donald Trump’s tariffs and the Iran conflict for the rising cost of living.
At the beginning of the year, inflation had settled back toward its lowest levels since early 2021. But the war sent gasoline, diesel and other prices soaring, boosting inflation and ultimately borrowing costs.
Diesel prices can be hard to isolate in the CPI. Higher fuel costs tend to first affect transportation services and later move through to food, durable goods such as furniture, and other products that have higher freight costs, though the effect can be lagged.
Separately, the Social Security Administration said Wednesday that beneficiaries would receive a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment in 2027, the most in four years. The adjustment is calculated using CPI data from the third quarter.

sources.news_title: Inflation rose in September, crucial pre-election report shows
sources.text:
Inflation accelerated in September as gas and energy prices, driven higher by the war in Iran, continued to squeeze household budgets, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday.
The report lands at a critical moment, two weeks before the Federal Reserve’s next interest rate decision and less than three weeks before the midterm elections in which affordability has been a central issue.

Consumer prices rose 0.6% from August to September and 3.7% from a year earlier. That compares with 0.4% monthly increase and 3.4% annual inflation rate in August. The latest figures were slightly higher than economists’ expectations.
Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, rose 0.3% last month, the same as the month prior, and rose 2.6% from a year earlier.
Gasoline shot up 9.1% in September, accounting for over half of the monthly all items increase, and the energy index increased 5.2% over the month. Grocery prices fell 0.1% in September.
“Inflation is uncomfortably high,” said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. With inflation now outpacing wage growth, he told Straight Arrow, it is “undermining families’ purchasing power.”
Core inflation, added Oliver Allen, a senior U.S. economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, was “too hot for comfort.” Allen told Straight Arrow that higher energy costs are “now clearly feeding through” to prices for goods and services.
Cost of living is key election issue
Wednesday’s report is the last Consumer Price Index reading before the Nov. 3 midterms, when voters will decide which party controls Congress. For many voters, cost of living will be top of mind when they head to the polls.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in late August found that 47% of registered voters said the cost of living would be the single most important factor in deciding their 2026 midterm votes.
A separate survey from the Pew Research Center released earlier this month found that 74% of Americans were very concerned about gas and energy prices, while 73% said the same about food and consumer goods. Concern was widespread across the political spectrum, though Democrats expressed more concern than Republicans.
Americans may share their frustration with rising prices, but they are divided over which party they believe can fix the problem.
An AP/ NORC poll published earlier this month found that 38% of voters said they trust the Democratic Party to handle the cost of living, while 27% said they trust the Republican Party on this issue.
Another 27% said they trust neither party to do a good job handling.
The majority of voters, however, blamed President Donald Trump for high costs more than factors outside of his control. A separate AP/NORC poll found that 65% of U.S. adults said higher-than-usual prices are the result of Trump’s policies, while only 17% approved of Trump’s handling of the cost of living.
Will the Fed hike rates?
Wednesday’s slightly hotter-than-expected reading could strengthen the case for the Fed to raise its benchmark interest rate when policymakers announce their next decision on Oct. 28.
Higher interest rates can help cool inflation by slowing borrowing and spending. But Zandi said that rate hikes cannot address the main drivers of the recent surge in prices. The “proximate cause” of higher inflation, he said, is the fallout from the Iran war on energy markets and global shipping, which is “not something the Fed can fix.”
Still, Zandi said “the Fed is worried that the higher inflation will become more entrenched,” and he predicted that policymakers will raise rates at their final meeting of the year in December. Allen and his team now expect the same, reversing their previous forecast that the Fed would hold rates steady through year-end.
In September, the central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%, its first rate increase in three years.
Although Wednesday’s Consumer Price Index is a widely followed measure of inflation, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge is the personal consumption expenditures price index, known as the PCE.
By that measure, prices rose 3.4% in August from a year earlier. The increase was less than economists expected, reducing market expectations that the Fed would raise rates again in October.
Core PCE, which strips out food and energy prices and is closely watched for signs of underlying inflation, rose 3% from a year earlier.
The next PCE report is scheduled for release on Oct. 29, one day after the Fed’s next rate decision.

sources.text:
Inflation heats up to 3.7% in September — more than expected amid soaring energy costs
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Inflation heated up in September at a faster pace than expected amid rising energy costs – putting an October interest-rate hike back on the table less than a month away from the midterm elections.
The Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% over the past 12 months, heating up from 3.4% the previous month and above expectations of a 3.6% rise, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said Wednesday. It rose at a 0.6% pace over the month.
Core CPI – which excludes volatile food and energy prices, giving a better look at underlying inflation – also heated up to 2.6%, above 2.4% in August and higher than estimates of a 2.5% rise.
Rising energy costs amid the war in Iran largely drove the inflation reading. Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% in September – 34.2% higher over the past year – and accounted for more than half of the overall inflation reading.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq tumbled 1.1% and 1.9%, respectively, and long-term US Treasury yields jumped higher as traders feared another interest-rate hike this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished with a small loss.
The Fed has been squarely focused on tackling inflation and hinted at a second rate hike this year. But it was expected to hold off until December to avoid appearing politicized by raising rates during the election cycle.
“The pass-through of higher energy costs into other ‘core’ items may be occurring more rapidly than previously thought,” Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21shares, wrote in a note Wednesday.
“[Federal Reserve Chair Kevin] Warsh will have an important opportunity tomorrow, should he consider it necessary, to prepare investors for a possible rate hike at the next meeting when he makes his final public appearance at the IMF meeting ahead of the Fed blackout window.”
Traders priced in a coin toss between a rate hike and holding rates steady at the October meeting – far higher odds than immediately before the report, when there was a 78% chance the Fed would hold rates steady, according to CME FedWatch.
Fuel oil jumped 15.3% in September, up 74.2% over the past 12 months – an ominous sign as Americans brace for the winter season, since the pricier fuel is used to heat homes.
President Trump has unveiled several efforts aimed at boosting diesel and crude oil supplies, though experts have warned they could have little impact on prices.
In the meantime, analysts pointed to signs that higher energy prices are starting to bleed into other sectors.
Transportation costs, for example, rose 0.6% in September, a faster pace than the previous month.
Higher diesel costs can also easily bleed into grocery and apparel prices, since the fuel is used for heavy trucks that transport goods cross-country.
Food at home declined 0.1% in September, though it’s up 1.8% on an annual basis, while food away from home ticked up 0.2%, up 3.5% over the year. Fast-food chains in particular have been struggling to hold onto low-income diners as their costs soar.
New vehicles rose 0.2% in September while used cars and trucks increased 0.7%, though the latter is down 1.5% over the year.
Airline fares – another category closely tied to energy, since jet fuel accounts for the bulk of carriers’ operating costs – jumped 2% in September.
Shelter costs rose 0.4% in September after rising 0.3% in August.

sources.news_title: US inflation rises more than expected ahead of midterm elections
sources.text:
US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
- Published
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.
The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.
Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher petrol prices, which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.
The elections are being fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US.
What is inflation?
Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.
Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).
It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.
The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.
What causes inflation?
There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.
If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.
Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.
Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.
Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.
What is the current rate of inflation?
Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices.
Vehicle fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.
In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.
Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher.
At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year.
Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.
Will the inflation hike change Social Security payments?
Shortly after the latest inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.
The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.
The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.
How have tariffs affected inflation?
Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.
While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.
Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.
In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.
Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.
Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.
Has inflation been worse lately?
While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years.
During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.
Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.
Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.
Can inflation ever go down?
It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.
A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.
Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.
Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

Inflation worsens to 3.7% in sign that prices remain elevated
Gas, clothes and airfares got more expensive in September
Associated Press
Key Takeaways:
- U.S. inflation accelerated in September, with consumer prices rising 3.7% from a year earlier and 0.6% from August.
- Higher gasoline, clothing and airfare costs contributed as inflation persisted despite falling sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022.
- Core prices rose 2.6% annually and 0.3% monthly, posing an ongoing challenge for the Federal Reserve.
WASHINGTON — U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes, and airfares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before the midterm elections that have focused heavily on issues related to affordability.
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Oct. 14, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month.
The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but this year has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn't all linked to gas prices, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that also use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed's 2% target.
Ongoing inflation has taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living issue. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much.

The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year.
By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war's disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can't address those bottlenecks.
Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It's already pushed up the price of airfares about 22% from a year ago.

Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones.

sources.news_title: US consumer prices accelerate in September
sources.text:
US consumer prices accelerated in September amid a surge in gasoline costs, dealing another blow to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November 3 midterm elections and putting an interest rate increase later this month back on the radar.
The US Consumer Price Index rose 0.6% last month after climbing 0.4% in August, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said today.
In the 12 months to September, the CPI advanced 3.7% after rising 3.4% in August.
Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI would gain 0.6% over the month and increase 3.6% on a year-over-year basis. Gasoline prices soared 7.1% in September, data from the US Energy Information Administration showed.
The report followed surveys this month showing a further deterioration in consumer sentiment and a plunge in Trump's approval rating, driven by angst over the rising cost of living.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed about 78% of Americans blamed Trump's policies, including tariffs on imports and the US-Israeli war with Iran, for rising prices, which are outpacing wages.
Underlying inflation picks up
Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI gained 0.3% in September, matching the gain in August.
In the 12 months to September, core CPI inflation increased 2.6% after advancing 2.4% in August.
The US Fed tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index for its 2% inflation target. The core CPI measure is lagging core PCE inflation, which increased 3% in August, because of the different weights assigned to the components in the baskets.
The Fed last month raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4% range, the first hike in three years, and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead.
Before today's figures, financial markets assigned a roughly 22% chance of a rate hike at the October 27-28 policy meeting, CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed.
The odds of a rate increase this month diminished following underwhelming payroll gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE inflation readings for July and August. Economists had expected the Fed to raise rates in December.

sources.news_title: US inflation jumps more than expected to 3.7% in September
sources.text:
U.S. consumer inflation jumped more than expected in September, government data showed Wednesday, as the U.S. war with Iran continued to push energy costs higher, deepening strains on American households ahead of next month's midterm elections.
The uptick underscores voter worries over high costs of living, and comes as President Donald Trump is campaigning in U.S. states to shore up support for his Republican party as it tries to retain control of Congress.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.7% year-over-year in September, the Department of Labor said, more than the 3.6% analysts forecast according to MarketWatch.
This was a notable acceleration from 3.4% in August, in one of the last major economic reports before the Nov. 3 vote.
Inflation picked up pace on a month-over-month basis too, accelerating from 0.4% in August to 0.6% last month.
Gasoline costs accounted for more than half of the jump, surging 9.1% on a monthly basis, Wednesday's report said.
Energy prices have jumped since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February, prompting Tehran to block off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for oil and gas shipments.
Average prices at U.S. gasoline pumps have surged more than 45% since the Middle East war to $4.33 per gallon, according to AAA data.
Diesel prices have surged even more, by 67.7%, boosting the cost of transporting goods and threatening further spillovers to consumers.
"Again, the Iran-U.S. conflict has led to higher motor fuel costs that everyone is experiencing," ING economist James Knightley told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
"The U.S. is also seeing substantial increases in airline fares," he said, adding that this will likely contribute to additional price pressures.
With the underlying U.S. economy remaining strong as massive spending linked to the artificial intelligence sector boosts demand for chips and labor, economists warn that higher costs could continue filtering through to households.
Excluding volatile food and energy prices, core CPI was up 2.6% from a year ago.
But Knightley does not expect the latest report to prompt the Federal Reserve (Fed) to raise interest rates at its Oct. 27-28 meeting.
Several Fed policymakers have suggested "that we don't need to see back-to-back interest rate increases," he said, instead leaning towards "a slow and steady" approach.
Industries sensitive to interest rates, like housing, are already under pressure from steeper borrowing costs.
"I think the Federal Reserve just wants to be a little bit careful and cautious in terms of its policy tightening," Knightley said.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump Suffers Inflation Nightmare Just Weeks Before Midterms
sources.text:
The final inflation report voters will see before the 2026 midterms showed prices rose even faster than expected in September, another blow for President Donald Trump and Republicans as they face significant headwinds in an election focused heavily on affordability.
According to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Wednesday morning, consumer prices rose 0.6 percent in September, compared to 0.4 percent the month prior. On an annual basis, headline inflation accelerated to 3.7 percent from 3.4 percent.
The 12-month rate came in slightly faster than analyst forecasts of 3.6 percent and, outside of May and April, reached its highest level since September 2023.
Core inflation—which strips out the more volatile food and energy categories—came in at 0.3 percent and 2.6 percent on a monthly and annual basis, respectively. This compares with 0.3 percent and 2.4 percent in August, and forecasts of 0.2 percent and 2.5 percent.
The White House has blamed rising prices on the previous administration, with National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett telling Fox News this week that voters’ economic frustrations should be directed at “the runaway inflation that Joe Biden gave us.” The administration has also argued that increased fuel prices driven by the Iran war will fall quickly at the end of the conflict.
Speaking to reporters after his Arizona midterm rally Wednesday, Trump responded to the latest inflation figures by saying, “We’re doing great,” and argued that his administration had inherited high inflation from former President Joe Biden. He also predicted the Iran war would “end very shortly,” saying energy prices would then “fall very rapidly, very fast.”
Why This Report Mattered
The next CPI will be released on November 10, making Wednesday’s reading the final one ahead of the November 3 midterms. Polls indicate that Election Day will be heavily influenced by voters’ views of the economy.
Some 37 percent of respondents told Economist/YouGov pollsters that inflation was their top issue in this year’s elections, beating all other choices and marking the highest share for rising prices since tracking began in 2022. In the survey of 1,381 registered voters conducted October 2 to 5, jobs and the economy came in second at 12 percent, followed by health care (8 percent) and immigration (7 percent).
Surveyed voters have routinely picked soaring prices as their top election issue, a concerning signal for the administration and Trump’s party given their downbeat feelings about the topic.
The University of Michigan’s latest consumer sentiment index showed that assessments of current economic conditions slipped to a record low of 44.7 in October from 50.9 in September.
Just 21 percent of those polled by Pew Research Center between September 28 and October 4 rated the economy as either excellent or good, with 37 percent describing conditions as fair and 42 percent as “poor.” Nearly three-quarters (73 percent) said they were “very concerned” about the price of food and other consumer goods, and that number rose to 74 percent for the cost of gasoline and energy.
An AP-NORC poll of 2,140 adults, fielded September 24 to 28, found that 65 percent blamed stubborn inflation on Trump, with 26 percent approving of his broader economic stewardship and only 17 percent of his approach to the cost of living.
This level of blame for higher costs rises to 78 percent in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll of 4,506 American adults. Sixty-eight percent of respondents said they were dissatisfied with Trump’s handling of inflation, and 57 percent of polled Republicans said prices were rising faster than their wages.
Beyond electoral implications, Wednesday’s report will also be the final CPI reading used to determine next year's Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA). Recent surveys show that seniors, in particular, worry these increases will fall short of helping with rising costs. An AARP survey found that 76 percent of Americans aged 50 and over think a 3.5 percent increase for 2027 would fail to meaningfully address growing affordability challenges.
Economists also believe faster inflation could increase the odds that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates again. In September, the central bank’s policymaking committee increased rates for the first time since 2023 amid what officials described as "elevated" inflation and uncertainty.
While the Trump administration is pushing for lower rates to boost economic activity, the CME FedWatch tool shows the odds of another 25-basis-point hike at the October 28 meeting have doubled to 44 percent after Wednesday’s reading.
“Not a good CPI number,” Robin Brooks, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, posted on X. “Last month it was wireless services that spiked core inflation and were a reasonable excuse for the Fed to pause later this month. But today's reading puts an October hike back on the table. If the Fed doesn't hike, debasement wins.”
What Was in the Report?
According to the BLS, energy was once again a leading driver of gains. The index rose 5.2 percent in September—with gasoline up 9.1 percent—and accounted for more than half of last month's overall gains. The energy index is up 20.4 percent from the same month in 2025, largely driven by the war in Iran and related supply issues.
While down from their recent peak of around $4.50 per gallon, U.S. gas prices broke a separate record this week. According to AAA, the average cost has stayed above $4 for now 158 days, surpassing the previous record set in 2022 under then-President Joe Biden.
Beyond gas, fuel oil rose 15.3 percent in September and is up 74.2 percent over the previous 12 months, while airline fares rose 22.4 percent over the same period, both contributing to the 3.7 percent annual rate.
This headline figure is now comfortably higher than the 3 percent wage growth recorded in the BLS’s recent employment report, meaning that rising prices have outpaced Americans’ pay increases on average over the past year.

sources.news_title: Inflation jumps to 3.7% as gas and diesel prices squeeze consumers ahead of the midterms
sources.text:
Prices rose across broad swaths of the U.S. economy in September as high energy costs triggered by the Iran war pushed up prices in many major consumer categories.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics said Wednesday that overall prices rose 3.7% from a year ago and 0.6% from August. Categories including housing, clothing, and restaurant and takeout food all saw price increases. Only three major categories saw price declines: groceries, medical care commodities and utility gas service.
“The index for gasoline rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for over half of the monthly all items increase,” the BLS wrote in its report.
The report adds to ongoing concerns that persistent inflation is taking a toll on consumers, particularly as wage growth has been stagnant. As of September, the growth in wages was pacing at 3% on an annual basis. Paychecks have not grown faster than inflation since March.
The overall increase was slightly more than had been expected by economists polled by Dow Jones, who forecast a jump to 3.6%.
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, also rose to 2.6% from a year ago, or 0.3% from August. This was also slightly more than had been expected.
Wednesday’s number is the final inflation report before November’s pivotal midterm elections, in which business owners and consumers have said they will be voting with their bottom line in mind.
“This was a disappointing number,” Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, said on Fox Business. Still, he maintained that “a lot of Trump policies are helping to keep inflation down.”
Since August, oil prices have risen to more than $106 per barrel from about $80. The price of unleaded gas, which most consumers use, has risen 45% since late February, when the United States and Israel launched the Iran war. The price of diesel, which powers businesses, farms, the shipping industry and other critical sectors, has soared 70% over the same period.
As early voting kicks off this week, the data also comes at a precarious moment for Republicans defending majorities in the House and the Senate. Polls consistently find that inflation and the high cost of living are top issues this year for voters in both parties.
Stocks fell sharply Wednesday. Before the data, market odds showed that traders had expected the Federal Reserve to wait until December to raise rates. After the data, odds rose above 55% for an October hike.
The Nasdaq Composite closed down 1.8%, and the S&P 500 tumbled 1.1%. The Russell 2000 index, which tracks small and medium-size companies, slid 1.9%. The stocks that sold off the most were interest rate sensitive, such as those in the technology and industrial sectors, which are involved in the ever-expanding AI data center build-out.

The artificial intelligence boom also reared its head last month, as categories that track the price of computers, software and accessories posted record year-over-year price increases.
Ahead of Wednesday’s report, economists had been watching recent price hikes on Apple products and whether they have an impact on the overall inflation figure. The smartphone category rose 0.4% month over month.
Airline fares were also being closely watched, given soaring jet fuel costs. Prices in that category rose 0.2% from August, posting their smallest increase since June.
Despite elevated prices and consumers who say they are being stretched to the limit, data shows that spending has remained strong.

“While much has been made of the AI boom, the consumer is still driving much” of the economy’s momentum, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser said Tuesday.

sources.news_title: Consumer Prices Rise Sharply
sources.text:
Consumer prices rose sharply in September.
The consumer price index rose 0.6 percent in September compared with August, driven higher by rising gasoline prices, the Labor Department said Wednesday. Over the year, the consumer price index is up 3.7 percent.
Core prices, a measure that excludes food and energy prices, rose 0.3 percent in September. Compared with a year ago, core prices are up 2.6 percent. That is a decline in year-over-year core inflation from last month’s 2.5 percent.
Economists had forecast CPI would increase by 0.6 percent from the prior month and 3.7 percent from a year ago. Core prices were expected to rise 0.2 percent for the month and 5.2 percent over the past 12 months.
Gas prices rose 9.1 percent in September, which the Labor Department said accounted for over half of the monthly headline increase. The energy index increased 5.2 percent over the month following a 2.1-percent increase in August. For the year, energy prices are up 20.4 percent.
There was some good news for consumers in the grocery aisle. The index for food at home fell 0.1 percent. Prices for dining out rose 0.2 percent.
Electricity prices rose 0.2 percent in September after falling 0.2 percent in August. This follows a 0.1 percent increase in July and a 1.0 percent decline in June. For the year, electricity is 4.4 percent higher.
Apparel prices rose 0.3 percent in September after being flat in August, rising 0.1 percent in July, and falling 0.6 percent in June. For the year, clothing prices are up 3.4 percent.
Shelter prices rose 0.4 percent in September after rising 0.3 percent in August, bringing the yearly gain to 3.2 percent. Rents rose 0.2 percent. Hotel and motel prices jumped 2.0 percent in September after a 2.4 percent rise in August.
Medical care services prices rose 0.3 percent and are up 2.5 percent from a year ago. Medical care goods fell 0.7 percent. These are down 3.3 percent from a year ago. Prescription drug prices declined 1.2 percent for the month after being flat the previous month. They are down 4.5 percent from a year ago. Non-prescription drug prices rose 1.3 percent after falling 1.0 percent the previous month. For the year, they have fallen by 0.9 percent.
Prices of major appliances were unchanged in September after jumping 1.4 percent in August. Compared with a year ago, major appliance prices are down 2.3 percent. Furniture prices fell by 0.8 percent in September after falling 0.9 percent in August. They are down 2.4 percent from a year ago.
Prices of new cars and trucks rose 0.2 percent compared with August. Compared with a year ago, they are up 0.6 percent. Used car and truck prices climbed 0.7 percent after rising 0.4 percent the previous month. Compared with September of last year, however, they are down 1.5 percent.

sources.news_title: September 2026 CPI: Gasoline prices surge 9.1% in a month
sources.text:
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.6% on a seasonally adjusted basis in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday, driven largely by a surge in gasoline prices that pushed the annual inflation rate to 3.7%.
Gas prices climbed 9.1% in September, accounting for more than half of the overall monthly increase in consumer prices and driving the annual inflation rate to 3.7%
Gasoline prices climbed 9.1% over the month, accounting for more than half of the overall monthly increase, according to the BLS. Over the past 12 months, gasoline is up 34.2%. September's energy index advanced 5.2%, following a 2.1% increase in August, and has climbed 20.4% compared with a year earlier.
The all-items index rose 3.7% for the 12 months ending in September, up from the 3.4% annual rate reported for August.
Core CPI, which strips out food and energy, came in at 0.3% for September and 2.6% year over year — both figures topping the 0.2% monthly and 2.5% annual readings economists had forecast, according to the Wall Street Journal and CNBC.
Food prices were unchanged in September after rising 0.1% in each of the two preceding months, the BLS said. The food-at-home index slipped 0.1%, pulled down by lower prices for meats, poultry, fish, and eggs, along with dairy and related products. The food-away-from-home index rose 0.2% for the month and is up 3.5% over the past year.
Within the core index, the shelter index increased 0.4%, owners' equivalent rent rose 0.3%, and rent increased 0.2%. The used cars and trucks index gained 0.7%, airline fares rose 1.2%, and the recreation index climbed 0.5%. The communication index declined 0.2%.
Stock futures fell into negative territory following the release, while Treasury yields moved higher.
At its September meeting, the Federal Reserve under Chairman Kevin Warsh approved an interest rate increase — its first in over three years — bringing the target range for the benchmark funds rate to 3.75%–4%, according to CNBC. The majority of policymakers at that gathering signaled they expected a single additional rate hike before year's end. The central bank's next scheduled meeting falls on Oct. 27–28, and market participants broadly anticipate no action at that gathering, with a possible increase coming in December, according to CNBC.
The BLS noted that data for October and November 2025 are unavailable due to a lapse in appropriations that year. The next CPI release, covering October 2026, is scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026.

sources.news_title: Prices increased sharply in September in last inflation report ahead of elections
Inflation was hotter than expected in September, rising to 3.7%
sources.text:
It’s not just gas.
It’s the car repair, the doctor’s visit, the plane ticket, the computer upgrade, the new clothes.
Inflation rose faster than expected last month, and more broadly than expected, with price pressures extending well beyond the pump, new Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed Wednesday.
The latest Consumer Price Index showed that prices rose 0.6% in September from the month before, bringing the annual rate of inflation to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in August and above economists’ expectations for a 3.6% increase.
A closely watched gauge of underlying inflation also ran hot last month: Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% from August and 2.6% from a year earlier (economists were expecting increases of 0.2% and 2.5%, respectively).
Inflation is moving uncomfortably higher, further eroding Americans’ pay gains, compounding affordability concerns, and keeping the economy – and the Trump administration’s handling of it – in focus for voters in advance of the midterm elections.
“We’re in a world now of inflation at 3.7% and wage gains for the typical American at 3%; that’s a big gap,” said Heather Long, chief economist for Navy Federal Credit Union. “The inflation pressures are in quite a few areas, and it’s tricky to cut back. The anger about the economy that many Americans feel has justification.”
‘A greater desire by businesses to pass on higher costs’
The Iran war’s energy shock continues to ripple through the economy. Gas prices, which rose 9.1% in September, accounted for more than half of the monthly increase, according to Wednesday’s report.
“You see the energy crisis causing used car prices to rise, and airfare prices to rise, and recreation costs to rise; and on top of that, you’ve got medical care and apparel also rising,” Long said. “So, it’s this more broad-based problem than just a gas price spike.”
The price increases across various categories outside of food and energy were the most concerning aspects of Wednesday’s report, said Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon.
Core goods prices rose at the fastest rate since January 2025, he said. And some categories’ monthly price increases stretched back even further: The 1.1% increase in men’s boy’s apparel prices was the highest since April 2024, and the 4.2% hike in toy prices was the highest on record, BLS data shows.
“They don’t necessarily appear to be tariff-driven,” he said. “What appears to be driving some of these core price pressures is perhaps a greater desire by businesses to pass on higher costs.”
Wednesday’s report also continued to show the fingerprints of massive AI-related infrastructure spending. Computer software and hardware prices are rising at their fastest-ever annual rates.
Housing-related inflation, which is captured in the amorphous and weighty “shelter” category, rose 0.4% from August, the fastest rate in five months, BLS data shows. Rents also rose at a five-month-high rate of 0.4%, a likely side effect of a US housing market frozen by affordability issues and 7.5% mortgage rates, Long said.
However, some of the sharpest increases in the category were seen in lodging. In addition to pricier hotel rooms, services-related inflation was pushed up by higher prices for hotel rooms, hospital visits, nursing home care, rental cars, tuition, sporting events and intra-city transportation, Daco said.
Those increases are partly demand-driven (continued spending from a segment of consumers more resilient to price shifts) as well as reflective of higher diesel costs, he said.
Bracing for more rate hikes and erosion in consumer spending
For American consumers, there’s really no easy way to escape higher prices, said Navy Federal Credit Union’s Long.
“People are having to skimp on something; and for a lot of Americans, that’s the grocery store … they trade down to the store brands, eat a little less meat in order to have enough money to pay all their bills,” she said.
Grocery prices were a silver lining in September’s CPI report as they ticked down by 0.1% from August. To what extent that lasts remains to be seen: Economists expect that sharply higher diesel prices could push up food costs.
Inflation is expected to remain elevated through the end of the year, further eating away at Americans’ ability to spend, said EY-Parthenon’s Daco.
“What we are living through is really an erosion phenomenon, an income erosion phenomenon,” he said.
Wednesday’s data puts the Federal Reserve further from its 2% inflation target (measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index) and could prompt policymakers to hike interest rates again if price pressures persist.
The broadening of price pressures beyond the pump “bolsters the case for additional rate hikes,” Jeff Schulze, head investment strategist for Franklin Templeton Institute, wrote in a note Wednesday, but noted that recent commentary from Fed officials suggests the bar for such a move could be high when policymakers meet later this month to decide on borrowing costs.
Stocks fell and bond yields surged after the report reinforced traders’ expectations that the Fed will keep interest rates higher for longer to tamp down inflation. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped eight basis points to 5.3%.
Odds for a Fed rate hike in October rose to 49% Wednesday morning, up from 22% one day ago, according to CME FedWatch. Traders widely expect the Fed to raise rates at least once before year-end.
CNN’s John Towfighi contributed reporting.

sources.news_title: September CPI report shows inflation accelerated to 3.7% as energy costs soared
sources.text:
September CPI report shows inflation accelerated to 3.7% as energy costs soared
Inflation accelerated across the U.S. in September, rising at an annual rate of 3.7% as energy costs jumped, according to new government data.
The latest Consumer Price Index shows that stubborn price pressures persist just weeks before Americans vote in the midterm elections.
By the numbers
The CPI tracks changes in prices over time for a basket of commonly purchased goods and services. Economists expected the index to rise at an annual rate of 3.6% in September, according to FactSet.
Inflation picked up after two months of holding steady at an annual pace of 3.4%. Core CPI, which excludes the more volatile energy and gas categories, rose 2.6% from a year ago, accelerating from a 2.4% rate in August and higher than economists' forecast of 2.5%.
Inflation has risen sharply since the start of the year due to soaring energy prices, sparked by the war in Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.
The Labor Department said Wednesday that gasoline prices, which rose 9.1% in September from the prior month, accounted for more than half the monthly increase in the CPI report. Energy prices rose 20.4% from a year ago, while gasoline jumped 34.2%.
Prices at the pump have cooled slightly in recent weeks but remain elevated. The national average for a gallon of gasoline was $4.33 a gallon on Wednesday, AAA reported, up from $2.98 before the war started. The national average for diesel, which hit a record high in late September, was $6.29 a gallon.
Higher diesel prices increase the cost of transporting goods around the U.S., often leading to higher prices for consumers on everyday items like groceries.
"The CPI was clearly hot, and there aren't many ways to sugarcoat it," Wall Street analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a note to investors on Wednesday.
Energy played a "huge role," he added, noting that prices may not head lower anytime soon as the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine escalate.
"Energy prices being so high for so long is starting to seep into the broader economy," he said.
One category of spending that saw large price increases last month was airline fares, which are up 22.4% from a year ago, according to the CPI report. Increases in shelter and used car costs also pushed up the core inflation figure, experts noted.
Nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their views of the economy, according to a CBS News poll released earlier this month.
What this means for the Fed and interest rates
Economists say the September inflation figures could put pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate later this month, as consumer prices rise faster than the central bank's 2% annual target.
"Today's hotter-than-expected CPI report shows that inflation is still well above the Fed's target, and that the current rate-hiking cycle isn't likely to end anytime soon," David Royal, chief finance and investment officer at Thrivent, a financial services firm, said in an email.
The spike in core CPI shows price pressures are broadening into other categories beyond energy, experts noted, a sign inflation remains sticky.
In September, the Fed hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023, bringing the federal funds rate to between 3.75% and 4%. Fed officials also signaled that they expect to raise rates again later this year. The central bank has two more policy meetings this year, on Oct. 27-28 and Dec. 8-9.
"This is the type of move that could prompt the Fed to pull the trigger on another hike this month, rather than wait as Fed officials have recently suggested, with markets now shifting to a 50% chance of that happening, up from 20% prior to the data," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, said in a report.

sources.news_title: Consumer inflation rose at a faster pace than expected in September
sources.text:
Consumer inflation rose faster than expected in September, CPI report shows
Labor Department releases closely watched September CPI inflation report
Inflation accelerated in September as the pace of consumer price growth trended higher due to elevated energy prices.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said on Wednesday that the consumer price index (CPI) – a broad measure of how much everyday goods like gasoline, groceries and rent cost – increased 0.6% on a monthly basis and is up 3.7% from a year ago.
Expectations vs. reality
The monthly figure was in line with the estimates of economists polled by LSEG, while the annual figure came in hotter than the estimate of 3.6%. The monthly data rate picked up following a reading of 0.4% in August, while the annual figure also trended higher from 3.4% the prior month.
So-called core prices, which exclude volatile measurements of gasoline and groceries to better assess price growth trends, were up 0.3% on a monthly basis and 2.6% from a year ago. Both of those figures were hotter than the expectations of economists polled by LSEG, who predicted a monthly rise of 0.2% and an annual increase of 2.5%.
The monthly figure cooled slightly from August, when it rose 0.3%, while the annual figure rose from 2.4% in the previous report.
US ECONOMY GREW AT A FASTER PACE THAN EXPECTED IN SECOND QUARTER
The cost of living breakdown
High inflation has created severe financial pressures in recent years for most U.S. households, which are forced to pay more for everyday necessities like food and rent. Price hikes are particularly difficult for lower-income Americans because they tend to spend more of their already-stretched paychecks on necessities and have less flexibility to save.
Energy prices rose 5.2% on a monthly basis in September and have increased 20.4% from last year. That increase follows a 2.1% monthly increase in August.
Gasoline prices increased 9.1% from the prior month in September and are up 34.2% on an annual basis, and the BLS noted the gasoline index accounted for over half of the monthly rise in the headline CPI. Electricity costs increased 0.2% on a monthly basis and are up 4.4% over the past 12 months.
WHY THE FED ISN'T READY TO DECLARE VICTORY ON INFLATION
Food prices were unchanged for the month of September and are up 2.5% compared with last year. The food at home index decreased 0.1% on a monthly basis and is up 1.8% from a year ago. The food away from home index rose 0.2% for the month and is up 3.5% from last year.
The meats, poultry and fish index declined 0.4% from the prior month in September, and is up 2.2% from a year ago. Beef and veal prices fell 1% in September and are up 3.5% from a year ago. Egg prices declined 1.3% in September and are down 20.6% from last year as supply normalizes after an avian flu outbreak.
The fruits and vegetables index increased 0.5% on a monthly basis in September and is up 3.7% from a year ago. Coffee prices rose 0.9% in September and are up 7.1% compared with last year.
Housing prices rose 0.4% month over month in September and are 3.2% higher than a year ago. Tenants' and household insurance costs increased 0.2% on a monthly basis and were up 3% from last year.
The transportation services index showed prices up 0.6% on a monthly basis and are up 2.7% from a year ago. Airline fares increased 1.2% from the prior month in September and are up 22.4% from last year.
FEDERAL RESERVE HIKES INTEREST RATES FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 2023 AMID STUBBORN INFLATION
What experts are saying
Vanguard senior economist Adam Schickling said that the "latest inflation report reinforces what we've been saying for several months: inflation is proving more persistent than many expected, particularly across services. While energy remains a factor, the more important story is that demand has stayed remarkably resilient."
"We're entering a phase where stronger productivity, moderating wage growth, and more price-sensitive consumers should help bring inflation lower, but patience will be required," Schickling added.
Tim Urbanowicz, chief investment strategist for innovator ETFs at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said that "today's print puts the Fed's tactical breather priced into the market for October in question."
"With $100-plus crude adding friction to already sticky core prices, the latest data increasingly complicates the disinflation narrative and may limit the Fed's flexibility," Urbanowicz added.
What does it mean for the Fed?
The Federal Reserve will hold its next monetary policy meeting on October 27-28, and the market's expectation as far as interest rates shifted toward a rate hike.
The probability of the Fed leaving the benchmark federal funds rate at its current target range of 3.75% to 4% fell from 77.9% on Tuesday to 58.5% on Wednesday following the September CPI inflation report, the CME FedWatch tool showed.
The odds of a 25 basis point rate hike rose from 22.1% yesterday to 41.5% on Wednesday, the tool showed.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
How did the market respond?
The benchmark S&P 500 Index fell 0.95% during Wednesday morning trading.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.13%, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.42%.

In September alone, prices rose 0.6%, driven by a large increase in the price of gasoline.

Inflation accelerated last month to 3.7% in a sign that prices remain elevated as midterm elections near
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gasoline and many other goods and services became more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before midterm elections that have focused heavily on issues related to affordability.
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month.

Inflation surges as Iran war drives prices higher across economy

Inflation surges as Iran war drives prices higher across economy
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Surging prices for energy and other goods sparked renewed pressure on prices last month, pushing inflation to a recent high and raising questions about how long the Federal Reserve can afford to wait before raising interest rates again.
Consumer prices climbed 3.7% in September compared to the year prior, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, inflation accelerated by 0.6%, the biggest monthly jump since the early days of the war with Iran.
The continued climb in prices highlights the ongoing impact the war with Iran has had on energy prices around the world and the growing risks higher fuel costs will spread throughout the economy. Prices also climbed across other categories that are impacted by fuel costs. Airfare jumped 22% from a year earlier, while costs for apparel and toys that are sensitive to shipment costs and tariffs also moved higher.
The longer energy prices are elevated, the greater the risk of businesses passing higher transportation and production costs onto consumers, creating the risk of an energy shock becoming a more persistent source of inflation.
Core prices, which exclude food and energy, increased by 2.6% year-over-year and 0.3% from a month earlier. A continued increase in core inflation is a sign price pressures are expanding beyond areas that are more sensitive to swings in energy prices.
“The core inflation rate is more concerning, as it is more informative of the larger trends in the economy. The Fed raised interest rates in the middle of September, so these inflation numbers don’t fully incorporate those effects, but they do suggest that the Fed’s fight with inflation is not close to being won,” said Competitive Enterprise Institute senior fellow and economist Jeremy Nighohossian.
The massive data center build-out to power artificial intelligence is also a significant contributor to inflation with robust demand for computer chips, equipment and electrical components that also go into consumer goods like laptops and smartphones.
Wages have also struggled to keep up with the pace of inflation in recent months. Average hourly earnings fell 0.5% in August when adjusted for inflation and are down 0.7% compared to a year ago. Hot inflation and slowing wage growth means Americans are earning less for their time worked and budgets are not going as far, raising questions about how long consumers can sustain the levels of spending that have kept the U.S. economy afloat despite years of higher prices and uncertainties.
"Today's CPI figures are a reminder that the pressure on household budgets has not let up,” said Kath Gramling, global consumer goods, retail and travel lead at Accenture. “While seasonal shopping moments such as back-to-school may have provided a lift for retailers and brands, consumers are still navigating higher prices and making tougher spending decisions, approaching every purchase with discipline, prioritizing value and stretching each dollar as far as it will go.”
Inflation has been running hot for more than five straight years, fueling frustrations for American consumers about the cost of living and the state of the economy. Facing gas prices over $4 a gallon and higher expenses for food and other necessities, voters are increasingly aiming their frustrations at President Donald Trump and Republican majorities in Congress.
Wednesday’s inflation report is the final major price data to be released before the midterm elections, creating a challenge for Republicans’ closing messaging about their management of the economy. Public opinion surveys have increasingly found voters do not approve of Trump’s handling of the economy and that voters trust Democrats more to deal with affordability.
The hot inflation report also underscores the challenges facing the Fed. Most economists are anticipating the central bank to raise its benchmark interest rate at least one more time this year, though it is unclear on the timing. Officials will meet next week and then again in December.
Before Wednesday’s release, several officials have said they could afford to wait to see how the economy responds to the quarter-point hike that was approved during the September meeting. It’s unclear whether a single inflation report will be enough to persuade officials to change their stance, but markets are pressuring officials to act.
Markets are pricing in a hold at the October meeting with a roughly 59% chance, according to CME FedWatch. Investors view a hike in December as virtually certain, with a quarter-point bump at 57% and a half-point increase at around 37% as of Wednesday afternoon.
How far the Fed will have to hike rates is also an open question moving forward, including within the central bank. Eight of the 18 Federal Open Market Committee members who gave a forecast after the September meeting projected one more increase in 2027, though other officials have signaled one more may be enough to bring inflation back toward the 2% target sometime next year.
“I haven’t changed my view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike,” New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said Tuesday in an interview with Bloomberg News. “I don’t think at this time I have any reason to believe that we would need to do more.”

sources.news_title: Consumer prices rose 3.7% annually in September as gas prices skyrocket
sources.text:
September brought little relief to the accelerating cost of living, as consumer prices increased again and kept the inflation rate well above the Federal Reserve's goal.
The consumer price index, a broad measure of goods and services costs across the U.S. economy, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.6% for the month, putting the 12-month rate at 3.7%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones expected respective gains of 0.6% and 3.6%.
Stripping out volatile food and energy costs, the so-called core CPI rose 0.3% for the month and was up 2.6% on an annual basis, compared with respective estimates for 0.2% and 2.5%.
The annual rate for headline inflation was 3.4% in August while the core rate was 2.4%.
Surging energy costs were again the primary culprit in the inflation picture. The energy index jumped 5.2% as tensions continued between the U.S. and Iran in a war launched in late February that shows no signs of ending anytime soon.
Gasoline prices soared 9.1%, accounting for about half the gain in headline CPI, according to the BLS. Over the past year, gas has posted a 34.2% rise while fuel oil has roared higher by 74.2%.
Food prices were flat on the month and up 2.5% from a year ago. However, shelter prices increased 0.4% and used car and truck prices jumped 0.7%. Apparel prices, which are sensitive to tariffs, increased 0.3% and are up 3.4% on an annual basis.
Stock market futures turned negative following the release while bond yields were sharply higher. Futures traders also raised the odds of a rate hike when the Federal Open Market Committee next meets on Oct. 27-28 to about 54%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds for a rate rise before the end of the year increased to better than 96%, with a near 50-50 chance of the Fed boosting rates by half a percentage point by December.
This is the final CPI reading that FOMC officials will get before that meeting. The BLS on Thursday will release the September reading on the producer price index, a measure of wholesale costs.
"CPI came in hot and it wasn't just fuel prices, as core inflation ran at a 3.7% annualized pace in September and 3.2% over three years," said Sonu Varghese, chief macro strategist at Carson Group. "The only surprise is that investors keep getting surprised by broad-based inflation. And we've yet to see the full impact of higher diesel prices and the AI boom."
Inflation as measured by the CPI has surpassed the Fed's 2% benchmark since March 2021. The gauge had been trending lower at the start of 2026, but then spiked following the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran.
Over the past few months, the year-over-year trend has moderated but still has held well above target.
Fed officials responded in September by approving their first interest rate hike in more than three years, a quarter percentage point move that took the benchmark funds rate to a target range of 3.75%-4%. Markets expect the Fed to skip an October increase but to hike again in December.
The type of supply shocks that have driven the energy surge generally are considered temporary, and policymakers often will look through them when considering where to set rates. However, Fed officials fear that the longer the war drags on, the higher the likelihood that the spike will make its way through the broader economy and become embedded in consumer and business expectations.
Prices also have faced pressure from President Donald Trump's tariffs as well as demand for goods associated with the artificial intelligence build-out.
In recent days, a number of key policymakers have expressed the belief that the Fed doesn't need to rush to implement another hike. However, most say they expect another increase this year. Market pricing implies the Fed could raise rates at least twice more in 2027.
Fed officials follow the CPI and a host of other metrics but use the Commerce Department's personal consumption expenditures price index as their primary forecast and policymaking metric. The PCE numbers for September won't be released until later this month.

sources.news_title: U.S. inflation rises to 3.7% in September report
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – U.S. inflation rose 0.6% in September for an annual rate of 3.7%, according to a new report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The September rate marks a significant increase from the overall 3.4% inflation in July and August. The price index for gasoline rose 9.1% in September, accounting more than half of all price increases. The overall energy index rose 5.2% in September after a 2.1% increase in August.
Across the country, states have passed temporary fuel tax suspensions as oil and gas prices continue to rise. Orphe Divounguy, founder and chief economist of Quantitative Research Group and a former Zillow economist, said the suspensions do not substantially change a household's fuel bill.
The suspensions, in Ohio, North Carolina and Georgia began in October. The delayed timeline means state progress has little effect on September's report.
"The benefit is a smaller bill than the household would otherwise face; it does not necessarily free up money for other spending," Divounguy told The Center Square. "Actual relief depends on local prices and how much of the tax cut reaches consumers."
Annual core inflation increased by 0.3% in September for an increase of 2.6% over the year after August saw a 2.4% increase. Divounguy said rising energy prices continuing to drive up core inflation could be a cause for concern.
"The question is whether higher energy costs keep spreading into other prices, or whether weaker demand forces businesses to absorb more of those costs," Divounguy said.
Jeffrey Roach, chief economist for LPL Financial, highlighted how energy prices are having a greater effect on other economic indicators. He said the Federal Reserve's latest interest rate hike will make future decisions more difficult.
"Inflation pressures are broadening beyond energy, suggesting the last mile back to target could remain bumpy and keep interest rates elevated," Roach said in a statement to The Center Square. "The latest report complicates the Fed’s decision this month, as the road back to price stability is looking increasingly difficult to navigate."
The September jobs report, released on Oct. 2, showed wage growth slowed to 3%, lower than overall inflation. Divounguy warned of a continued gap between prices and wage growth remaining a persistent problem for American families.
"Households are feeling the pressure," Divounguy said. "When spending outpaces income, households have less room to save."
Overall, the energy index rose by 20.4% in the last year. Fuel oil rose by 74.2% over the last year. Food at home saw a decrease of 0.1% in September as it rose 1.8% over the year.
"Families should plan around their actual grocery bills, fuel use, utility rates, rent renewals, insurance premiums and debt payments," Divounguy told The Center Square. "Their experience depends on what they buy, which can differ considerably from the national average."
