sources.news_title: Inflation climbs in September as gas prices surge
sources.text:
Inflation climbed to a 4-month high in September as the Iran war continued to drive up gasoline prices, according to federal government data released on Wednesday. The reading came in slightly above economists’ expectations.
Prices rose 3.7% in September compared to a year earlier, marking an uptick from an annual inflation rate of 3.4% in the prior month.
Inflation stands well above a rate of 2.4% recorded in February prior to the outbreak of the Iran war.
The fresh data arrived as affordability marks a top concern for voters ahead of early November’s midterm elections.
Gas prices jumped more than 9% in September from August, accounting for more than half of the overall price increase last month, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Shelter prices — which include home-owner payments and rental charges — also rose in September.
Food prices proved stable, however. The price of food stayed flat in September from August, putting annual inflation for food at 2.5%. That figure, which includes prices for groceries and food eaten away from home, stands well below the annual pace of overall price increases.
The Middle East conflict drove up fuel prices and catapulted inflation to a three-year high in May, but inflation eased slightly over the summer after a preliminary peace agreement established an on-again, off-again pause in fighting.
The tentative accord between the U.S. and Iran expired in August, however, giving way to continued attacks on oil infrastructure and ships in the region.
Oil exports from the Gulf have improved in recent weeks but heightened shipping costs and persistent risks have kept the national average gas price above $4.30 a gallon, AAA data shows. Prior to the Iran war, the average price of U.S. gas stood below $3 a gallon.
Diesel prices, which feed into supply costs for groceries and just about every other product bought in stores, stood at $6.29 a gallon, according to AAA. That figure amounts to an increase of about 66% since the outbreak of the Iran War.
Last month, consumer sentiment dropped close to the lowest level ever recorded in the 74-year history of the University of Michigan’s monthly survey.
By some measures, the economy remains robust.
Gross domestic product grew over three months ending in June, defying fear of a downturn triggered by the Iran war. Consumer spending, which accounts for about two-thirds of U.S. economic activity, rose 0.6% in August from July, the largest monthly increase since March 2025, government data on last month showed.
In other areas, however, the economy has wobbled. The inflation report came days after monthly jobs data showed sluggish hiring in September.
Employers added 29,000 jobs last month, a sharp slowdown from 162,000 jobs added in August, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics said earlier this month. The figure came in well below economists’ expectations.
Prior to the latest jobs report, hiring had proven largely resilient this year, even as shoppers and businesses weathered higher costs.
The combination of elevated inflation and a sturdy labor market prompted the Fed to raise interest rates a quarter of a percentage point last month, marking the central bank’s first rate increase since 2023.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said at a press conference in Washington, D.C., last month.
In theory, an increase to the benchmark interest rate should slash inflation by slowing the economy and eating away at demand, though the policy typically yields results after a lag time lasting several months.
The next meeting of Fed policymakers takes place on Oct. 28, just days before the midterm elections. Investors peg the chance of another quarter-point rate increase at about 45%, according to CME Group’s FedWatch Tool, a measure of market sentiment.

sources.news_title: Red hot U.S. CPI report fuels AI rout
sources.text:
Hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data sent the Nasdaq to a sharply lower close on Wednesday, with worries about more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve pummeling shares of Oracle, CoreWeave and other AI stocks sensitive to higher borrowing costs.
Increased bets that the Fed will need more rate hikes to tame inflation dealt a sharp blow to some of the market’s biggest gainers of 2026. Oracle lost 8.8%, while AI-infrastructure firms CoreWeave and Nebius tumbled 15% and 10%, respectively.
Dell and Hewlett Packard Enterprise sank 11.4% and 8.2%, respectively, after Barclays downgraded the AI server makers to “equal-weight” from “overweight.”
The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index dropped 4.3%, down for a sixth straight session, its longest losing streak since May 2025.
US consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged and price pressures broadened beyond energy, data from the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics showed.
Interest-rate traders are pricing in a 37% chance that Fed policymakers will raise rates this month, up from 22% on Tuesday, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.
“The reading was hotter than expected, not just with energy but elsewhere, suggesting higher tariffs and conflict-driven disruptions are bleeding into other categories,” said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide. “Investors are coming to terms with ‘higher-for-longer’ inflation.”
The S&P 500 declined 1.11% to end the session at 7,718.94 points, its biggest one-day drop since July 29.
The Nasdaq declined 1.88% to 26,692.87 points, its biggest daily drop since July 23. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.09% to 51,621.48 points.
Canada’s S&P/TSX Composite index also closed in the red, with a loss of 1.11%. The technology sector lost 2.3%, though it was a 4.2% drop in the heavily weighted materials sector that mostly contributed to the Canadian index’s decline. The increased bets for Fed rate hikes hurt the gold sector and sent the U.S. dollar stronger against major currencies. A stronger greenback puts commodity prices, priced in U.S. dollars, under pressure.
Eight of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by information technology, down 2.6%, followed by a 1.78% loss in communication services.
After hitting a record high last week, the S&P 500 remains up almost 13% in 2026, with most of that gain fueled by AI-related stocks. The median S&P 500 stock has gained 4% in 2026, and over 200 of the index’s components are in negative territory.
Bank of America fell 4.8%. The lender’s profit fell in the third quarter as it set aside $1.2 billion to cover regulatory fines for failures to detect potential money laundering. Morgan Stanley dropped almost 3%, despite a rise in quarterly profit.
The S&P 500 Banks index dipped 0.7% to its lowest close since June.
Before the inflation data was released, Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said the central bank had time to wait and see how markets and the economy evolve after its September rate rise before deciding further action.
Bending Spoons rallied 41% after Berkshire Hathaway invested another $330 million in the owner of Vimeo and AOL, a big endorsement from the high-profile investor whose moves traders closely follow.
Volume on US exchanges was relatively heavy, with 18.0 billion shares traded, compared to an average of 17.6 billion shares over the previous 20 sessions.
Declining stocks outnumbered rising ones within the S&P 500 by a 1.1-to-one ratio. The S&P 500 posted 15 new highs and 11 new lows; the Nasdaq recorded 27 new highs and 521 new lows.
US Treasuries rallied sharply on Wednesday afternoon, reversing an earlier selloff spurred by the latest hot inflation report and leaving yields on most maturities lower for the day.
The turnaround highlighted an increasingly vigorous debate in the market, centering on accelerating consumer price data on the one hand and a string of comments from Federal Reserve officials on the other suggesting that the central bank is not in a rush to hike rates further to try to tame stubborn inflation.
The 2-year US Treasury yield, which typically moves in step with interest rate expectations for the Fed, rose 0.9 basis points to 4.802% after earlier touching 4.9521%, its highest level since September 29.
The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 2.7 basis points to 5.19% after hitting 5.3293% in morning trading.
After earlier spiking on the U.S. inflation data, Canada’s five-year and 10-year bond yields by late Wednesday were nearly unchanged.
Reuters, Globe staff

The monthly rate clocked in at 0.6%. More than half of the increase was explained by gas prices.
Consumer prices rose above expectations in September, increasing 0.6% compared to the previous month, according to the latest figures.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics noted that the annual figure stood at 3.7%, compared to the 3.6% expected by analysts.
More than half of the increase was explained by gas prices, which rose more than 9% last month.
"The energy index increased 5.2 percent over the month following a 2.1-percent increase in August. The shelter index rose 0.4 percent in September after rising 0.3 percent in August. The index for food was unchanged in September, as the index for food away from home increased 0.2 percent and the index for food at home fell 0.1 percent," BLS detailed.
Odds of a rate hike by the Federal Reserve climbed after the report. They stand at 56.3% for the October meeting, compared to 77.9% on Tuesday, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
New York Federal Reserve President John Williams reiterated on Tuesday his view that the central bank should hike rates once more this year and leave them unchanged next year, at least considering the current scenario.
"I don't think at this time I have any reason to believe that we would need to do more," Williams added in an interview with Bloomberg News. "it's still mid-October. This economy is being affected by lots of different influences, and we just have to keep watching the data."
Inflation is also impacting consumer sentiment, which hit a five-month low in October after dropping further over the first days of the month.
The survey of consumers from the University of Michigan showed the figure at 46.3, compared to 48.1 last month. It is also a 13.6% drop compared to the same month last year.
Surveys of Consumers Director Joanne Hsu detailed in a statement that "buying conditions for durables plummeted amid high prices and borrowing costs."
Looking at the partisan divide, she noted that "increases in sentiment among Democrats and Republicans were offset by a decline among independents this month."
"Overall, sentiment for lower-income consumers and those with smaller stock porfolios dropped steeply this month, groups that have fewer resources to weather increases in prices. The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but this year has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn't all linked to gas prices, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that also use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices.

Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients.

sources.news_title: Energy, gas costs push inflation higher. Paychecks are lagging behind
sources.text:
Energy, gas costs push inflation higher. Paychecks are lagging behind
For the third straight month, workers’ paychecks did not keep pace with rising prices, the Labor Department’s final inflation report ahead of the midterm elections revealed.
U.S. consumer prices rose 0.6% from the month before in September, above forecasters’ expectations. Over the year, prices for all items were up 3.7%, surpassing August’s 3.4% pace. In comparison, average hourly earnings for employees on private, nonfarm payrolls increased 3% over the year last month.
A 9.1% rise in gas prices led the month-over-month increase in prices.
As workers struggle with the cost of living, consumer confidence is sitting at a 12-year low and 52% of Americans surveyed by WalletHub said they believe inflation is going to “ruin” Christmas this year.
Voters may be looking for political candidates who can make their lives more affordable before heading to the polls on Nov. 3, but economists say there is no guaranteethat prices will come down any time soon. Several factors are contributing to inflation’s stubbornness, including — but not limited to — war in Iran, tariffs, and the AI buildout.
While those things remain largely out of the Federal Reserve’s control, its policymakers have committed to delivering price stability. They voted to raise the Fed’s benchmark for short-term interest rates to help tame inflation last month. The Labor Department’s September report, which shows year-over-year inflation is still well above the Fed’s 2% target, will help inform their next rate decision on Oct. 28.
What is the core US inflation rate?
“Core” consumer price inflation, the department’s way to measure price changes while excluding more volatile food and energy costs, rose 0.3% in September as recreation, used vehicles, education, airline fares, medical care, and apparel got more expensive.
Core CPI was up 2.6% over the year in September after a 2.4% increase in August. It’s closely watched for signs that price pressures are easing or evidence that supply shocks, like limited oil supply due to global conflicts, are beginning to raise the price of other goods and services.
“There is increasing evidence that the energy price shock caused by the war in the Middle East is starting to produce price increases in other core goods and services,” Christopher S. Rupkey, chief economist of FWDBONDS LLC, said in a note after the report’s release. “It is clear that as long as geopolitical risks lead to higher energy costs, there will be cost pressures on many businesses that force them to pass the inflation hot potato on to other consumers and companies.”
More fodder for the midterms
With midterm elections weeks away, Democrats blamed Republicans and President Donald Trump for September’s inflation increase.
“President Trump promised to end inflation and lower costs ‘on day one.’ More than 600 days into his second term, he has done the exact opposite, driving up costs for American families with his disastrous war in Iran and reckless tariff taxes,” Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan Boyle, the Democrats’ ranking member on the House Budget Committee, said in a statement.
White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett painted a rosier picture of the report in a NewsNation interview.
“The topline number was driven by a surge in energy prices, which we believe to be temporary, but there is a whole bunch of good news in the report,” Hassett said, highlighting price declines for some food products and a 1.2% drop in prescription drug prices.
Are gas prices still climbing?
A jump in gas prices drove the all-items increase again. They rose 9.1% in September, accounting for over half of the monthly all-items increase, the Labor Department said. Gas prices are up 34.2% over the year.
War in Iran, the Russia-Ukraine war, and conflict in the Red Sea are limiting the global oil supply. As of Oct. 14, futures for Brent crude, the international benchmark are trading at $106 per barrel and futures for West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, are trading near $96.
Consumers are well aware of higher prices at the gas pump. The national average price of a gallon of regular unleaded gasoline is $4.33, up from $3.08 this time last year, according to AAA.
As of Oct. 14, the national average price for a gallon of regular gasoline has remained over $4 for 158 days this year, according to GasBuddy, surpassing the previous annual record of 157 days set in 2022, the year Russia invaded Ukraine.
What about diesel?
Americans may be grateful their car doesn’t run on diesel, the average price of which is hovering near $6.30 per gallon, but much of the U.S. economy depends on it.
The rise in diesel costs is a point of concern for economists as it fuels the transportation of many goods sold in the United States and disproportionately affects truckers, farmers, and fishers. Over time, high diesel prices can lead to higher price tags for a wide range of products and services.
Under a new deal, Trump said Russia would supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the American and global marketplace to bring diesel costs down. Experts are skeptical that plan will work.
“That deal is unlikely to have a meaningful impact,” Jill Cetina, a professor of finance at Texas A&M University and former vice president of bank supervision at the Dallas Fed, said. “I would view that more as a symbolic thing.”
Some grocery costs ticked down but dining out stayed pricey
Americans may have paid a bit less when checking out at the grocery store in September depending on what they bought. The Labor Department’s food at home index ticked down 0.1% over the month, but grocery costs were up 1.8% over the year.
The monthly decline was driven by a 2% drop in milk prices and a 1% dip in beef prices. Still, some items got more expensive. Carbonated drink prices rose 1.5%, fruits and vegetable costs rose 0.5%, and the index for cereals and bakery products ticked up 0.1%.
Dining out again got pricier last month. The “food away from home” index rose 0.2% in September and was up 3.5% compared to September 2025.
What does this mean for the Fed?
The Federal Open Market committee, tasked with keeping unemployment low and prices stable, voted last month to raise the target range for short-term interest rates to 3.75% to 4% in a bid to tame the pace of rising prices, though monetary policy famously works on a lag.
After U.S. employers added a disappointing 29,000 jobs, past months’ payroll gains were revised down, and the unemployment rate ticked up in September, the question is whether the committee members will vote to raise the range again.
The hot September inflation report increases the odds of another hike after the Fed’s meeting at the end of the month, according to Bill Adams, Fifth Third Commercial Bank’s chief U.S. economist.
“If the Fed hikes in October, it would in part be because they see increased possibility that the Iran War’s disruptions to energy supplies persist into 2027,” Adams said in a note.
The day before the Labor Department inflation report’s release, 78% of traders bet on an October pause, and 70% expected a quarter-point hike in December, according to CME FedWatch. After the report’s release, 52% are betting on a quarter-point hike this month, and traders are about evenly split on whether the range will be 4% to 4.25% or 4.25% to 4.5% after the Fed’s December meeting.

sources.news_title: Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% in sign that prices remain elevated as midterm elections near
sources.text:
Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% in sign that prices remain elevated as midterm elections near
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gasoline and many other goods and services became more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before midterm elections that have focused heavily on affordability.
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month.
The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn’t all linked to oil and gas, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month and higher than economists had expected. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed’s 2% target.
Higher inflation will likely put more pressure on the Fed to lift its key interest rate at its next meeting Oct. 27-28. Economists noted that the report showed price increases were spread more broadly across the economy than in recent months.
“The report was worse than expected,” Bill Adams, chief U.S. economist at Fifth Third Bank, said in a note to clients. “Price increases were widespread. … Consumer demand seems to be holding up better than the downbeat consumer surveys would suggest, helping businesses maintain pricing power.”
Wednesday’s figures are the last major inflation data to be released before the upcoming elections. Ongoing inflation has taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living issue. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Higher prices are eroding Americans’ earnings. The Labor Department also said Wednesday that average weekly paychecks, when adjusted for inflation, shrank last month compared with a year ago for the first time since May.
Gas prices jumped 9.1% just from August to September, the government’s consumer price index report said. Rising gas costs are a highly visible sign of inflation and often drive down measures of consumer sentiment about the economy.
With fuel much more expensive, air fares rose 1.2% last month and have soared 22% compared with a year ago. Hotel prices rose 2% from August to September and are up 4.4% compared with a year earlier.
Consumers saw some relief in grocery prices, which actually declined 0.1% last month and are up just 1.8% from a year ago. Ground beef prices fell 0.8% in September, though they are still up 5.4% from last year.
The cost of toys, new and used cars, sporting goods, and shoes all rose at a rapid clip last month, the government said.
The government also said Wednesday that Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% cost of living increase, based on the inflation figures.
The Middle East and Russia-Ukraine conflicts have also sharply inflated the cost of diesel fuel, which is used by long-haul trucks. Higher diesel prices will increase shipping expenses, which in turn could push up prices for a range of goods.
Ralph Newhouse, CEO of Chefman, which makes countertop appliances, said that rising diesel prices could force him to raise prices in the coming months.
The Mahwah, N.J.-based company, which makes milk frothers, air fryers, blenders and other appliances in China, last increased its prices in 2024. This year, it has used its $20 million in tariff refunds to offset the rise in fuel costs, but may not be able to do so much longer.
“We’re at the point right now that if we continue to see any additional rises in (diesel) prices, then these conversations are going to be forced upon us. We just day by day, hope and pray that we don’t have to have this conversation.”
Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn’t moving quickly enough back to the central bank’s target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9%.
Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year.
Still, Wednesday’s report has led many Wall Street investors to project that the Fed will now act in two weeks. The odds of a rate increase at the central bank’s October meeting have doubled, though remain at just 50-50, according to futures pricing tracked by CME Fedwatch.
Stock prices fell slightly after the report, while greater expectations for rate hikes pushed up bond yields, which will raise borrowing costs throughout the economy.
By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war’s disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can’t address those bottlenecks.
Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It’s already pushed up the price of air fares about 22% from a year ago.
Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients.
The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones.
Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge.
On September 1, Nintendo increased the price for its Switch 2 gaming system by 11% to $499.99. And Apple’s newest iPhone, the iPhone 17, cost about 10% more than its previous upgrade, though some of that likely reflects greater capabilities.
___
AP Retail Writer Anne D’Innocenzio contributed to this report from New York City.

sources.news_title: US Inflation Jumps to 3.7% as Gas Prices Squeeze Family Budgets
sources.text:
Rising energy costs are pushing prices higher across America, putting fresh pressure on household budgets as colder weather approaches.
US inflation reached 3.7% in September 2026, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday, October 14. Consumer prices rose 0.6% in just one month, largely because of a sharp increase in gasoline costs. For families already struggling to balance groceries, transportation, housing and heating, the latest inflation report delivers another unwelcome financial challenge. This spike in prices highlights the pressing issue of US inflation September 2026.
The figures also leave the Federal Reserve facing a difficult question: how aggressively should it fight inflation when higher interest rates can make borrowing more expensive?
What the September Inflation Report Shows
The annual Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September. CPI measures the prices consumers pay for a broad selection of goods and services. According to the official BLS September report, the latest monthly changes include:
- Overall consumer prices: up 0.6%.
- Gasoline: up 9.1%.
- Energy overall: up 5.2%.
- Fuel oil: up 15.3%.
- Shelter: up 0.4%.
- Food overall: unchanged.
- Core prices, excluding food and energy: up 0.3%.
“The index for gasoline rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for over half of the monthly all items increase,” the BLS stated in its report.
Gasoline Is Driving Much of the Increase
Gasoline prices rose 34.2% over the previous 12 months, according to the national index. Fuel oil increased 74.2% over the same period. The global energy disruptions associated with the conflict involving Iran have added pressure to oil markets. However, the BLS report measures price changes; it does not assign every price movement to a single cause.
Higher transportation expenses reach beyond the gas pump. Delivery companies, independent contractors, commuters and businesses that depend on vehicle fleets may all face higher costs. Whether those expenses are passed on to customers depends on market conditions and individual businesses.
Why Core Inflation Still Matters
The September report was not just about fuel. Core inflation, which leaves out the often-volatile food and energy categories, rose 0.3% during the month and 2.6% over the year. That annual figure was 2.4% in August.
The BLS reported monthly increases in categories including recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, medical care and apparel. One piece of better news: grocery prices dipped 0.1% during September, while the overall food index held steady.
Slower Inflation Does Not Mean Prices Fall
Inflation is the rate at which the overall price level rises. Even when that rate slows, families may still be paying more than they paid a year ago. A representative $1,000 basket of goods and services would cost about $1,037 after a 3.7% increase. That is an illustration of the inflation rate, not a forecast of any one household’s spending.
What It Means for Utica and the Mohawk Valley
National inflation numbers cannot tell us the exact prices in Utica, Rome, Herkimer or every surrounding town. They do, however, identify the pressures that local households may face, especially during the transition to winter.
Home Heating Deserves Attention Now
The national fuel-oil index jumped 15.3% in September alone. For households that heat with oil, that is an important warning to review winter budgets and compare suppliers. Actual local bills will vary by fuel, supplier, contract and consumption. Eligible New York households can review the Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP) for help with heating expenses.
Commuters May Feel the Squeeze
Transportation costs can be hard to avoid in a region where many residents drive to work, medical appointments or shopping. As a simple illustration, a 9.1% increase on a $200 monthly gasoline budget adds $18.20 if the same quantity is purchased. That does not mean gasoline will increase another 9.1% each month.
Will the Federal Reserve Raise Interest Rates?
The Federal Reserve seeks stable prices and maximum employment. Its longer-run inflation target is 2%, although the measure it targets is the personal consumption expenditures price index, not CPI. The September CPI report gives policymakers another reason to examine persistent price pressure before their next decision.
Higher policy rates can restrain spending and borrowing, but they cannot directly restore damaged oil infrastructure or end an overseas supply disruption. That is why the trade-off matters: policymakers must consider the risk of inflation spreading further against the risk of slowing the economy and hiring too much.
For consumers, interest-rate changes can influence variable-rate credit cards, car loans, savings yields and, indirectly, mortgage rates. Market expectations about the next decision can change rapidly; they should not be mistaken for an official announcement.
Affordability Takes Center Stage Ahead of the Midterms
With the November 3 midterm elections approaching, household costs are likely to remain an important issue in political debate. Republicans and Democrats differ over responsibility and remedies. International energy shocks can push prices higher beyond a president’s direct control, while government choices on energy, trade, taxes and spending can also affect the economy. Voters have reason to judge proposals by their likely impact, not simply by political slogans.
Five Practical Steps to Prepare for Rising Prices
- Review fuel spending: Compare nearby pump prices and combine trips when practical.
- Plan for winter: Check heating contracts and assistance eligibility before cold weather sets in.
- Watch variable-rate debt: Review credit card terms and prioritize costly balances where possible.
- Compare grocery totals: Plan meals and check unit prices rather than relying on advertised discounts alone.
- Protect a small cash cushion: Even modest emergency savings can reduce reliance on expensive credit.
Residents who need help finding community resources can also visit 211 Central New York.
What Happens Next?
September’s numbers show inflation moving in the wrong direction. Energy prices explain much of the monthly increase, but core prices also rose. The question for families is immediate: can earnings keep up with the next grocery trip, commute and heating bill?
As policymakers consider their next steps, an improving economy should mean more than a favorable headline number. It should mean people can afford ordinary needs and still set aside something for tomorrow.
What has strained your household budget most this year: gasoline, groceries, housing or heating? Share your experience with the Utica Phoenix.

sources.news_title: Consumer Price Index inflation climbed at worse than expected 3.7% rate in September
sources.text:
Before this morning’s release of the Consumer Price Index for September, economists were expecting annual all-items inflation to have increased at a 3.6% rate. That would have been an ugly increase in inflation from the 3.4% anual rate in August.
Turns out the actual numbers were more like ugly squared. The Consumer Price Index, released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics Wednesday morning, showed overall prices rose 0.6% month over month in September, the largest monthly increase in five months. Compared with the same time last year, prices were 3.7% higher.
The bulk of the increase stemmed from energy prices. Gasoline prices, which in late September rose to the highest level in four months at nearly $4.50 a gallon, surged 9.1% month over month. That accounted for more than half of the overall monthly increase in prices. Gasoline prices are up 34.2% over the past year.
Prices for fuel oil, used for heating in many homes in the Northeast, also shot higher, rising 15.3% in September, or 74.2% on an annual basis.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and food prices, edged higher as well, but by a smaller percentage. Over the course of September, core prices were up only 0.3%. Over the past year, they are up only 2.6. That’s comforting news for American families that don’t drive a car or eat.
Tariffs are still hitting some sectors: Prices on toys were up 4.2% in September. But other categories that are heavily exposed to tariffs showed fairly minimal effects. Apparel was up 0.3% last month, and prices on household furnishings fell 0.2%. Spending on the A.I. buildout helped to push up prices for computers and related equipment by 9.7% over the past year. Software prices have risen 28.4% over that time period. Smartphone prices have dropped nearly 10% over the last year.
This morning’s numbers, combining higher inflation and weaker wage growth, means that Americans are earning less for every hour of work in real terms. Average hourly earnings, adjusted for inflation, fell 0.5% in August, and are down 0.7% from a year earlier. It was the sixth straight month of year-over-year declines in real earnings. Average hourly earnings are now back to almost exactly where they were when President Donald Trump was sworn into office for the second time. On average, Americans have experienced zero wage growth, in real terms, since he returned to the White House.

sources.news_title: September CPI Hits 3.7% as Gasoline Jumps 9.1% in a Month
sources.text:
U.S. inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September as gasoline prices jumped 9.1% in a single month, but the more important surprise for markets came underneath the headline: core inflation rose 0.3%, above the 0.2% economists had expected.
The Consumer Price Index increased 0.6% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis, matching the broad consensus, and rose 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Forecasts had generally centered on 3.6% to 3.7% for the annual headline rate.
Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% from August and 2.6% from a year earlier. Both were above consensus forecasts of 0.2% and 2.5%, respectively.
That makes the core figures the part of Wednesday’s report markets are likely to keep trading. The headline acceleration was heavily telegraphed by the surge in fuel prices. A stronger core reading suggests inflation pressure is extending beyond the direct energy shock.
Gasoline Rose 34.2% From a Year Ago
Energy was responsible for much of the headline move.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics said the energy index rose 5.2% in September after increasing 2.1% in August. Energy prices were 20.4% higher than a year earlier.
Gasoline alone increased 9.1% month over month and 34.2% year over year. The BLS said gasoline accounted for more than half of the monthly increase in the all-items CPI.
Fuel oil was even more extreme, rising 15.3% in September and 74.2% over 12 months.
That energy pass-through matters because investors already knew September would contain a large fuel component. The question before the release was whether underlying inflation would remain contained once food and energy were stripped out.
It did not come in as softly as expected.
Shelter rose 0.4% in September and 3.2% from a year earlier. The BLS also reported monthly increases in recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, medical care and apparel.
Core CPI Is the Number That Changed the Fed Debate
Before the release, economists generally expected core CPI to increase 0.2% month over month and 2.5% annually. The actual readings of 0.3% and 2.6% therefore represent an upside miss on both measures.
That matters because the Federal Reserve has already restarted its hiking cycle.
On September 16, the Fed raised its target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00%, its first rate increase since July 2023. The September CPI report is also the final CPI print before the October 27-28 FOMC meeting.
Markets responded by sharply repricing the probability of another move this month. At around 2:05 p.m. ET Wednesday, CME FedWatch showed roughly a 42% probability of a 25-basis-point hike in October, up from about 22% before the CPI release. Earlier post-data readings reached as high as 47.1% as fed-funds futures adjusted to the inflation surprise.
The distinction between headline and core therefore matters. A 0.6% headline increase driven largely by gasoline was already broadly expected. A 0.3% core reading was not.
The latter gives policymakers more reason to ask whether higher energy costs, tariffs and other supply pressures are beginning to spread into prices that tend to be more persistent.
Gold Falls Below $4,100 as the 2-Year Yield Rises
Rates and precious metals moved quickly after the release.
The U.S. 2-year Treasury yield, which is particularly sensitive to changes in expectations for Fed policy, was around 4.87% in Reuters’ latest U.S. market read, up 7.2 basis points on the day.
Gold moved in the opposite direction. Spot gold was down 1.8% at $4,083.94 an ounce at 2:05 p.m. ET, its lowest level since October 7, as the dollar and Treasury yields rose.
That is a significant reversal from the setup before the report. Earlier Wednesday, FinanceFeeds had gold near $4,155 ahead of CPI, with $4,000 as the downside reference if core inflation came in at 0.3% or higher. The actual print landed precisely on that hot-core scenario.
Oil remains a complicating factor for the Fed because it is simultaneously lifting headline inflation and threatening further pass-through into other prices. FinanceFeeds’ CPI-day Brent analysis had crude near $106 a barrel before the release, with geopolitical disruption around Saudi Arabia and the Strait of Hormuz keeping the energy risk premium elevated.
Bitcoin Falls Toward $81,800 After the CPI Release
Bitcoin also weakened as rate expectations moved higher.
The cryptocurrency had traded above $84,000 earlier Wednesday but was around $81,800-$81,900 in early-afternoon U.S. trading, down roughly 1.6% on the session.
The immediate post-CPI move had already pushed Bitcoin below $83,000. FinanceFeeds tracked Bitcoin at $82,651 shortly after the release, when the inflation surprise first revived October rate-hike bets.
The subsequent move lower fits the broader rates reaction rather than requiring a crypto-specific explanation: Treasury yields rose, the dollar strengthened and investors priced a greater probability that U.S. monetary policy will become tighter again.
The Fed Now Has a Harder October Decision
The CPI report does not make an October rate increase certain.
Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said Wednesday that policymakers have time to “wait and see” how markets and the economy respond to September’s hike before deciding whether further action is necessary.
But Wednesday’s data changed the starting point for that debate.
Headline inflation at 3.7% can still be explained partly by an unusually large energy shock. The harder number for policymakers to dismiss is core CPI at 0.3% for the month and 2.6% for the year, both above forecasts.
With no another CPI report arriving before the October decision, this is the inflation snapshot the Fed will carry into the meeting. The gasoline surge explains why inflation accelerated. The core miss explains why markets can no longer treat the late-October meeting as an easy hold.

sources.news_title: US Inflation Rises To 3.7%, Will This Lead To A Fed Interest Rate Hike?
sources.text:
- Headline inflation in the US rose to 3.7% year-on-year in September, while core inflation climbed to 2.6% in the latest BLS CPI report.
- Surging energy commodity prices primarily drove the higher readings.
- The chart shows an alarming 74.2% spike in fuel oil and 34.2% in gasoline compared to the previous year.
Surging energy costs continue to drive up Consumer Price Index (CPI) readings. The numbers remain well above the US Federal Reserve’s goal, putting another interest rate hike on the table. However, many analysts believe the central bank will hold rates steady at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.
Headline Inflation Rises to 3.7%, Core Inflation Spikes to 2.6%
The US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) released its latest CPI report on Wednesday, showing the average change over time of prices paid by urban households for consumer goods and services. The numbers give people, especially those living solely on a day-to-day wage, more reasons to plan their spending carefully.
Headline inflation rose to an unadjusted rate of 3.7% year on year in September 2026, up about 0.6% month on month at a seasonally adjusted rate. Sharply rising energy commodities drove the increase, led by a whopping 15.3% rise in fuel oil costs and 9.1% in gasoline prices in just a month. Meanwhile, zooming out on the chart shows an alarming 74.2% spike in fuel oil and 34.2% in gasoline.
Overall, energy commodities and services ballooned 20.4% over the year, up by 5.2% on the month. These accounted for roughly half of the index’s increase. But then again, it’s worth noting that the surges were broad-based, with shelter, vehicle, and apparel costs also logging substantial gains.
On the other hand, core inflation, which excludes the volatile prices of food and energy, was at 2.6% on the year, up by 0.3% on the month.
Fed Interest Rate Expectations
Some analysts are sounding alarms over a potential interest rate hike following the alarming CPI report. However, CNBC expects the Fed to pause rates at this month’s FOMC meeting, as it just raised rates in September to 3.75%-4%.
CME’s Fedwatch reflected the same sentiment, indicating a 62.9% chance of a hold and 37.1% for a hike. Nonetheless, that’s not a reason to celebrate yet, as the central bank will likely move the dial up by a quarter-percentage point in December.
How Crypto Reacted to the News
Bitcoin (BTC) fell from roughly $84,000 to $81,000 in the last 24 hours, as sharp inflation generally fuels odds of an interest rate increase. Typically, this scenario makes safer traditional investments such as US Treasuries and high-yield savings more attractive for investors than risk assets, which BTC and most cryptocurrencies are positively correlated with in the short- to medium-term trend.

sources.text:
US consumer prices accelerated in September, with the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rising 0.6% for the month, largely due to a 9.1% jump in gasoline prices.
The broadening inflation pressures raised concerns among economists that underlying inflation could persist, complicating the Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision this month.
The big picture: Financial market expectations for a Fed rate hike at the upcoming meeting surged to roughly 52%, up from 22% before the CPI data was released.
- The report highlighted that energy prices, influenced by the US-Israeli conflict with Iran, are impacting fuel and potentially food costs.
- Food prices were flat in September, but some categories such as nonalcoholic beverages and produce saw noticeable increases.
By the numbers: Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% – above economist forecasts – and was driven by higher shelter, recreation, and transportation costs.

sources.news_title: U.S. Consumer Inflation Accelerates in September as Energy Costs Surge
sources.text:
U.S. consumer inflation accelerated again in September as gasoline prices surged and annual core inflation reversed August’s decline.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Oct. 14 that its Consumer Price Index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.6% month-over-month, following August’s 0.4% gain. Prices rose 3.7% year-over-year, up from 3.4%. The monthly increase matched economists’ expectations, while the annual reading exceeded forecasts of 3.6%.
Meanwhile, core CPI, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.3% for a second consecutive month, above expectations for a 0.2% gain. Annual core inflation climbed to 2.6% from 2.4%, exceeding forecasts of 2.5%.
Energy prices rose 5.2%, accelerating from August’s 2.1% increase. Gasoline jumped 9.1% and accounted for more than half of September’s overall monthly CPI gain. Fuel oil increased 15.3%, while electricity rose 0.2% and natural gas declined 0.3%.
Shelter increased 0.4%, compared with August’s 0.3% gain. Food prices were unchanged, as grocery prices declined 0.1% and food away from home increased 0.2%.
Used vehicles rose 0.7%, recreation increased 0.5% and airline fares climbed 1.2%. Medical care edged up 0.1%, while communication prices declined 0.2%.
Year-over-year, energy prices increased 20.4%, including gains of 34.2% for gasoline and 74.2% for fuel oil. Shelter rose 3.2% and food increased 2.5%.
MDM Analysis
September’s report suggests inflation’s summer improvement remains fragile. Energy drove the headline increase, but another above-forecast core reading gives the Fed additional reason to consider further tightening. For distributors, the practical concern is simultaneous pressure from fuel-related operating costs and borrowing costs, with less room for customers to absorb price increases. The report strengthens the case for cautious margin and inventory planning.

sources.news_title: Energy to Blame as Inflation Rises, Setting Up Rate Hike
sources.text:
Despite the Federal Reserve’s attempts to combat inflation, the latest data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reveals that such progress may be minor, or nonexistent.
The September CPI report saw a 0.6% monthly increase, with annual inflation gaining traction once again at 3.7%. The latest data is up from August’s report, which saw a monthly increase of 0.4% and an inflation rate of 3.4%.
Core inflation—or the all items less food and energy index—remains unchanged at 0.3% on a monthly basis, but it did increase by 2.6% annually.
Overall, the data “came in slightly hotter than expected,” according to Realtor.com® Senior Economist Jake Krimmel.
“Today’s numbers all but guarantee a hike by December though, while further opening the door for one or more hikes in early 2027. We are in ‘when’ not ‘if’ territory when it comes to the next Fed rate increase,” he noted.
Mortgage rates are already up almost 80 basis points since August, according to Freddie Mac, as housing markets stare down the slower fall and winter seasons. The rapid run-up in rates has largely been blamed on the Iran war as well as a sharp increase in treasury yields driven by spiraling government debt.
Prior to the report’s release, Krimmel projected headline inflation to rise to 3.6%, and although the actual rate is fairly close, it may not bode well for the Fed.
“(The) report is also the last inflation read before the Fed announces its next move on Oct. 28,” Krimmel said in a statement prior to the September report’s release. “At a minimum, the Fed will want confirmation that inflation is not getting worse, but that alone won’t mean they see it as acceptable.”
The big picture
According to economists, housing is sure to take a hit. Lisa Sturtevant—chief economist at Bright MLS—said that persistently high inflation is “dealing another blow to an already cooling housing sector.”
Lately, mortgage rates have soared in the mid-7% range, with the latest Freddie Mac survey reporting an average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage of 7.4%.
“With average mortgage rates at a near three-year high, there has been a sharp pullback in home sales,” Sturtevant added. “Prospective homebuyers are dealing with both high home prices and high mortgage rates. They are also dealing with higher costs across everyday living expenses, which makes saving for a downpayment and qualifying for a mortgage even more difficult.”
She also broke down the monthly inflation increase by category, and stated that “rising energy prices were the key driver of the inflation uptick.”
The gasoline index shot up this month by 9.1%. Previously, gasoline increased by 3.9% in August, putting energy costs on the forefront of everyone’s minds.
Combining energy commodities and energy services, the energy index increased by 5.2% for September. The jump in the energy index—which clocked in at 2.1% the previous month—generally contained the highest contributions by category. Gasoline already spiked month-to-month, but fuel oil also joined the trend by increasing 15.3%.
In terms of outlook, economists acknowledge that the real estate market may continue to face severe headwinds, as uncontrolled inflation will squeeze buyers already facing affordability struggles.
“This is a tough print for housing, not because of what higher inflation means for right now but because of what it may mean moving forward,” Krimmel said. “On real wages, earnings growth of 3% now trails 3.7% inflation, so buyers’ paychecks are losing ground just as monthly payments climb.”
Sturtevant warned real estate professionals to “expect the housing market to slow down considerably this fall.”
“While year-to-date sales are currently tracking at about last year’s levels, the combined headwinds of higher mortgage rates, higher inflation, and weak consumer confidence will drag activity lower. We could potentially see existing home sales below 4 million for 2026 for the first time since the 1990s,” she concluded.
Although the latest data doesn’t signal good news, Krimmel remains optimistic and explains the steps needed to address elevated inflation and jumpstart the housing market.
“Getting inflation under control by early 2027 likely means lower mortgage rates while also bringing consumers closer to real wage gains, which would improve purchasing power, help ease the lock-in effect, and get both affordability and market activity moving back toward normal,” he said.

sources.news_title: October Fed Rate Hike Odds Surge to 43% as U.S. CPI Inflation Hits 3.7%
sources.text:
TLDR:
- Polymarket’s October rate hike odds rose about 25 percentage points to 43%, while unchanged rates held 57%.
- U.S. CPI inflation climbed to 3.7% in September, exceeding the 3.6% forecast and August’s 3.4% reading.
- Core CPI gained 0.3% monthly and 2.6% annually, both exceeding forecasts of 0.2% and 2.5%, respectively.
- September PPI arrives October 15; the October 27–28 Fed decision comes before September PCE on October 29.
An inflation miss of just 0.1 percentage point triggered a much larger market repricing on October 14, lifting October rate-hike odds to 43%. September’s consumer price report delivered the catalyst, with annual U.S. CPI inflation reaching 3.7% against a 3.6% forecast. That comparison became a focal point for markets assessing whether inflation progress had stalled before the interest rate decision.
On Polymarket, the probability of a 25-basis-point increase climbed approximately 25 percentage points during Wednesday’s trading. However, unchanged rates retained a 57% probability ahead of the October 27–28 policy meeting. The figures captured a rapid shift in expectations without making another increase the favored outcome.
The report also showed core inflation running above forecasts, placing attention on price pressures beyond gasoline. The difference matters as energy-driven increases and broader inflation carry distinct implications for the central bank’s 2% inflation objective.
September CPI Hits 3.7% as Core Inflation Exceeds Forecasts
Headline prices increased 0.6% in September, accelerating from August’s 0.4% monthly gain. Similarly, gasoline costs jumped 9.1% and accounted for more than half the increase. Meanwhile, the broader energy index climbed 5.2%, explaining much of the immediate pressure on household budgets. That left other categories contributing to a report dominated, but not defined, by energy.
Yet the increase extended into other spending categories. Shelter prices rose 0.4%, alongside higher prices for used vehicles, airline fares, medical care, and apparel. Those movements showed that inflation was not confined to fuel. These increases showed price pressure outside energy, an important distinction when interpreting the core inflation figures.
Core consumer prices, excluding food and energy, advanced 0.3% monthly, above the expected 0.2%. Annual core inflation reached 2.6%, compared with forecasts of 2.5% and August’s 2.4%. Both annual inflation readings remained above the central bank’s target.
CME Hike Odds Reach 43.7% Ahead of PPI and October Meeting
The Fed had already increased its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00% on September 16. Meeting minutes showed most policymakers considered another increase appropriate before year-end, while keeping decisions dependent on incoming economic data.
The shift was visible beyond Polymarket. CME FedWatch put the likelihood of an October increase at 43.7%, up from 22.1% before the inflation release. That represented a 21.6-percentage-point increase in expectations. Two-year Treasury yields climbed, the dollar strengthened, and U.S. equities declined as financial markets reacted.
Higher borrowing costs also affect liquidity conditions surrounding Bitcoin and Ethereum, although the inflation report provided no cryptocurrency price figures. Attention now turns to September’s Producer Price Index on October 15. September Personal Consumption Expenditures data are also scheduled for October 29, one day after the policy meeting concludes. For now, unchanged rates remain the leading October outcome.

sources.news_title: Consumer Prices Rose at 3.7% Annual Rate in September - The MortgagePoint
sources.text:
The cost of living continues to accelerate, and the consumer price index showed little relief in September, with inflation remaining well above the Federal Reserve’s goal.
The consumer price index measures the cost of goods and services across the U.S. economy, and it rose a seasonally adjusted 0.6% for the month, putting the 12-month rate at 3.7%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday.
Economists surveyed by Dow Jones expected respective gains of 0.6% and 3.6%, CNBC reported.
Stripping out volatile food and energy costs, the so-called core CPI rose 0.3% for the month and was up 2.6% on an annual basis, compared with respective estimates for 0.2% and 2.5%, CNBC reported.
Surging Energy Costs
The annual rate for headline inflation was 3.4% in August while the core rate was 2.4%, CNBC said.
The primary cause of inflation continues to be surging energy costs. The energy index rose 5.2% as tensions continued between the U.S. and Iran in a war launched in late February that shows no signs of ending soon.
Gasoline prices soared 9.1%, accounting for about half the gain in headline CPI, according to the BLS. Over the past year, gas has posted a 34.2% increase while fuel oil has jumped higher by 74.2%.
Shelter prices rose 0.4%, and used car and truck prices jumped 0.7%. Apparel prices, which are sensitive to tariffs, rose 0.3% and are up 3.4% on an annual basis. Food prices were flat on the month and up 2.5% from a year ago.
Stock market futures turned negative following the release, while bond yields were sharply higher. Futures traders also raised the odds of a rate hike when the Federal Open Market Committee next meets on Oct. 27-28 to about 54%, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool.
CNBC noted that this is the final CPI reading that FOMC officials will receive before that meeting. On Thursday, the BLS will release the September reading on the producer price index, a measure of wholesale costs.
Consumer Price Index Tops Benchmark Since 2021
“CPI came in hot, and it wasn’t just fuel prices, as core inflation ran at a 3.7% annualized pace in September and 3.2% over three years,” said Sonu Varghese, Chief Macro Strategist at Carson Group. “The only surprise is that investors keep getting surprised by broad-based inflation. And we’ve yet to see the full impact of higher diesel prices and the AI boom.”
CNBC reported that inflation as measured by the CPI has surpassed the central bank’s 2% benchmark since March 2021. The gauge had been trending lower at the start of 2026, but rose following the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran.
In recent days, some key policymakers have said the Fed doesn’t need to rush into another hike. However, most say they expect another increase this year.

sources.news_title: U.S. Inflation Climbs to 3.7% as Gas Prices Surge

(AURN News) — Prices are climbing again. New government figures show the annual inflation rate rose to 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August. In September alone, consumer prices jumped 0.6%. That’s one of the biggest monthly increases this year.

sources.news_title: Inflation Jumps to 3.7% as Gasoline Prices Surge Ahead of Midterms
sources.text:
U.S. inflation accelerated in September as gasoline prices surged, adding pressure to consumers and creating another economic challenge for Republicans weeks before the midterm elections.
Consumer prices rose 3.7% over the 12 months through September, up from 3.4% in August, according to data released Wednesday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Prices increased 0.6% from the previous month, the largest monthly gain in five months.
Both figures came in slightly above economists’ expectations, which had called for annual inflation of 3.6%.
Gasoline was the biggest driver of the monthly increase. Prices at the pump rose 9.1% in September, accounting for more than half of the overall monthly increase, the Labor Department said.
The report arrives as higher energy costs strain household budgets and voters prepare to head to the polls in November. Inflation and the cost of living remain central economic concerns, putting pressure on an administration that has promised to make everyday expenses more affordable.
Gasoline drives inflation higher
Energy prices climbed 5.2% in September after rising 2.1% in August. Gasoline prices were up 34.2% over the previous 12 months, reflecting substantial pressure from energy-market disruptions linked to the war with Iran.
Higher fuel costs affect more than drivers. Diesel is essential to trucking, agriculture, shipping and other industries, meaning rising prices can increase the cost of transporting goods and operating businesses.
Beyond energy, housing costs rose 0.4% in September. Restaurant and takeout prices increased 0.2%, while apparel prices also moved higher.
Food prices were unchanged overall. Grocery prices edged down 0.1%, while prices for food consumed away from home rose 0.2%. Natural gas service prices fell 0.3%.
The figures show that the latest inflation increase was concentrated heavily in energy, although several other categories continued to put upward pressure on household expenses.
Core inflation also rises
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy because their prices tend to be more volatile, increased 0.3% in September and 2.6% over the past year. The annual rate was up from 2.4% in August.
The core figures suggest that price pressures extend beyond gasoline, even as energy has been the main source of the latest acceleration.
For consumers, the combination of higher fuel costs and continued increases in other expenses makes it harder to regain purchasing power. Wage growth has also struggled to keep pace with inflation, limiting the relief workers receive from larger paychecks.
Inflation creates a political challenge
The latest report comes as Republicans defend their majorities in the House and Senate ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Higher prices have remained a key concern for voters across party lines, and rising gasoline costs are especially visible to consumers. The new figures give Democrats another opportunity to challenge the administration’s economic record, while Republicans face pressure to demonstrate that their policies can bring costs down.
The report does not determine how voters will respond, but it underscores the political stakes surrounding affordability as campaigns enter their final weeks.
Markets reassess the outlook for interest rates
The inflation report also complicates the Federal Reserve’s efforts to control price increases without unnecessarily slowing economic activity.
Before the release, investors had debated whether the central bank would raise interest rates again in October or wait until later in the year. The latest data added to concerns about persistent inflation, although market expectations for an immediate rate increase remained uncertain.
Higher interest rates can make mortgages, credit cards, auto loans and other forms of borrowing more expensive. Treasury yields, which influence borrowing costs throughout the economy, can also rise as investors reassess the outlook for inflation and monetary policy.
For households already facing higher fuel and living costs, additional increases in borrowing expenses would create another financial strain.
The September report offers a fresh indication that inflation remains above the Federal Reserve’s long-term 2% target. Whether the increase proves temporary or signals more persistent price pressure will depend in part on energy prices and how inflation develops across the wider economy.

sources.news_title: US CPI Sept 2026: Inflation Hits 3.7% as Gas Prices Surge
sources.text:
Inflation picked up in September as soaring gasoline prices drove much of the increase, while shelter costs and underlying inflation also rose, according to figures released Wednesday by the Labor Department.
Prices paid by U.S. consumers rose 0.6% in September, according to the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, matching expectations and following a 0.4% increase in August.
The CPI, a key measure of inflation, tracks changes in prices paid by American consumers for a broad range of goods and services, from groceries to gasoline.
Looking at food costs, prices were unchanged in September after rising 0.1% in each of the previous two months. Grocery prices edged down 0.1% following no change in August, while restaurant prices rose 0.2% after two consecutive monthly increases of 0.3%.
Over the past 12 months, overall food prices rose 2.5%, easing from 2.7% in August. Grocery prices increased 1.8%, down from 2.2%, while restaurant prices climbed 3.5%, slightly above August’s 3.4% annual gain.
Continuing a recent trend, rising energy costs helped push overall consumer inflation higher. Gasoline prices surged 9.1% in September after a 3.9% increase in August. Compared with a year earlier, pump prices were up 34.2%, following a 27.4% annual increase in August.
Gasoline prices accounted for "over half of the monthly all items increase," the CPI report noted, up from over one-third in August.
The broader energy index, which includes gasoline, electricity and fuel oil, climbed 5.2% in September following a 2.1% gain in August. Over the past 12 months, energy prices jumped 20.4%, accelerating from a 16.3% annual increase in August.
Excluding the volatile food and energy components, core consumer prices rose 0.3% in September for the second consecutive month, exceeding most forecasts by one-tenth of a percentage point.
Shelter costs climbed 0.4% in September following a 0.3% gain in August. Over the past 12 months, shelter prices increased 3.2%, up from 3.0% in August.
The shelter component of the CPI includes apartment rents, owners’ equivalent rent — an estimate of what homeowners would pay to rent their homes — lodging away from home such as hotels and motels, housing at schools, and tenants’ and household insurance.
In other key categories:
- Clothing prices rose 0.3% in September after holding steady in August and were 3.4% higher than a year earlier.
- New vehicle prices edged up 0.2% in September following a 0.3% increase in August, bringing their annual gain to 0.6%.
- Used car and truck prices climbed 0.7% in September after rising 0.4% in August but remained 1.5% below year-earlier levels.
- Airline fares increased 1.2% in September, slowing from a 2.7% jump in August, while prices were 22.4% higher than a year ago.
The headline annual inflation rate climbed to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August, exceeding expectations by one-tenth of a percentage point.
Core inflation rose to 2.6% over the 12 months through September, topping forecasts by one-tenth of a percentage point. August’s 2.4% reading had been the lowest core inflation rate since March 2021.
The core CPI, also known as the "all items less food and energy" index, is among the inflation measures monitored by Federal Reserve policymakers to assess price trends and guide monetary policy decisions.

sources.text:
In brief
- U.S. consumer prices rose 3.7% year over year in September, above the 3.6% forecast, as gasoline jumped 9.1% in a single month.
- Odds of an October Fed rate hike roughly doubled from 22% after the report, and the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to about 5.3%.
- Bitcoin fell 1.5% to $82,142 and is holding the $81,847 to $82,305 Fibonacci golden zone, with $81,603 as the next support.
Bitcoin fell 1.5% to $82,142 on Wednesday after U.S. inflation came in hotter than expected, dragging most of the crypto market down with it. Ethereum dropped 2.8% to $2,440, Solana lost 1.9% and XRP slid 1.3%, while total crypto market cap shed 0.7% to $2.8 trillion.
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% over the past year, up from 3.4% in August, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Economists expected 3.6%. Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% in a single month and accounted for more than half of the increase.
Core CPI, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 2.6% annually against a 2.5% forecast. That is the reading the Federal Reserve watches most closely, since it shows whether price pressure is spreading into rent, airfares, and services.
Expensive gasoline starts with expensive oil, which has traded above $90 a barrel for most of the past two months amid the war between the U.S. and Iran. Pricier fuel raises the cost of shipping and producing almost everything.
When inflation runs hot, the Fed raises interest rates to cool spending. It already hiked in September to a 3.75%-4.00% range, and traders now see roughly 44% to 49% odds of another hike at its October 27-28 meeting, up from 22% before the report, according to CME FedWatch.
The 2-year Treasury yield, which closely tracks Fed rate expectations, jumped about 10 basis points to roughly 4.9%, while the 10-year climbed to about 5.3%, near 24-year highs.
Higher yields hit crypto directly. A government bond paying 5.3% with almost no risk competes with Bitcoin, which pays nothing. Rising rates also make borrowing more expensive and tend to strengthen the dollar, draining the cheap money speculative assets feed on, which is why the S&P 500 fell 0.6% and the Nasdaq 0.8% on the same news.
Crypto also swings harder than stocks because many traders borrow to bet on rising prices, and when the price drops past a set level, exchanges automatically close those positions, a process called liquidation, and that forced selling can push prices lower and trigger more liquidations in a chain.
At the moment, more than $281 million in crypto derivatives positions have been liquidated in the past 24 hours, with most of it coming in just the last four hours—and the majority of that coming from Bitcoin long positions (the bulls betting the price would go up, and now paying the price when it dropped).
Bitcoin price: The macro picture is punching hard
On the daily chart, Bitcoin opened at $83,066 and now trades near $82,211, sitting inside the Fibonacci "golden zone" it reclaimed on Tuesday. That zone marks an area where pullbacks within uptrends often attract buyers.
The average price of the last 50 days remains above the 200-day average, a setup traders read as an intact long-term uptrend. The Average Directional Index, which gauges trend strength on a 0-to-100 scale where readings above 25 confirm a trend, sits at 27.7 with buyers still ahead, down from 29.9 on Tuesday, meaning traders are bullish, just not as much as they used to be.
The Relative Strength Index, a momentum gauge from 0 to 100, slipped to 48.7, just under the 50 line that separates bullish from bearish momentum. The Squeeze Momentum Indicator has been on for eight sessions, meaning volatility is compressed and a big move is building, and its -0.76 reading leans bearish by a small margin.
A daily close below $81,603 would break the golden zone and bring the $80,365 swing low into play, with the trend band near $80,284 right under it; losing that would expose $78,003. On the upside, bulls need to reclaim $84,245 before targeting $85,301, $86,644 and the October high of $87,422.
The next test arrives Thursday with the Producer Price Index, which tracks what businesses pay for goods and services, and the Fed announces its rate decision on October 28.

sources.news_title: US Inflation Hits 3.7% Ahead of Midterm Elections
sources.text:
US inflation has risen more than expected, reaching 3.7% for the year ending September 2026, according to official statistics released prior to the upcoming midterm elections. This marks an increase from the 3.4% recorded for the previous month, August. The rise in inflation has been attributed primarily to soaring gasoline prices, which have surged due to disruptions in Middle Eastern energy supplies linked to the ongoing US-Israel conflict with Iran.
The inflation data comes at a critical time, as candidates in the midterm elections are focusing on the cost of living challenges faced by many Americans. The heightened prices are likely to influence voter sentiment and decisions as they head to the polls next month.
Inflation is defined as the rate at which the prices of goods and services increase over time. For instance, if the price of a loaf of bread rises from $1 to $1.10 over a year, the annual inflation rate for that item would be 10%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) measures inflation using the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which tracks price changes across a diverse range of goods and services essential for daily living.
Factors Driving the Current Inflation Surge
The recent increase in inflation can be attributed to multiple factors, including supply chain constraints and rising demand. When demand for a product exceeds its supply, producers often raise prices. A pertinent example is the recent surge in gasoline prices, which have reportedly increased by 34.2% over the past year. In September alone, fuel prices jumped by 9.1%, contributing significantly to the overall inflation rate.
Energy inflation has also seen a notable rise, with a year-on-year increase of 20.4%. Prices for fuel oil, which is commonly used for home heating, have soared by 74.2%. Experts are monitoring the situation closely, particularly to see if these energy costs will begin to influence other sectors, such as food prices, which have remained relatively stable for now.
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, stands at 2.6%. This figure indicates that while energy costs are driving overall inflation, other essential goods and services have not experienced the same level of price increases.
Impact of Tariffs on Inflation
The introduction of tariffs by President Donald Trump has also played a role in shaping inflation trends. Since taking office for a second term, Trump has imposed tariffs on a wide range of imports. Although some initial tariffs were reduced following trade agreements, a new 10% global tariff was announced to replace those that were struck down by the Supreme Court in February.
Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York indicates that these tariffs have contributed to rising prices for consumer goods. Higher import taxes generally lead to increased costs for US companies unless foreign suppliers reduce their prices. The New York Fed found that US businesses absorbed nearly 90% of the tariff costs, resulting in an estimated 0.25% price increase for consumer goods for every percentage point rise in average tariffs.
While inflation currently exceeds the Federal Reserve’s target of 2%, it has been significantly higher in previous years, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic and following geopolitical events such as the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The Federal Reserve aims to maintain a stable inflation rate to support economic growth and consumer purchasing power.
