sources.news_title: Hot U.S. CPI Sends Bitcoin Lower as Rate Hike Fears Return
sources.text:
TL;DR
- September CPI rose 3.7% year over year, above the 3.6% forecast, while core inflation also exceeded expectations and Bitcoin fell about $1,000.
- The hotter inflation print pushed Treasury yields higher and revived concern the Federal Reserve could raise rates in October instead of waiting until December.
- CoinMarketCap later showed Bitcoin near $82,903, with a 24-hour range between $82,283 and $84,049, leaving traders focused on whether macro pressure triggers sustained selling.
Bitcoin fell sharply after U.S. September inflation came in hotter than expected, reviving concern that the Federal Reserve could raise rates again sooner than markets had anticipated. Headline CPI rose 0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year, above the 3.6% annual consensus, while core CPI increased 0.3% monthly and 2.6% annually. Bitcoin dropped about $1,000 after the release to $82,800, while CoinMarketCap later showed BTC near $82,903. The inflation surprise immediately pressured Bitcoin as traders reassessed the probability of an October rate hike. The monthly increase matched economist forecasts.
Treasury Yields Jump as Markets Reprice Fed Risk
The report also hit broader risk markets. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield jumped 9.3 basis points to 5.308%, while the 2-year yield rose 13.1 basis points to 4.924%. Nasdaq 100 futures fell 0.65%, S&P 500 futures slipped 0.3% and gold dropped 1.5% to $4,116 per ounce. The synchronized move across bonds, equities, gold and Bitcoin points to a broad repricing of rate expectations rather than an isolated crypto-specific selloff. That backdrop extends the recent link between inflation data and Bitcoin volatility as macro releases continue to shape short-term positioning. Other risk assets weakened alongside Bitcoin.
Before the CPI release, market pricing had largely favored a pause at the Federal Reserve’s October meeting and another 25-basis-point increase at the final meeting of the year in December. Several Fed officials had also signaled that another increase before year-end remained possible. The stronger inflation print now raises the possibility that policymakers could move earlier, although the data alone does not guarantee an October hike. For Bitcoin, the immediate concern is that higher-for-longer rate expectations can tighten financial conditions and reduce appetite for risk assets. The reaction contrasts with recent relief after softer inflation indicators. Core inflation also exceeded consensus forecasts.
CoinMarketCap’s later snapshot placed Bitcoin’s 24-hour range between $82,283 and $84,049, showing that the post-CPI decline kept BTC inside a volatile but familiar trading zone. The release therefore changed the macro backdrop more decisively than it changed Bitcoin’s broader technical structure in the immediate aftermath. The next test is whether rate-hike fears produce sustained selling or whether buyers absorb the shock above the lower end of the current range. That uncertainty arrives as Bitcoin’s October momentum remains vulnerable to repeated reversals driven by macro catalysts. That kept BTC inside its daily range.

sources.news_title: US inflation rises more than expected ahead of midterm elections - The Ghana Report
sources.text:
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.
The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.
Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have spiked following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.
The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US.
What is inflation?
Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increase over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.
Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).
It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.
The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples’ spending and lifestyle habits change.
What causes inflation?
There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.
If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices – the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.
Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.
Reuters Labubu dolls of various colours including pink, deep red and beige on displayt at Pop Mart’s Skullpanda pop-up shop in Manhattan in New York CityReuters
Supply and demand: Labubu dolls illustrate how inflation can rise
Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.
Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.
What is the current rate of inflation?
Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices.
Car fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.
In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau or Labor Statistics.
Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.
Experts said the US Federal Reserve – which sets the country’s interest rate – will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher.
At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year.
Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.
How have tariffs affected inflation?
Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.
While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.
Trump argued the tariffs would increase America’s tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Reuters US President Donald Trump smailes and points at the camera against a blue and white backdrop at a rallyReuters
US President Donald Trump raised tariffs
Higher tariffs – which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import – directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.
In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.
Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.
Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.
What tariffs has Trump introduced and why?
Has inflation been worse lately?
While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like – it has a target of 2% – it has been much higher in previous years.
During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.
Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.
Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.
Can inflation ever go down?
It’s important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down – it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.
A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve’s target rate illustrates.
Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn’t impact people’s purchasing decisions.
Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect prices to fall further. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

sources.news_title: US Inflation Reaches 4-Month High as Bitcoin Bulls Retreat
sources.text:
Bitcoin’s price tumbled below $83,000 Wednesday after U.S. inflation climbed to 3.7%, its highest reading in four months. Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% in September, rattling Wall Street and complicating the Federal Reserve’s next move as another inflation report approaches.
US Inflation Reaches 4-Month High as Bitcoin Bulls Retreat
Key Takeaways
- U.S. inflation reached 3.7% in September as gasoline prices jumped 9.1%, driving more than half the monthly increase.
- Bitcoin dropped roughly $1,000 after the CPI release, falling below $83,000 as Treasury yields climbed.
- The Federal Reserve faces another inflation test Oct. 15, when September’s PPI figures are released.
Gasoline Prices Push U.S. Inflation to 3.7%
America’s inflation problem just got more expensive, and the war in Iran is helping foot the bill. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported Wednesday, Oct. 14, that the consumer price index (CPI) increased 0.6% in September, following August’s 0.4% advance. Annual inflation accelerated from 3.4% to 3.7%, edging past economists’ 3.6% forecast.
The biggest culprit wasn’t housing or groceries. Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% in a single month, accounting for more than half of the overall increase. Compared with September 2025, gasoline costs, which followed crude prices, climbed an eye-watering 34.2%. The broader energy index increased 5.2% monthly and 20.4% annually. Food prices held steady for September, while shelter costs rose 0.4%.
Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, also delivered an unwelcome surprise. It increased 0.3% monthly and 2.6% annually, exceeding forecasts of 0.2% and 2.5%, respectively.
Wall Street Retreats as Bitcoin Loses $1,000
Financial markets didn’t take the news kindly. Dow Jones futures slipped approximately 0.2%, S&P 500 futures declined 0.3%, and Nasdaq 100 futures dropped 0.6% following the 8:30 a.m. Eastern release. Treasury yields climbed as traders reconsidered how aggressively the Federal Reserve might tighten monetary policy. The two-year yield approached 4.91%, while the 10-year yield neared 5.29%.
Bitcoin’s price took an immediate hit. The cryptocurrency fell from approximately $83,800 toward $82,800, shedding roughly $1,000 as the inflation figures crossed trading desks. Leveraged long liquidations added pressure, leaving traders watching support between $81,000 and $82,000.
The reaction followed September’s Federal Reserve rate increase, which lifted the benchmark target range to 3.75% to 4%. With inflation running hotter than anticipated, hopes for an early return to easier monetary conditions have taken another beating.
Thursday’s Producer Inflation Report Takes Center Stage
The next economic test arrives Thursday when the BLS releases September’s producer price index (PPI) at 8:30 a.m. Eastern. The report measures prices received by producers and could reveal whether higher energy costs are spreading further through the economy.
Retail sales figures are also scheduled for Thursday, giving investors another window into consumer spending. The Federal Reserve meets Oct. 27-28, with policymakers weighing stubborn inflation against September’s disappointing addition of just 29,000 jobs. Presently, Polymarket bettors give a quarter-point Fed hike a 44% chance, and odds climbed following the CPI release before dipping again.
For bitcoin traders, reclaiming the $84,000 zone would help restore the market’s footing. But another hot inflation reading on Thursday could leave Wall Street confronting an uncomfortable possibility: The energy shock isn’t finished working its way through prices.

sources.news_title: Inflation Hits 3.7%, Putting Mortgage Rate Relief At Risk
sources.text:
Inflation Hits 3.7%, Putting Mortgage Rate Relief At Risk
September’s inflation pickup puts recent rate improvements at risk, potentially eroding affordability gains from lower home prices and seller concessions
September’s inflation report put recent borrowing-cost improvements at risk, complicating the outlook for loan officers counting on better pricing to move purchase and refinance borrowers forward.
The Consumer Price Index rose 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. Prices increased 0.6% over the month on a seasonally adjusted basis, following August’s 0.4% increase.
“The hotter report raises the odds of an October Fed rate hike, likely extending the wait for lower mortgage rates and offsetting some of the affordability gains from rising incomes and cooling house prices,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson said in comments following the release.
Recent Rate Gains Face Pressure
Rates had edged to another two-week low Tuesday, with its daily index for a top-tier 30-year fixed loan at 7.46%.
Reuters reported Wednesday morning that the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield rose approximately nine basis points to 5.304%. That move puts upward pressure on financing costs, although Treasury yields and retail loan pricing do not move in identical increments.
For LOs, further pricing deterioration could change payment estimates for unlocked purchase loans and narrow savings for prospective refinance customers. Financing can respond to changing investor expectations before the Fed announces its next decision.
Gasoline Led, But Core Inflation Didn’t Cool
Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% on a seasonally adjusted basis, accounting for more than half the monthly CPI increase.
Core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3%, matching August’s pace but exceeding the 0.2% forecast cited by Williamson. Annual core inflation increased to 2.6% from 2.4%.
Underlying inflation therefore held its rounded monthly pace rather than accelerating, but failed to deliver the slowdown economists had anticipated. Headline annual inflation remained below May’s 4.2%, and food prices were unchanged in September.
Shelter prices rose 0.4%, following August’s 0.3% increase. Within that category, residential rent increased 0.2%, owners’ equivalent rent rose 0.3%, and lodging away from home increased 2%. CPI shelter measures rental costs and rental equivalence; it does not measure home-sale prices or mortgage interest expenses.
Less Room To Count On Rate Relief
Williamson said the report could bring forward a rate increase that markets had largely expected in December. The Fed meets Oct. 27–28, and its next move remains dependent on incoming data. Its 2% inflation objective is measured using the separate Personal Consumption Expenditures price index.
“For prospective home buyers, that could keep mortgage rates elevated for longer as investors adjust to the prospect of more persistent inflation, pushing meaningful affordability relief further out,” Williamson said.
He also warned that elevated rates reinforce the lock-in effect, limiting inventory and slowing sales.
For originators, the immediate question is whether current pricing still supports the borrower’s transaction. Further rate increases could raise payments on unlocked purchase loans or reduce the savings available through refinancing.
On purchase deals, price reductions, seller credits toward eligible closing costs, and permanent rate buydowns can address different affordability needs. Their value depends on the borrower’s upfront cash and ongoing payment.
September’s report gives LOs less reason to count on near-term rate relief to make those numbers work.

sources.news_title: US Inflation Climbs to 3.7% in September, Oil Prices Still to Blame
sources.text:
American households got no relief from rising prices in September. The consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.6% for the month, pushing the annual rate to 3.7%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday, figures slightly above what economists surveyed by Dow Jones had expected: 0.6% and 3.6%, respectively. Stripping out volatile food and energy costs, core CPI climbed 0.3% for the month and 2.6% over the past year, versus estimates of 0.2% and 2.5%. In August, headline inflation stood at 3.4% and core inflation at 2.4%.
Energy remains the main culprit behind the rising cost of living, with the energy index jumping 5.2% as tensions between the US and Iran, which erupted into war in late February, show no sign of easing. Gasoline prices soared 9.1%, accounting for roughly half of the overall gain in headline CPI, according to the bureau. Over the past year, gas prices have risen 34.2%, while heating oil has surged 74.2%. Food prices held flat for the month, up 2.5% from a year earlier, while shelter costs rose 0.4% and used car and truck prices climbed 0.7%.
A Fed already on the move
Inflation, as measured by CPI, has remained above the Fed’s 2% target since March 2021. The gauge had been trending lower at the start of 2026, before spiking after the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran. Over recent months, the year-over-year trend has eased somewhat but remains well above the central bank’s target. In September, the Fed approved its first rate hike in more than three years, a quarter-point move that took the benchmark range to 3.75%-4%. Markets expect the Fed to pause in October before hiking again in December.
The kind of supply shocks driving energy prices higher are generally viewed as temporary, and policymakers tend to look past them when setting rates. But the longer the war drags on, the greater the Fed’s fear that the price spike will spread through the broader economy and become embedded in consumer and business expectations. Several key officials have said in recent days they see no need to rush another hike, though most still expect one before year’s end; market pricing implies at least two more increases in 2027. Fed officials track CPI alongside a host of other metrics, but rely primarily on the Commerce Department’s personal consumption expenditures price index for forecasting and policy decisions; September’s PCE data won’t be released until later this month.

sources.news_title: September Inflation Surges to 3.7%, Analysts React
Soaring gasoline prices: US consumer inflation up more than expected as midterms loom
sources.text:
US consumer inflation was hotter than anticipated in September, government data showed Wednesday, as Washington's continued war with Tehran pushed energy costs higher, deepening strains on American households ahead of next month's midterm elections.
The uptick underscores voter worries over high costs of living, and comes as President Donald Trump is campaigning in US states to shore up support for his Republican Party as it tries to retain control of Congress.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.7 percent year-on-year in September, the Department of Labor said, more than the 3.6 percent forecasted by analysts according to MarketWatch.
This was a notable acceleration from 3.4 percent in August, in one of the last major economic reports before the November 3 vote.
Inflation picked up pace on a month-on-month basis too, accelerating from 0.4 percent in August to 0.6 percent last month.
Gasoline costs accounted for more than half of the monthly CPI jump, surging 9.1 percent in September.
The higher-than-expected inflation reading has raised the odds of a second straight interest rate hike at the US central bank's October 27-28 policy meeting, although many expect the Federal Reserve to proceed cautiously.
Economist James Knightley at ING noted that Fed officials John Williams, Philip Jefferson and Christopher Waller have suggested "that we don't need to see back-to-back interest rate increases," instead leaning towards "a slow and steady" approach.
He expects the Fed will want to be "careful and cautious in terms of its policy tightening."
Traders see a 37.1 percent chance that the Fed will raise rates by another 25 basis points in October, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool. The probability was around 22 percent a day prior.
"We expect at least two more rate hikes by early 2027, starting in December," said KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk. "September gave the Fed more reason to hike, even if officials hold in October."
Industries sensitive to interest rates, including housing, are already under pressure from steeper borrowing costs.
Yields on US government bonds spiked after the inflation report. The 10-year Treasury yield, which influences rates on mortgage and auto loans, rose to 5.3 percent from 5.2 percent. But it has since moderated.
"Energy lit the match; sticky services, shelter and goods prices kept the fire burning," said KPMG's Swonk of the inflation report.
Energy prices have soared since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, prompting Tehran to block off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for oil and gas shipments.
Average prices at US gasoline pumps have surged more than 45 percent since the start of the Middle East war to $4.33 per gallon, according to AAA motor club data.
Diesel prices have soared even more, by 67.7 percent, boosting the cost of transporting goods and threatening further spillovers to consumers.
"Again, the Iran-US conflict has led to higher motor fuel costs that everyone is experiencing," ING's Knightley told AFP.
"The US is also seeing substantial increases in airline fares," he said, adding that this will likely contribute to additional price pressures.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was up 2.6 percent from a year ago.
Although high gasoline and diesel prices drove about half of the September spike in inflation, "it's starting to spill into other areas," warned Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union.
"Airfares, used cars and recreation all had big price jumps," she added. "Americans are seeing their pay totally wiped out by inflation. That's been the case for half a year now."
With the underlying US economy remaining strong as massive spending linked to the artificial intelligence buildout boosts demand for chips and labor, economists also caution that higher costs could continue filtering through to households.

sources.news_title: Yikes! Big Inflation Overshoot Upends Fed’s ‘Patience’ Message
sources.text:
Underlying inflation in the US ran hotter than expected last month, Wednesday’s update from the outfit formerly known as the world’s preeminent macro statistics agency showed.
Core CPI rose 0.335% MoM, the BLS said. That constituted a meaningful overshoot versus what I thought was a rather optimistic consensus, which expected a downshift from August’s monthly pace to 0.2%.
As the figure below shows, September marked the third straight month during which the unrounded core measure picked up. The YoY pace, at 2.6%, was likewise warm.
Headline CPI rose 0.6% MoM, 0.649% unrounded. The 3.7% YoY pace there was also a tenth higher than expected.
Aside from another benign read on grocery prices (which allegedly fell last month from August and rose just 1.8% from September of 2025), there wasn’t a lot to like in Wednesday’s report.
The energy gauge posted its largest increase since the beginning of the war, rising more than 5% MoM. The gas index was up more than 9% (accounting for more than half of the overall, headline inflation increase) and the fuel oil measure more than 15%.
The used vehicles gauge posted its largest MoM gain in nearly a year, apparel prices their largest monthly advance since May, transportation services the briskest monthly pace since March and, insult to accumulated injury, the shelter gauge its quickest increase since April.
The CPI-derived versions of the so-called “supercore” measure the Fed eyes (i.e., core services excluding housing) were warm for a second month. Stripping out the rent and OER measures, core services prices rose 0.42% in September atop a 0.51% increase in August. Core services excluding the shelter gauge posted a 0.34% advance on top of the prior month’s 0.42% gain.
There was no respite in core goods. That gain was 0.25%, double the prior month’s advance and the quickest of Donald Trump’s second term. The category that captures the impact of the AI buildout — “computers and associated equipment” — showed a near 4% MoM advance, the quickest since inflation took off in early 2021.
So, again, there were no silver linings in this week’s marquee US macro release, which served to underscore households’ concerns about prices headed into the midterms. A New York Fed poll last week showed consumers’ near-term inflation expectations were the highest since May of 2023 in September, and the preliminary read on University of Michigan Sentiment for October saw the current conditions gauge hit a new all-time low.
If you’re wondering whether the CPI release puts an October Fed hike back on the table, the answer’s probably “no.” Fedspeak, including Wednesday remarks from Miki Bowman, has uniformly suggested another hike isn’t in the offing, and that December’s gathering is the next “live” meeting.
That said, STIRs moved dramatically in the wake of the CPI release. Prior to the hot core readout, market-implied odds of a move on October 28 weren’t even 25%. Following the report, those chances rose all the way to a coin flip.
The figure above shows you the knee-jerk move at the front-end of the curve. Twos were cheaper by 15bps, resulting in a fairly sharp bear flattener. Had the move in twos held (it didn’t) it would’ve been the largest close-to-close increase of the year.
“Overall, it was a troubling round of inflation data that undermines the argument for a gradual pace of future rate hikes, and revives the prospects for a quarter-point Fed hike in two weeks,” BMO’s Vail Hartman said, adding that the stakes are now higher for Kevin Warsh’s remarks at the IMF meetings in Thailand.
“Forward guidance is by no means guaranteed,” Hartman went on. “[But] the Chair has shown a willingness to provide implicit signals about the future path of policy rates in recent public appearances.”
I wonder if Lisa Cook will be banging on the table to raise, knowing it’s probably her last meeting.
Inflation can drop to 0% and people will still be complaining about it, Trump can’t win on that one. Everybody is comparing prices to what they were 3-4 years ago, that’s where people see inflation. Out for dinner, grocery shopping, its 30-50% more, even McDonalds costs an arm and a leg.
The bond market therefore mortgage rates see the future. A steady rise in mortgage rates has the potential for people to question the ‘cost’ of the big beautiful.

sources.news_title: Dollar Breaks Higher as Core CPI Pushes October Fed Hike Odds Above 40% - ActionForex
sources.text:
The Dollar Surged Broadly as Stronger US Core Inflation Forced a Sharp Reassessment of Fed Rate Expectations
What’s happening: The Dollar surged broadly on Wednesday after September’s US core CPI beat expectations, reversing the recent retreat in Treasury yields. The Dollar Index broke above 102.60 to reach 102.72, the 2-year Treasury yield jumped toward 4.94% and the 10-year yield rebounded above 5.30%. According to CME FedWatch, the probability of a Fed hike at the October 28 meeting surged from 22.1% a day earlier to 43.7%, against 17.7% a week ago.
Why it matters: A hold remains narrowly favored at 56.3%, but the repricing suggests markets are no longer confident that the Fed can afford to pause tightening. The next confirmation points are 102.77 in the Dollar Index, 4.960% in the 2-year yield and 5.365% in the 10-year yield. Sustained breaks would signal that the recent correction in yields has ended and that the Dollar’s broader advance is regaining momentum.
The Dollar surged broadly on Wednesday as stronger-than-expected US core inflation triggered a sharp reassessment of Fed rate expectations. The Dollar Index broke above 102.60 to extend its medium-term uptrend, while the 2-year Treasury yield jumped toward 4.94% and the 10-year yield rebounded above 5.30%. Most notably, the probability of another Fed hike at the October 28 meeting surged from 22.1% a day earlier to 43.7%, according to CME FedWatch, compared with just 17.7% a week ago. Although a hold remains narrowly favored at 56.3%, the repricing suggests markets are no longer as confident that the Fed can afford to pause tightening.
Core Inflation Surprise Reverses Treasury Yield Retreat
The catalyst was September’s upside surprise in core CPI, which held at 0.3% mom rather than moderating to the expected 0.2%. Annual core inflation accelerated from 2.4% to 2.6%, exceeding forecasts of 2.5%. Headline CPI also strengthened from 3.4% to 3.7% yoy, driven largely by surging gasoline prices. Importantly, firmer underlying price pressures extended across goods and services, making the report more concerning than an energy-driven headline increase alone. For a detailed breakdown, see our US Core CPI Beats Forecasts as Inflation Pressures Broaden Beyond Energy.
September US CPI: Actual vs Forecast
| Measure | Previous | Forecast | Actual | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Core CPI (m/m) | 0.3% | 0.2% | 0.3% | 
| Core CPI (y/y) | 2.4% | 2.5% | 2.6% | 
| Headline CPI (y/y) | 3.4% | 3.60% | 3.7% | 
The Treasury market responded by rapidly unwinding the correction that had developed since last week’s yield peaks. The 2-year yield surged as high as 4.939%, approaching the September high of 4.960%. A break above that level would strengthen the case for resumption of the larger uptrend. Meanwhile, the 10-year yield’s rebound through 5.278% suggests its pullback from 5.365% completed at 5.173%, bringing a retest of 5.365% back into focus. The sharp recovery in shorter-term yields is particularly significant, reflecting renewed uncertainty over how much additional monetary tightening will be required.
CME FedWatch: October 28 Fed Hike Probability
| Timing | Probability of a hike | 
|---|---|
| A week ago | 17.7% | 
| A day earlier | 22.1% | 
| Wednesday | 43.7% (hold at 56.3%) | 
Dollar Breakout Adds Pressure to Equities and Precious Metals
The Dollar Index climbed to 102.72, breaking above its previous 102.607 high and strengthening the case for continuation of the broader advance. Immediate focus is now on the 100% projection at 102.77. A decisive break above that level, accompanied by sustained trading above the rising channel ceiling, would raise the possibility of upward acceleration toward the 138.2% projection at 104.36.
Cross-Asset Moves
- Dollar Index: climbed to 102.72, above its previous 102.607 high
- 2-year Treasury yield: surged as high as 4.939%
- 10-year Treasury yield: rebounded through 5.278% and above 5.30%
- Nasdaq futures: down around 0.67%
- S&P 500 futures: down around 0.31%
- Dow futures: down around 0.18%
- Gold: down around 1%
- Silver: down more than 2%, extending its recent underperformance against Gold
The renewed rise in yields and Dollar also weighed on risk assets and precious metals. Nasdaq futures underperformed S&P 500 and Dow futures, while Silver fell by more than twice as much as Gold. The cross-asset reaction was consistent with investors adjusting to a more restrictive interest-rate outlook, with higher yields and a stronger Dollar adding pressure to non-yielding metals.
Oil and Fiscal Risks Complicate the Bond Outlook
Energy prices provided another source of inflation concern, with Brent holding around $106 as Middle East supply risks persisted. The International Energy Agency warned that constraints in diesel markets could continue well into 2027. Meanwhile, Saudi authorities reported an overnight attack on a Saudi Aramco administrative building in Dhahran, while a Saudi-led coalition reportedly struck Houthi energy facilities in Yemen. No disruption to Saudi oil production was confirmed. These developments cannot explain September’s inflation figures, but they highlight the possibility of continued energy-price pressure in subsequent months.
Separately, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned that economic growth alone would not be sufficient to address America’s mounting debt burden. Speaking at the IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, she said, “Growth of course helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments,” arguing that fiscal measures would also be necessary. Her warning contrasts with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s emphasis on stronger growth as a means of reducing the debt ratio. The IMF projects US growth of 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, below the administration’s ambition for sustained growth above 3%. While the immediate Treasury rebound was driven by inflation and Fed repricing, persistent deficits and borrowing requirements represent a separate longer-term risk to bond yields.
Inflation Repricing Puts Dollar and Yields Back on an Upward Path
Wednesday’s CPI surprise has shifted the near-term market narrative from a possible extension of the Treasury rally toward renewed risks of higher yields and a stronger Dollar. The change in October Fed pricing is especially revealing: a rate hike is no longer a relatively remote possibility, even though a pause remains marginally more likely.
For now, the Dollar’s break above 102.60 and the 10-year yield’s recovery through 5.278% favor further upside tests. The next confirmation points are 102.77 in Dollar Index, 4.960% in the 2-year yield, and 5.365% in the 10-year yield. Sustained breaks would reinforce the view that the recent correction in yields has ended and that the Dollar’s broader advance is regaining momentum.
Related Coverage
US Inflation, the Fed and Silver
- US Core CPI Beats Forecasts at 2.6% as Inflation Pressures Broaden Beyond Energy: the full breakdown of September’s report, with core at 2.6% and gasoline lifting headline inflation to 3.7%.
- Fed’s Williams Sees One More Hike in 2026, But No Clear Need for More in 2027: a more measured tightening path than market pricing implies, with inflation expected to fall toward 2% in 2027.
- Fed’s Collins Backs Another 2026 Hike as Strong Economy Gives Room to Fight Inflation: resilient growth and employment give the Fed room to tighten, while energy costs, tariffs and AI investment keep inflation risks elevated.
- Silver Breaks Support Despite Lower Yields. Is $50 Back in Sight?: the technical view on Silver’s slip below 58.46, with downside risk building toward 55.30 as the Gold/Silver ratio strengthens.
Europe: BoE and ECB
- BoE’s Pill Sees Inflation Risks Bringing MPC Together, but Four Hikes May Be Too Many: further tightening may be needed, but the BoE’s chief economist questions market pricing for four hikes as wage growth moderates.
- ECB’s Lagarde Puts France’s Bond Troubles Back on Paris, Watches Inflation Spillovers: France is expected to fix its debt problems through domestic fiscal action, while the ECB monitors whether energy-driven inflation spreads into wages.
China Trade and Inflation Data
- China’s Export Boom Pushes Trade Surplus to Record $133.5B, but Imbalances Deepen: September exports rose 36.3% on AI-related technology shipments, even as subdued domestic demand and trade tensions expose weak spots.
- China PPI Surges to Four-Year High, but CPI Shows Little Sign of Stronger Demand: producer prices at 5.0% against consumer prices at just 0.9%, a gap that points to persistently weak domestic demand.
FAQ
Why did the Dollar surge on Wednesday?
Stronger-than-expected US core CPI triggered a sharp reassessment of Fed rate expectations. Core CPI held at 0.3% month-on-month against an expected 0.2%, and annual core inflation accelerated from 2.4% to 2.6%, above the 2.5% forecast. The Dollar Index broke above 102.60 to reach 102.72, while the 2-year Treasury yield jumped toward 4.94% and the 10-year yield rebounded above 5.30%.
How much did the odds of an October Fed hike change?
According to CME FedWatch, the probability of a Fed hike at the October 28 meeting surged from 22.1% a day earlier to 43.7%, compared with 17.7% a week ago. A hold is still narrowly favored at 56.3%, but the repricing suggests markets are no longer as confident that the Fed can afford to pause tightening.
Which levels matter next for the Dollar and Treasury yields?
The next confirmation points are 102.77 in the Dollar Index, 4.960% in the 2-year yield and 5.365% in the 10-year yield. A decisive break above 102.77 with sustained trading above the rising channel ceiling would raise the possibility of a move toward the 138.2% projection at 104.36. Sustained breaks in yields would reinforce the view that the recent correction has ended.
Key Takeaways
- The Dollar surged broadly on Wednesday as stronger-than-expected US core inflation triggered a sharp reassessment of Fed rate expectations.
- September core CPI held at 0.3% m/m against an expected 0.2%, while annual core inflation rose from 2.4% to 2.6% and headline CPI from 3.4% to 3.7%.
- CME FedWatch put the chance of an October 28 Fed hike at 43.7%, up from 22.1% a day earlier and 17.7% a week ago, with a hold still narrowly favored at 56.3%.
- The 2-year yield surged as high as 4.939% and the 10-year yield rebounded through 5.278%, unwinding the correction from last week’s peaks.
- The Dollar Index climbed to 102.72, with 102.77 the immediate focus and 104.36 the next projection if a decisive break follows.
- Higher yields and the stronger Dollar weighed on Nasdaq futures (down around 0.67%), Gold (down around 1%) and Silver (down more than 2%).
- Brent near $106 and the IMF’s warning that growth alone cannot address US debt are separate, longer-term risks to bond yields rather than explanations for Wednesday’s move.
What to Watch Next
The October 28 Fed meeting is the key decision point, and the shift in hike odds from 22.1% to 43.7% shows how quickly pricing can change if inflation data keep surprising to the upside. Watch whether the 2-year yield clears the September high of 4.960% and whether the 10-year yield retests 5.365%.
Beyond inflation, energy and fiscal risks remain in the background. The IEA’s warning that diesel constraints could last well into 2027, Middle East supply risks around Brent’s $106 level and the IMF’s call for fiscal measures could each add to bond-market pressure in the months ahead.

sources.news_title: Inflation uptick puts pressure on Fed to hike again
sources.text:
- Key insight: Inflation appears to have gained steam last month, raising the likelihood that the Federal Open Market Committee — or at least a substantial chunk of its voting members — decide to raise interest rates again later this month.
- Expert quote: "The FOMC took an important first step at our September meeting by raising the target range for the federal funds rate 25 basis points. Still, I currently estimate the target range needs to rise an additional 50 basis points or more to appropriately balance the outlook and risks for our dual mandate goals." —Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas President Lorie Logan
- Forward look: The CPI report is the last major economic indicator ahead of the FOMC's communications blackout period before its next meeting on Oct. 27 and 28.
A surprise jump in inflation last month could force the Federal Open Market Committee to raise interest rates for its second consecutive meeting — or at least strongly consider it.
Price growth regained momentum in September, according to the latest consumer price index reading, with headline inflation rising 3.7% on an annualized basis and core inflation jumping 2.6%.
The Wednesday release from the Bureau of Labor Statistics upends a monthslong trend of declining inflation. The August CPI report showed headline inflation at 3.4% and core at 2.6%. Soaring energy prices in September drove the higher-than-expected reading, but rising prices for used cars, transportation and shelter all contributed as well.
The September inflation print aligns with economic outlooks offered by several Federal Open Market Committee members in recent weeks that described underlying price growth as being too strong and in need of further Fed intervention.
"The FOMC took an important first step at our September meeting by raising the target range for the federal funds rate 25 basis points," said Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan in a speech on Oct. 1. "Still, I currently estimate the target range needs to rise an additional 50 basis points or more to appropriately balance the outlook and risks for our dual mandate goals."
Wednesday's report is the last major economic indicator ahead of the FOMC's next meeting on Oct. 27 and 28. It comes just days before the Fed's pre-meeting communications blackout period, which begins next week. In the meantime, markets are bracing for public commentary from several Fed officials in the days ahead, including Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who is set to speak at an event in Thailand early Friday morning.
After the FOMC increased the federal funds rate by 25 basis points last month, financial markets have been left to wonder if the central bank will embark on a series of hikes or if the increase will be a one-off measure. With persistently high inflation having been the impetus for the hike last month, all eyes have been on the October CPI reading to set the tone for what comes next.
"Looking ahead, I will consider what policy rate may be needed to continue to guide inflation down to our target," said Fed Gov. Lisa Cook in late September. "Of course, the number and magnitude of any future adjustments will be informed by observations of the economy's reaction to our policy actions thus far and the inflation and labor data over the coming months."
Read more
- Inflation likely to spark more rate hikes: Boston Fed's Collins
- Why Citi remains cautious on key profitability metric
- Goldman's Solomon wants 'clear human accountability' on AI
- BofA gets $1.21B penalty for money laundering
The October CPI reading showed a monthly increase of 0.4 percentage point increase in headline inflation and a 0.3% percentage point increase in core CPI, which factors out food and energy prices. On Tuesday, the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's Inflation Nowcast tool projected increases of 27 basis points and 20 basis points, respectively.
During the past two weeks, markets have largely come to expect the FOMC to hold its benchmark interest rate between 3.75% and 4% at its policy meeting this month. As recently as Sept. 28, federal funds futures markets were pricing in a 70% chance of a quarter-point hike, according to the CME Group's Fedwatch tool. Market sentiment shifted substantially since then, with only 21% of contracts predicting a hike before the CPI report.  
The shift coincided with a series of public remarks from FOMC participants that left the door open for the committee to leave rates unchanged. First, on Sept. 29, New York Fed President John Williams said the September hike meant "there is no need for urgency, and we have time to gather more information."
On Oct. 1, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson acknowledged that bond yields had continued to rise after the FOMC's rate hike — a potential signal that markets were anticipating further tightening — but said the committee would not be pressured to adhere to the private sector's expectations or timeline. 
"My colleagues and I will need to come to our own judgment, which may take more time," Jefferson said. "I will continue to assess whether underlying trends suggest that inflation will return to target with sufficient speed."
Even if the Fed does hold rates steady this month, that does not mean further hikes are not in the offing. In his pivotal speech, Williams noted that he still expects policy to be tightened "late this year." Several other FOMC voters also said they expect more hikes eventually, but did not commit to a specific schedule.
Markets have followed this logic, albeit to different ends. As of Tuesday, nearly 90% of fed futures contracts expected a rate hike by the end of the year, according to CME Group, with 70% favoring one hike and almost 18% predicting two.
If the FOMC does use this week's CPI report to justify another rate hike, it may have to do so over the objections of a handful of participants who have favored a wait-and-see approach to inflation.
"I don't currently see an urgent need for further action," Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said last week. "And I think we need to better understand the totality of the data but remain attentive to the risks."
